title: Ranch Operations Dashboard - rules, data and integrations registry
status: Audit registry. The dashboard is a portfolio demonstration with fictional data and is not production-ready. Current thresholds are demo or ranch-set values, not validated operating thresholds.

legend.classification_rule: Where a checker dispute was credible, the stricter class was applied and classification_note says why. A rule that bundles supported guidance with a design choice takes the stricter class; the note names the supported part.

verification.verified: the citation checker confirmed the claim on the page
verification.partly: the page supports only part of the claim, or a detail is wrong (see checker_note)
verification.unverified: the page could not be confirmed (empty, blocked, or not checked)
verification.failed: unreachable, or (integrations only) checked and found not to support the use

legend.rejected_sources: Sources the checker marked claim_supported 'no' for this use. They are not listed as support.
legend.kind: vendor = vendor specification or vendor-authored material, kept apart from independent outcomes; product-documentation = agency or university product pages the research had labelled 'field-study'.

recommended_phase.3: Add later (at most three items: water supply coverage; forage observations at moves; drought/precipitation snapshot)

data_fields.required.phase-1 required: needed by phase-1 rules or the phase-1 data contract
data_fields.required.optional: used when present, or by phase-2 features; the page works without it

legend.research_refs: 0-based indexes into the research files' arrays.
legend.web_checks: Every web check in the evidence went through a summarising fetch tool; direct downloads were refused by the proxy. Quotes are as the tools returned them.
legend.critic_recheck: Present on a source when the citation critic re-opened it (WebFetch) to confirm a number a recommendation depends on.

health_scope: Health content stays on observation, scheduling, records and escalation to a veterinarian. No diagnosis and no treatment protocols.

rules.rule: CURRENT: critical when a tank's latest level_pct < 25 (RULES.waterCritical). Action shown: 'Check the float and the supply line today'.
rules.decision_supported: Whether someone goes to a tank now.
rules.required_inputs: Today: level_pct only. To be meaningful it also needs tank capacity in gallons, usable volume (sensor offset), head and class drinking there, daily high temperature, and supply type and inflow.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h)

rules.context_research: Any tank and any season, applied the same way whether or not cattle are in the pasture.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). No published cut-off was found; vendor help pages show the critical level as a user setting (Ranchbot example 10-20%). In this demo the 25% value acts as a synthetic setting and must be labelled that way.
rules.evidence: No extension, NRCS or peer-reviewed source I found sets a % full alarm level. Vendor documentation treats the level as user-set. Ranchbot's alert help page gives EXAMPLES only: 'Critical, low level ... example of 10-20%' and 'Warning, low level ... 40-50%'. My diagnostic (node docs/audit/diagnostics/water.research.mjs) converts 25% into hours of water with zero inflow at 90F. I assumed capacities and took intake from NRC/K-State tables. Output: 'Cows 180 hd ~4932 gal/day | small: 25%=1.2 h ... | storage: 25%=12.2 h' and 'Heifers 45 hd ~707 gal/day | small: 25%=8.5 h ... | storage: 25%=84.9 h'. So the same 25% reading means about 1 hour of water or about 3.5 days depending on tank and herd. In the synthetic data, healthy tanks never go below about 55% (the generator refills +30 when level < 55). Observed: 'lowest level per tank: {"T1":56.3,"T2":11.8,"T3":65,"T4":10,"T5":56.2,"T6":59.9,"T7":55.7,"T8":55.1}'. So only the planted tanks ever test the 25% line. In this demo the specific value 25 behaves as a synthetic demonstration setting.
rules.limitations: Percent of what? Ranchbot's offset help article (vendor) shows that a probe sitting on 10 in of mud in an 80-in tank reads 50%, while usable water is 37.5%. An outlet pipe halfway up makes the lower half unusable. Percent also ignores inflow: a float-fed tank refilling at full flow is fine at 20% for minutes. A storage tank on solar is not fine at 30% before a cloudy stretch. LoneStar (vendor) claims accuracy of 'about 10%', which is as wide as the gap between some thresholds.
rules.configurable: Yes. It must be per tank. The right number depends on capacity, head, class, temperature and the time it takes to reach the tank. One global percentage cannot be right for a 1,000-gal float tank and a 10,000-gal storage tank at once.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without capacity_gal, head and class present, and a temperature or season, the dashboard should not say 'someone goes now' with confidence. It should say 'low by percent; hours of water unknown' and ask for capacity. Without a sensor offset or calibration record, near-threshold readings should be marked uncertain.
rules.recommendation: Keep a % line on the chart for orientation, but drive severity from estimated hours of water remaining (see the proposed hours-of-water rule). If % stays, store it per tank as a ranch setting and label the default as a demo value, not guidance.
rules.phase_note: Keep it, label 25% as a ranch-set demo value in the rules table, and judge only tanks that reported recently; a silent tank is CAN'T TELL (RULE-WAT-04), not OK. T2 (planted) must still be found. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: How to set up water tank alerts & notifications
sources.supports: Low-level alerts are user-set percentages. The examples are warning 40-50% and critical 10-20%. Rapid-drop alert example: 11.81 in in 60 min. No defaults are stated.
sources.checker_note: Written by Kadee Petty, September 20, 2023. Warning: 'When the tank is low e.g. you may set this at 40-50% level'. Critical: 'e.g. you may set this to 10-20% level'. Rapid drop: 'When water level has fallen rapidly (excessive rate of fall) e.g. 11.81 inches in 60mins'. No defaults are stated. All values are 'e.g.' examples, and the page says triggers can be edited 'depending on your water tank and operations'.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): warning 'e.g. you may set this at 40-50% level'; critical 'e.g. you may set this to 10-20% level'; rapid drop 'e.g. 11.81 inches in 60mins'; examples, not defaults; Kadee Petty, 2023-09-20. Confirmed.

sources.title: What is offset and how to update it
sources.supports: % full depends on where the 'true bottom' is set. A probe on 10 in of mud in an 80-in tank reads 50% when usable water is 37.5%. Offsets are not applied retrospectively.
sources.checker_note: August 11, 2023 (Kadee Petty). Example: an 80-in tank with 10 in of mud reads '40 / 80 inches (50%)'. After a +10 in offset it shows 50/80 (60%), with 'only 30 inches or 37.5% available space'. 'Changes to offset will NOT be applied retrospectively.' 'Field validation means offset can be +/- 240 inches' confirms the ±240 data-field claim.

sources.title: Water Tank Level Monitoring System
sources.supports: Vendor claims the hydrostatic pressure sensor is 'accurate to about 10%', affected by water temperature, barometric pressure and sediment. Satellite 4 readings/day, cellular 24/day. Battery-life statements on the page conflict (2-3, 5 and 10 years).
sources.checker_note: Title 'Water Tank Level Monitoring System 2026 - LoneStar Tracking', footer (c) 2026. 'The LST Vita water level sensors are accurate to about 10%'. Listed factors: 'water temperature, changes in barometric pressure and sediment in the bottom of the tank'. Sensor wire 15 ft. Cellular '24 / day', satellite '4 / day', and also 'once every 1 hour' (a conflict). Battery claims conflict: 5 years, '10 years on 2 D cells', and 2-3 years in the table. Price $250.00 plus subscription, $99/yr after the first year. Sends SMS/email low alerts and a 'returned to normal' notice. Has a hydrostatic pressure sensor. Minor: cellular is named 'Global 4G Cat M1'. Myriota is not named on this page (it appears on the Myriota partner page). No API or export is mentioned. The page metadata lists price 100 USD, which conflicts with the visible $250.

sources.title: Calculating Water for Cattle
sources.publisher: Colorado State University Extension, Golden Plains Area
sources.supports: Tank volume formula and capacities at 24-in depth (10 ft = 1,000 gal; 12 ft = 1,690 gal). 2 gal per 100 lb body weight on days over 90F. Windmill or solar pumps deliver 2-4 gpm.
sources.checker_note: Scott Stinnett, CSU Extension Golden Plains, June 17, 2021. Formula: π x diameter² ÷ 4 x depth. At about 24 in: 10 ft ≈ 1,000 gal and 12 ft ≈ 1,690 gal. On days over 90F: 'provide 2 gallons of water per 100 pounds of body weight'. Cattle drink '2 gallons to as much as 5 gallons in a single trip'. Windmill/solar pumps 'may provide 2 to 4 gallons per minute'; home wells 3-6 gpm. 'Cows normally drink first and lower the tank water level' (calves). All cited claims match.

rules.rule: CURRENT: warning when the latest level_pct < 40 (RULES.waterLow). Action shown: 'Look at it on the next pass'.
rules.decision_supported: Whether to add the tank to the next routine check.
rules.required_inputs: Today: level_pct only. It also needs capacity, head and class, temperature, inflow, and when the next pass is due.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h)

rules.context_research: All tanks, all seasons.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). The only figure found is a Ranchbot vendor example (warning at 40-50%).
rules.evidence: No public guidance sets 40%. The only 40% figure I found is a Ranchbot vendor EXAMPLE ('Warning, low level ... example of 40-50%'). Diagnostic output at 90F with zero inflow: 'Cows 180 hd ... small: 40%=1.9 h' and 'Heifers 45 hd ... storage: 40%=135.9 h'. 'Next pass' is too slow in the first case and needlessly early in the second. In the synthetic month no healthy tank ever dropped below 55.1%, so the 40% warning never fires on normal data.
rules.limitations: 'Next pass' has no defined time. The dashboard has no route or check-schedule field, so it cannot tell whether the next pass comes before the water runs out.
rules.configurable: Yes. Per tank, expressed as hours of water left compared with the hours until the next scheduled check.
rules.missing_data_blocks: No capacity, head or temperature means no time-to-empty estimate. No check schedule means the 'next pass' advice cannot be tested.
rules.recommendation: Replace with: warn when estimated hours of water (with expected inflow) is less than the hours until the next scheduled visual check plus a margin. Keep 40% only as a labelled demo default.
rules.phase_note: Keep it and label 40% as a ranch-set demo value. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Water Essential for Cattle in High Heat (NDSU news release, Karl Hoppe)
sources.supports: 'With 100-degree weather, checking water supplies on a daily basis may not be often enough.' The right check interval depends on heat.
sources.checker_note: Undated on the page, so the URL-path-only dating is correct. Karl Hoppe, Carrington REC. Quotes: 'With 100-degree weather, checking water supplies on a daily basis may not be often enough.' Cattle can drink '20 or more gallons a day'. 'Spring-fed ponds that have water one day may be dry the next day.' As evidence for the visual_check log data field it supports only more frequent checks in heat, not the log's structure.

rules.rule: CURRENT: critical when the level fell >= 30 points between the latest reading and the most recent reading at least 24 h earlier (RULES.waterDropPts). Action shown: 'Check for a leak or a stuck float; haul water if it can't be fixed today'.
rules.decision_supported: Whether there is a supply failure: a leak, a float stuck shut, or a pump or pipeline failure.
rules.required_inputs: Today: level_pct time series. To tell failure from normal use it also needs expected consumption (head x gal/head/day / capacity), inflow and pump schedule, tank type, and reporting interval.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h)

rules.context_research: All tanks, regardless of tank type, herd size or cattle presence.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D). Healthy demo tanks fall at most 18.2 points a day and the planted T4 leak 46, so 30 separates the fictional data only. A storage tank's normal pump-off draw can exceed it (49 points/day in the research example).
rules.evidence: The threshold sits between the generator's noise and its planted leak. Observed on repo data: 'max 24h fall per tank over September: {"T1":16.1,"T2":15.3,"T3":16.2,"T4":46,"T5":14.5,"T6":11.8,"T7":14.9,"T8":18.2}'. Healthy tanks max out at 18.2 points and the planted T4 leak is 46 points, so 30 separates them by construction. The generator moves level by uniform(-6,6) per 6 h, so a healthy 24 h fall can never exceed 24. On realistic tanks the rule misfires both ways. (1) False alarm: hypothetical storage tank TX with the Cows, normal 35-point draw with the pump off, gives "C: storage tank, normal 35-pt draw with pump off, 60% now -> [ 'critical: Dropped 35 points in 24 hours, now 60%' ]". Diagnostic section 3: 'Cows on 10000 gal: 49 pts/day at 90F -> WOULD trip the leak rule with no leak'. (2) A slow leak on a large tank below 30 points/day, or a small leak masked by refills, never fires. NRCS 614 lists leak checks in operation and maintenance but gives no rate. Vendors offer a user-set rate-of-change alert (Ranchbot example: 11.81 in per 60 min).
rules.limitations: Points per day mean nothing without capacity and head. A 24 h window on 6-hourly data only compares two snapshots. A float-fed tank that empties and refills within an hour (Bartlett: refill in 1 hour or less) can look normal at every 6 h snapshot. A float stuck OPEN (overflow) cannot be seen in level at all, since the tank reads full. That needs a flow meter or a visual check.
rules.configurable: Yes. Express it as observed fall minus expected consumption over the window, per tank type.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without capacity, head present, and supply type and schedule, a large fall should be reported as 'unexplained fall; leak not confirmed', not as a diagnosed leak.
rules.recommendation: Treat the 30-point figure as a demo setting. Propose an expected-versus-observed drawdown rule (see the proposed leak and stuck-float rule) and keep a separate per-device rapid-drop alert in inches per hour if the device supports it.
rules.phase_note: Bound the comparison window (the reading about 24 h before the latest, within one reporting interval, not any older reading) and measure it against as_of. Word the row 'unexplained fall; leak not confirmed'. T4 must still be found. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Watering Facility (Code 614) Conservation Practice Standard
sources.supports: Operation and maintenance includes regular checks for leaks and checking 'the performance of the automatic water level device'. No numeric leak rate is given.
sources.checker_note: NRCS CPS Watering Facility Code 614, August 2023. 'To determine the storage volume, use the availability of water, replenishment rate, location, and planned operation.' 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days), a battery backup system, or an alternate water source.' O&M: 'Check for leaks, site erosion, and damage to fences' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' No numeric leak rate. Weak use: it is cited as evidence for the tank_id/pasture_id field, which it does not address, and for tank_shutoff/planned_move_in only through the phrase 'planned operation'.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days)' (Considerations; 'consider', not 'shall'). O&M: 'Check for leaks' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' August 2023. Confirmed.

sources.title: The ABCs of Livestock Watering Systems (Ben Bartlett)
sources.publisher: LPES Small Farms Fact Sheets / MidWest Plan Service
sources.supports: Group-drinking tanks hold at least 1/4 of daily need and should refill within one hour. Typical floats have a 1/8-inch opening, which is a bottleneck. Hot weather and dry forage can raise needs more than fourfold.
sources.checker_note: 'The ABCs of Livestock Watering Systems', Ben Bartlett (MSU), LPES Small Farms Fact Sheets, MidWest Plan Service, Iowa State University, (c) 2006. Quotes: 'the tank should hold at least ¼ of the daily requirement'; 'If the tank cannot be refilled in one hour or less, use a larger tank size'; 'The typical tank float has only a 1/8-inch opening'; 'provides total daily needs in four hours or less of pumping'; 'allow 5% to 10% of the animals to drink at one time'; 'Hot temperatures and dry forage can increase these water needs over fourfold'; 900 ft travel distance. I did not separately confirm the 'worked gpm examples'. This document says nothing about well testing.

rules.rule: CURRENT: serious when the last reading is >= 24 h before as_of (RULES.sensorSilentHours). The tank's level and drop are then not judged at all ('continue').
rules.decision_supported: Whether to send someone to look at the tank and sensor because the data is stale.
rules.required_inputs: Today: last reading time and as_of. It should also use the device's expected reporting interval, last-known level and hours of water, whether cattle are present, and temperature.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h)

rules.context_research: All tanks. The severity does not change with last-known level, cattle presence or heat.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). Vendor pages describe a 'Delay' status and a 3-4 day inspection point; none sets 24 h for this ranch.
rules.evidence: Vendor documentation agrees the data goes stale but sets no hour figure. Ranchbot (vendor help page): Delay means values 'are likely out of date'. Monitors 'transmit data at irregular intervals'. If Delay lasts more than 3-4 days, a manual inspection may be needed. Farmbot's April 2026 help article (vendor) says the same in substance. The Myriota/LoneStar partner page (vendor) states '4 measurements per day' for satellite units (LoneStar's own page gives conflicting cadences), so 24 h is about 4 missed reports. On repo data T6 (empty pasture P6) is flagged: 'serious | Tank T6 (Cedar Draw) | ... No reading for 42 hours; last level 98.5%'. I ran a hypothetical through findExceptions. Same pasture as the Cows, last reading 26 h ago at 20%: "A: silent 26 h, last reading 20%, cows present -> [ 'serious: No reading for 26 hours; last level 20%' ]". A reporting tank at 24% with the same cows: "A2 ... -> [ 'critical: Down to 24% full' ]". Less information about a lower tank with cattle on it therefore gets a LOWER severity.
rules.limitations: 24 h is stricter than vendor guidance (3-4 days) but may be too slow in heat (NDSU: daily checks 'may not be often enough' at 100F). Satellite gaps and data spikes are common in field reports (USU). Vendor battery help pages (Farmbot; Ranchbot's battery page, not its Delay page) say a charged battery runs 3-5 days without sun, so a cloudy spell can cause a gap that clears by itself. This is a vendor statement, not an independent test.
rules.configurable: Yes. Set silence thresholds per device as a multiple of its expected interval. Escalate by the last-known hours of water and cattle presence.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without the expected reporting interval per device, the dashboard cannot tell 'late' from 'normal irregular transmission'. Without capacity and head, it cannot tell whether the last-known level outlasts the silence.
rules.recommendation: Keep a staleness flag, but (a) set severity to the higher of the stale flag and an 'assume the worst' estimate from the last-known level, head and heat, so silent + low + cattle present = critical; (b) show the silence as a device-maintenance task separate from the water-supply alarm; (c) downgrade when no cattle are in the pasture.
rules.phase_note: Measure silence from as_of, not from the newest reading in the file. A silent tank is CAN'T TELL: show its last level and time and 'check by eye'. T6 must still be found. The ranking inversion (silent at 20% with cattle ranks below a reporting tank at 24%) is handled in phase 2 by RULE-WAT-07. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: What does Monitor Status 'Delay' mean?
sources.supports: Delay = values likely out of date. Irregular transmission intervals. Causes include cloud cover draining the battery, poor connectivity, and animal or weather damage. Manual inspection if Delay persists more than 3-4 days.
sources.checker_note: February 16, 2024. Delay = values 'are likely out of date and are no longer accurate'. Monitors 'transmit data at irregular intervals' but must update 'within a maximum transmission time period'. Causes: cloud cover 'for a few days', connectivity, battery, and 'an animal or a severe weather event may damage it'. 'longer than 3-4 days, a manual inspection may be required.' Caveat: this page has no '3-5 days' battery figure. That figure, which the research credits to Ranchbot in the Delay-rule limitations and the integrations, is on Ranchbot's battery page (5702599). The page also does not support the data field's timezone requirement, which comes from the repo.

sources.title: What does Device Status 'Delay' mean?
sources.supports: Same guidance. Also: pump automation pauses when a linked monitor is in Delay.
sources.checker_note: April 13, 2026 (Jen Duff). Same Delay definition, 'irregular intervals', 'maximum transmission time period', and 'longer than 3-4 days' manual inspection. Cloud cover 'for a few days'. Pump automation: 'automation will be paused if it is enabled' when a linked monitor is in Delay. It groups causes differently from Ranchbot ('Transmission Missed', 'Transmission Failure', other), so 'same guidance' is accurate in substance only. I did not verify the help centre's 'Integrations' collection.

Costs: monitor $1,800.00, installation $100.00, website $3-10.00/month. Payback is 'just over 2 years' for one rancher who drives 20 miles one way 2-3 times a week. rules.rule: CURRENT GAP + PROPOSED: water severity should account for whether cattle are on the tank's pasture now or are planned to move there. Today the level and drop rules give the same severity with or without cattle, and the subject line only names a group when one is present. Proposed: a critical or silent tank in an occupied pasture is also shown as a reason on that group's grazing row, and a low or silent tank in the planned destination is flagged before the move. Tanks in empty pastures keep their row but rank lower; they are never hidden.
rules.decision_supported: [water research rule 4] Priority of a water exception. | [grazing research rule 7] Whether to move early (water failure), or delay or redirect a planned move (destination water not ready).
rules.required_inputs: [water research rule 4] moves.csv open stays (already loaded), plus a planned move-in date for the pasture. | [grazing research rule 7] Tank-to-pasture mapping (water.csv already has pasture_id), latest level and sensor status, the stay's planned destination.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Rotational grazing on 8 pastures with a planned stay length per pasture; each tank serves one pasture (demo)

rules.context_research: [water research rule 4] Rotational grazing, where most pastures are resting at any time. | [grazing research rule 7] All pastures with stock water. Distance to water also affects distribution (SD TN9 calls a field 'very large' when water is more than about 1 mile away, in a passage about when season-long use can still allow recovery).
rules.classification_research: water R4: C-ranch-management-choice + grazing R7: A-supported-general
rules.classification_note: CHANGED for the grazing part. Water research rule 4 was C. Grazing research rule 7 was A; the checker (grazing dispute 0) found that only 'provide water during occupancy' (NRCS CPS 528) is general guidance. Showing tank status on the grazing row and letting the destination tank delay a move are ranch choices, and the SD TN9 '>1 mile' passage was misread. Stricter class C applied to the merged rule; the occupancy principle alone is A.
rules.evidence: [water research rule 4] Observed on repo data at as_of 2026-09-30T18:00: 'grazing now: Cows@P7, Heifers@P4, Yearlings@P3'. Exceptions: 'critical | Tank T2 (Windmill) | ... Down to 11.8% full' (no group in P2) and 'serious | Tank T6 (Cedar Draw)' (no group in P6). Only T4 has cattle: 'critical | Tank T4 (Lone Tree, Heifers here now) | Dropped 46 points in 24 hours, now 10%'. The tank actually serving the 180 pairs (T7) reads 61.3%, which my diagnostic converts to '3.0-3.7 h' if it were a 1,000-gal tank with no inflow. | [grazing research rule 7] CPS 528 (June 2025) General Criteria: 'Provide adequate quantity, quality, and distribution of drinking water for animals during periods of occupancy.' SD TN9 p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' SD TN9 (p.2-3): a 'very large field' is one where water is more than about one mile away; the passage concerns recovery under season-long use and does not require herding or water relocation. OBSERVED: exceptions.js already names the group present in a water alert (whoIsThere). Grazing rows never mention water, and no check looks at the destination's water.
evidence_corrections: SD TN9's '>1 mile = very large field' passage is about when season-long use can still allow recovery, not a requirement to herd or relocate water (grazing checker).
rules.limitations: [water research rule 4] An empty pasture's low tank still matters before the next move-in, and a leak there still wastes water or drains shared storage. Some managers shut floats off in resting pastures on purpose, which makes 'low' expected. | [grazing research rule 7] Tank level thresholds are covered by the water topic (separate researcher). This rule only links them. Pastures with several water sources need all of them mapped.
rules.configurable: [water research rule 4] Yes. It is a ranch policy whether resting-pasture tanks alert, and how far ahead of a planned move. | [grazing research rule 7] Yes. Which water severities block a move is a ranch choice.
rules.missing_data_blocks: [water research rule 4] There is no field saying a tank was deliberately shut off, and no planned move-in date, so the dashboard cannot tell 'resting, shut off' from 'resting, failing'. | [grazing research rule 7] A silent sensor at the destination should read 'water unknown: check by eye before moving', never 'ready'.
rules.recommendation: [water research rule 4] Rank tanks with cattle on them first. For resting pastures, flag 'needs attention before move-in on <date>' at a lower severity, unless the tank feeds shared storage or a pipeline. | [grazing research rule 7] Add destination water status to the upcoming-moves view. Add a water reason to the grazing row when the occupied pasture's tank is critical or silent, without duplicating the water exception row (cross-reference only).
rules.phase_note: Phase-2 default 'consequence-aware ranking'. Needs head present per pasture (derived from groups.csv and moves.csv) and, for the destination check, moves.planned_next_pasture. In the demo, T2 and T6 sit in empty pastures and T7 serves the cows.

sources.title: Watering Facility (Code 614) Conservation Practice Standard

sources.checker_note: NRCS CPS Watering Facility Code 614, August 2023. 'To determine the storage volume, use the availability of water, replenishment rate, location, and planned operation.' 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days), a battery backup system, or an alternate water source.' O&M: 'Check for leaks, site erosion, and damage to fences' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' No numeric leak rate. Weak use: it is cited as evidence for the tank_id/pasture_id field, which it does not address, and for tank_shutoff/planned_move_in only through the phrase 'planned operation'.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days)' (Considerations; 'consider', not 'shall'). O&M: 'Check for leaks' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' August 2023. Confirmed.

sources.title: Grazing Management (Code 528) Conservation Practice Standard
sources.supports: Drinking-water quantity, quality and distribution during occupancy.
sources.checker_note: Cover and footer: 'GRAZING MANAGEMENT', 'CODE 528', 'June 2025'. General Criteria, verbatim: 'Develop and implement a monitoring strategy that supports adaptive management and documents decisions based upon ecological triggers and thresholds to optimize the conservation outcome.' 'Manage livestock numbers and grazing periods to adjust the intensity, frequency, timing, duration, and distribution...' 'Provide adequate quantity, quality, and distribution of drinking water for animals during periods of occupancy.' 'Provide desired plants sufficient recovery time from grazing/browsing to meet planned objectives.' 'Deferment or rest should be planned for critical periods of plant or animal needs.' PARTLY: 'Implement longer rest periods before perennial forage dormant seasons to extend root growth' is NOT a General Criterion. It sits under 'Additional Criteria to Reduce Runoff and Compaction and Enhance or Maintain Key Soil Health Components...'. The rest rule quotes it next to the general criteria without saying it applies only to that purpose. The CPS gives no support for 'planned_next_pasture' (data field) beyond the general water and monitoring criteria; that link is loose.

sources.title: Prescribed Grazing, Range Technical Note No. 9
sources.supports: Dependable water access (App. B p.16: 'ensure animals have access to dependable water'). The passage on fields more than 1 mile from water describes when continuous season-long use can still allow recovery; it does not say such fields need herding or water relocation. Supplement placement away from water was not confirmed by the checker.
sources.checker_note: Fetched with WebFetch; curl gave 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Metadata is correct: 'Prescribed Grazing', Range Technical Note No. 9, April 2017, running header 'SOUTH DAKOTA TECHNICAL GUIDE NOTICE SD-424'. VERIFIED: p.4 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' and 'Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules.' p.3 'Keeping the grazing periods as short as practical, especially during periods of fast plant growth, will minimize the opportunity ... to graze plant regrowth prior to plant recovery.' p.3, once-over use ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed only one time'): rangeland 'minimum of 45 consecutive days of rest during the growing season', pasture 30. p.3, 2+ grazings ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed two or more times during a growing season'): 'Each pasture will be deferred for a minimum of 90 days during the growing season.' The p.4 Table 1 range values match the research: 20-30%* West fast 40, slow 60; East 35/55. 40-50%: West 50/70, East 45/65. Footnote: 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage.' Note: 'Under drought conditions, recovery periods may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Utilization limits match: 50% seasonal and 30% temporal (p.4), 65% browse and 60% dormant season (p.6). Table 3 (p.6, titled 'Minimum Height of Pasture Species') gives end stubble WWG 4, CWG 3, switchgrass 8, big & sand bluestem 6, KBG 2, sideoats 2, and begin heights WWG 6-10 etc., all as cited. Riparian 'residual heights of 4 to 8 inches is commonly cited as adequate' (Section IV, p.7). App. B p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' Phase I removes 10% in the first month; Phase II removes 20-40% and says 'Routinely monitor conditions such as soil moisture and plant growth on a weekly basis'; Phase III says 'measure remaining forage in all pastures', 'combine remaining herds into one herd', with 30%+ removal on p.16. All verified. MISREAD: the research says '>1 mile to water = very large field needing herding or water relocation'. The source says 'A very large field would roughly be where the distance to water is greater than one mile' ('could be considerably larger on smooth terrain'). Its point is that continuous season-long use gives adequate recovery only on very large fields where livestock are herded or redistributed by changing water. It does not say every field over 1 mile needs herding. The page number for this passage came back inconsistently from two fetches (p.2 and p.3).

rules.rule: PROPOSED: estimate how long the water in each tank will last for the cattle on it. Usable gallons (level x usable capacity, with and without expected refill) divided by demand (head present by class x gal/head/day for the day's temperature) gives hours or days of water. Warn below a ranch-set figure, for example less than the time until the next check plus the time needed to respond.
rules.decision_supported: [water research rule 5] Who goes, and how soon: haul water, fix the float, or move cattle. | [context research rule 10] Whether to haul water, fix supply, or move cattle before a tank runs dry
rules.required_inputs: [water research rule 5] tank_capacity_gal, sensor offset or usable volume, level, head and class per group present (groups.csv plus moves.csv), forecast or observed daily high, intake lookup table, supply type and design inflow, hours until next check, and travel time. | [context research rule 10] tank capacity (gal), usable fraction, refill rate or haul schedule, head per tank (from moves/groups), class, forecast max temp, intake table

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Float-fed, storage or hauled tanks with known capacity and head counts

rules.context_research: [water research rule 5] Pasture stock tanks in the Northern and Central Great Plains in the grazing season. Intake rises about 2.4-fold from 40F to 90F for growing, finishing and bull classes, but only about 1.4-1.6-fold for lactating cows. | [context research rule 10] Pasture tanks with float-fed or hauled supply; summer demand peaks
rules.classification_research: water R5: B-context-dependent + context R10: B-context-dependent
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B (both research rules). Checker water dispute 3 and context dispute 3: only the intake-by-class-and-temperature inputs are sourced (NDSU AS1763, UNL G2060, K-State MF3303). The formula (usable fraction, refill, head at the tank) and the alert threshold are unsourced design or ranch choices. Class C with B inputs.
rules.evidence: [water research rule 5] The intake tables agree in shape. NDSU AS1763 (rev. 2021, adapted from NRC updated 2016) and UNL G2060 (2011, adapted from NRC 1996 / Winchester and Morris 1956) give, in gal/head/day: growing 600 lb 5.3 at 40F to 12.7 at 90F; finishing 1,000 lb 8.7 to 20.6; lactating cows 900+ lb 11.4 (40F), 16.9 (70F), 17.9 (80F). K-State MF3303 (2016): a 1,100 lb cow with 25 lb milk needs 12.8 / 15.4 / 17.9 at 40/65/90F, plus about 1 gal per 10F above 40F. UNL BeefWatch adds 5-10 gal for the calf in heat. Rules of thumb: 1-2 gal per 100 lb (K-State 2018; UNL 2020). SDSU (2026), quoting A. DiCostanzo (UNL) for a feedlot animal: 0.66-1 gal per lb dry matter intake above 75F. Diagnostic output shows the spread this rule would capture: 'T4 P4 level 10% | Heifers 45 hd ... small 1000 gal -> 3.4-5.1 h | ... storage 10000 gal -> 34.0-50.8 h'. | [context research rule 10] NDSU AS1763 'Livestock Water Requirements' (revised Feb 2026; table from NRC 2016) gives gal/head/day by class and temperature. For example, Lactating 900 lb is 11.4 at 40 F, 16.9 at 70 F, 17.9 at 80 F, 16.2 at 90 F, and Growing 600 lb is 12.7 at 90 F. The page's extraction left the pregnant-cow columns unclear. Re-running context.research.mjs printed 'water.csv carries level_pct only, so gallons on hand = level_pct x capacity is NOT computable from repo data'. With an ASSUMED 10,000 gal tank it printed 'Cows @70F (lactating 900 lb row): 180 head x 16.9 = 3042 gal/day; tank 40% ... -> 1.31 days with zero refill'. NDMC Plan page: 'Upgrading or adding stock water tanks can improve grazing distribution and livestock health during drought.'
evidence_corrections: 'Use the 90F column (conservative)' is wrong for lactating cows: AS1763 gives 17.9 gal at 80F but 16.2 at 90F (G2060 gives 18.2).
'Intake roughly doubles from 40F to 90F' holds for growing, finishing and bull classes (about 2.4x) but not for lactating cows (about 1.4-1.6x), the demo's largest group.
SDSU hauling page: the 0.66-1 gal per lb dry matter figure is DiCostanzo's and refers to feedlot cattle.
rules.limitations: [water research rule 5] The tables are old (1956 data underlie NRC). The 90F lactating value differs between the two published tables: NDSU AS1763 gives 16.2 (lower than its 80F value of 17.9) and UNL G2060 gives 18.2. The citation checker confirmed both, and the citation critic re-read AS1763 on 2026-10-16 (80F 17.9, 90F 16.2). Moist forage lowers drinking, and humidity, solar load and salt raise it. Calves' share is uncertain. This gives an estimate, not a measurement. | [context research rule 10] Table values are estimates (the lactating row is not monotonic). Intake also varies with forage moisture and water quality (AS1764). Refill rate dominates for float-fed tanks. The 10,000 gal capacity is an assumption, not repo data.
rules.configurable: [water research rule 5] Yes. Intake table, temperature source, margin and response time should all be settings. | [context research rule 10] Yes. The alert threshold in days is C (ranch choice). Intake by class/temp is B, from a table. Current % thresholds are D (synthetic demo).
rules.missing_data_blocks: [water research rule 5] Do not compute or show hours-of-water when capacity or head is missing. Show 'capacity unknown' and fall back to a visual-check task. If no temperature is available, use the highest value in the class's row and label it an assumed hot-day figure (for lactating cows in AS1763 that is the 80F value, 17.9 gal, not the 90F value). | [context research rule 10] No capacity or refill data: show % only and state 'days of supply unavailable'. Never compute days from % alone.
rules.recommendation: [water research rule 5] Adopt as the primary water severity driver once capacity and head are recorded. Show the assumptions (capacity, head, temperature, intake column) beside each estimate. | [context research rule 10] Add capacity_gal and supply_type/refill_gph to a tanks table. Keep % thresholds labelled as demo settings until then.
rules.phase_note: Phase-3 item 'water supply coverage from capacity and head'. Needs tanks.capacity_gal, usable fraction, supply type and an intake lookup. Without them the page keeps the labelled % rules.

sources.title: Livestock Water Requirements (AS1763)
sources.data_years: Table adapted from NRC Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle, 8th rev. ed., updated 2016
sources.supports: Table 1: gal/head/day by class, weight and temperature (40-90F). Intake rises with weight, pregnancy, lactation and temperature.
sources.checker_note: AS1763 'Livestock Water Requirements', Meehan, Stokka and Mostrom, Revised March 2021. 'Adapted from Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle: Eighth Revised Edition: Updated 2016, 2016, NRC'. Raw table text, 90F row: '9.5 12.7 15.0 14.3 17.4 20.6 [blank] [blank] 16.2 19.0 20.6'. So growing 600 lb is 5.3→12.7, finishing 1,000 lb is 8.7→20.6, and lactating 900 lb is 11.4 / 16.9 / 17.9 / 16.2 at 40/70/80/90F, all confirmed. Note: in this table the lactating 90F value (16.2) is LOWER than the 80F value (17.9). The proposal to 'use the 90F column (conservative)' is therefore not conservative for lactating cows if AS1763 is the lookup. The flattened headers ('Lactating Cows 900 lb 1,400 lb; Mature Bulls 1,600 lb') make 1,400 lb look like lactating; G2060 shows it is mature bulls, which matches the researcher's reading.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): Table 1, lactating cows 900 lb 11.4/12.6/14.5/16.9/17.9/16.2 gal/head/day at 40-90F; growing 600 lb 5.3 to 12.7. 'Revised March 2021'; adapted from NRC 2016. Confirmed; 90F is not the highest lactating value.

sources.title: Water Requirements for Beef Cattle (G2060)
sources.data_years: Adapted from NRC 1996, derived from Winchester and Morris 1956
sources.supports: Same table with column headers (growing, finishing, wintering cows, lactating 900+ lb, mature bulls 1,400 and 1,600+ lb). Intake is constant up to 40F.
sources.checker_note: G2060, Rasby and Walz, March 2011. Source: 1996 NRC 7th rev. ed., derived from Winchester and Morris (J. Anim. Sci. 15(3), Aug 1956). Raw text: 'Lactating Cows4 / 900 11.4 12.6 14.5 16.9 17.9 18.2'. This confirms the 16.2 (NDSU) vs 18.2 (UNL) disagreement is real in the published documents and is not a WebFetch extraction error. The growing rows show '600' twice, which confirms that note. Footnote: 'Water intake is constant up to 40oF.' Other values: TDS '3,000 ppm TDS or less is usually satisfactory'; 5,000 ppm ≈ 10% performance reduction; 5,000-7,000 not for pregnant or lactating; NO3-N <100 safe, 100-300 caution, >300 unsafe; sulfate <500 calves, <1,000 adults.

sources.title: Estimating Water Requirements for Mature Beef Cows (MF3303)
sources.publisher: Kansas State University Research and Extension
sources.data_years: Equations from published literature: Murphy 1983, Hicks 1988, Meyer 2006, Winchester and Morris 1956, NRC 2000
sources.supports: Table 2: 1,100-1,500 lb cows at 0-35 lb milk, 40/65/90F. 0.85 lb (about 0.1 gal) more per F above 40F. 0.9 lb water per lb milk.
sources.checker_note: MF3303 (also ANSI-3299), Spencer, Lalman, Rolf and Richards, December 2016. Table 2: a 1,100 lb cow with 25 lb milk needs 12.8 / 15.4 / 17.9 gal at 40/65/90F. A 1,500 lb cow with 35 lb milk at 40F needs 16.3. Quotes: '0.85 pound of increased water intake per one degree increase in temperature beyond 40 degrees'; 'adjusted by 0.9 pound for each pound of milk'. Equations cite Murphy 1983, Hicks 1988, Meyer 2006, Winchester and Morris 1956, NRC 2000. The 40→90F rise for this lactating cow is only about 1.4x (12.8→17.9), not 'roughly doubles'.

sources.title: Estimating Water Requirements for Mature Beef Cows (AFS-3299)
sources.data_years: Same underlying studies; notes NRC (2000) relies on 1956 data
sources.supports: Identifies the data age and the gap for cows over 1,100 lb. Free water intake can be 'substantially lower' on moist feed.
sources.checker_note: AFS-3299, Lalman, Richards, Spencer and Rolf, published July 2017. NRC values 'were taken from research data published in 1956'. 'Current guidelines are restricted to 900- to 1,100-pound mature weight in gestating cows and 900-pound lactating cows only'. 'Free water intake could be substantially lower than the estimates' (moist feed). Gives about 1 gal per 10F. Table value for a 1,500 lb cow with 35 lb milk at 40F is 15.3, versus 16.3 in the K-State PDF, so the discrepancy is confirmed.

sources.title: How much water do cattle need and what water problems should cattle producers watch for?
sources.supports: Lactating cows about 2 gal per 100 lb. Spring-calving cows 20-24 gal in heat plus 5-10 gal for the calf. Calves struggle if cows empty a tank that refills slowly.
sources.checker_note: Walz and Berger. The page shows April 30, 2025 although the URL path says 2023, which matches the researcher's note. Quotes: 'lactating cows need two gallons of water per 100 pounds of bodyweight per day'; 'close to 20 to 24 gallons of water per day for themselves'; 'another 5 to 10 gallons for their calf when it gets hot'; 'calves may struggle to get a drink if there is a slow recharge'. Also sulfate <500 calves and <1,000 adults, and NO3-N <100 ppm.

sources.title: Water: Questions and Answers
sources.supports: 1-2 gal per 100 lb. About 1 more gal per 10F above 40F. At least 15 in of trough space per head. At least 10% of animals drinking at once, 30% where travel is long.
sources.checker_note: April 30, 2018. Byline Angie Denton; content by Justin Waggoner. Quotes: '1 to 2 gallons of water per 100 lbs of bodyweight'; 'additional gallon of water for every 10 degree increase in temperature' (above 40F); 'A minimum of 15 inches of linear trough space per head'; 'at least 10% of the animals ... drink ... at once', and 30% for larger pastures with long travel.

sources.title: Hauling Water to Cows: When water is not everywhere
sources.supports: 0.66-1 gal per lb DM above 75F (the article credits this to A. DiCostanzo, UNL, for 'a feedlot animal'; it is not a general cattle rule). Example: 100 pairs need 3,750 gal/day. Keep at least half of daily needs in stationary storage for hot days. An 8 ft tank holds 625 gal.
sources.checker_note: Taylor Grussing, 'Updated July 17, 2026'. Confirmed: '37.5 gal × 100 = 3750 gallons' for 100 pairs; 'stationary storage tanks to hold at least half your water needs will help with demand on hot days'; '625 gallon volume per 8-foot tank'. Partly: the 0.66-1 gal per lb DM above 75F figure is credited to Alfredo DiCostanzo (UNL) and applies to 'a feedlot animal'. The research presents it as an SDSU rule for cattle in general.

sources.title: Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle: Eighth Revised Edition (Summary; Chapter 9 Water)

Table 1 is 'Adapted from Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle: Eighth Revised Edition: Updated 2016, NRC'. Lactating cows 900 lb: 11.4 (40F), 16.9 (70F), 17.9 (80F), 16.2 (90F). rules.rule: PROPOSED: silence escalation. Mark a tank stale after N x its device's expected reporting interval. Severity = max(device-maintenance severity, worst-case water severity from the last-known level, head present and heat, projected to now).
rules.decision_supported: Whether a silent sensor is a maintenance chore or a reason to drive out now.
rules.required_inputs: expected_report_interval_h per device, last reading time with timezone, last level, capacity, head present, temperature, device battery and status.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h); devices with different reporting intervals

rules.context_research: Cellular, satellite and LoRaWAN monitors, which all report irregularly.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C).
rules.evidence: Repro case A (above): silent 26 h, last reading 20%, cows present gives only 'serious', while a reporting 24% tank is 'critical'. Vendor intervals vary: LoneStar satellite 4/day, cellular 24/day. Ranchbot and Farmbot say only 'irregular intervals'. NMSU LoRaWAN field test (2020 data): the water level sensor 'also timed out when the Wi-Fi system went down'.
rules.limitations: Vendor intervals are vendor claims. Real gaps depend on sky view, vegetation, snow on panels and backhaul.
rules.configurable: Yes. Interval multiple, and response time per tank.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without the expected interval, fall back to a fixed hour limit and label it as an assumption. Without capacity and head, treat silent + cattle present + last level below the ranch's comfort line as needing a visual check today.
rules.recommendation: Implement after capacity and head fields exist. Show 'last seen X h ago at Y% (about Z h of water then)'.
rules.phase_note: Part of phase-2 consequence-aware ranking. Uses expected_report_interval_h per device (default 24 h, labelled an assumption) and the last-known level and head present, so a silent tank with cattle never ranks below a reporting tank in a better state.

Listed factors: 'water temperature, changes in barometric pressure and sediment in the bottom of the tank'. Sensor wire 15 ft. Cellular '24 / day', satellite '4 / day', and also 'once every 1 hour' (a conflict). Battery claims conflict: 5 years, '10 years on 2 D cells', and 2-3 years in the table. Monitors 'transmit data at irregular intervals' but must update 'within a maximum transmission time period'. Causes: cloud cover 'for a few days', connectivity, battery, and 'an animal or a severe weather event may damage it'. 'longer than 3-4 days, a manual inspection may be required.' rules.rule: PROPOSED: leak and stuck-float screen. (a) Unexplained fall = observed fall minus expected consumption, over a window of at least two reporting intervals. (b) Any sustained fall in a pasture with no cattle. (c) A float-fed tank that fails to recover within its expected refill time. (d) A float stuck open or overflowing cannot be seen in level data, so add a flow-meter or visual check.
rules.decision_supported: Whether to send someone for a supply fault instead of a consumption problem.
rules.required_inputs: Level series, capacity, head and class present, intake table, tank type (float-fed vs storage), pump schedule or supply type, optional flow meter (gal/day).
