rules.context_research: Float-fed stock tanks and storage tanks on pipelines, wells, solar or windmills.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker water dispute 0: no cited source proposes or validates an 'observed fall minus expected consumption' detector. NRCS 614 says only 'check for leaks'; Bartlett and NRCS Missouri cover float sizing and refill; Tobin et al. detected water-system failure from cattle GPS and accelerometers, not tank level. The researcher found no validation study.
rules.evidence: NRCS 614 (2023) puts leak and float-performance checks in operation and maintenance. Bartlett (2006): tanks refill in an hour or less, with full-flow floats. The NRCS Missouri guide recommends full-flow floats and says small clamp-on floats 'do not refill tanks rapidly enough'. Diagnostic section 3 shows normal pump-off drawdown can exceed 30 pts/day (Cows on 10,000 gal: 49 pts/day), so a fixed point threshold cannot separate leak from use. Ranchbot (vendor) offers rapid-drop alerts, and its graphs give only Rising, Steady or Falling trend labels plus projections; it describes no leak signature. Farmbot's graph article also describes no leak or stuck-float signature. I found no independent study that validates level-curve leak detection. Tobin, Bailey and Trotter (2021, Arizona, 2018-2019 data) simulated water failure and detected it from cattle GPS and accelerometer behaviour, not from tank level.
evidence_corrections: NRCS Missouri 'Watering Systems for Serious Graziers' never mentions flow meters (it was cited for flow_meter_gal).
Tobin et al.: 2021-07-19 is the repository posting date; the article is REM 77(1):9-16, accepted 2021-02-24.
rules.limitations: Consumption estimates carry roughly ±30% uncertainty (temperature, forage moisture, calves). 6-hourly data cannot resolve fast float-tank cycles. Evaporation and ice confuse readings.
rules.configurable: Yes. Window, tolerance band, and refill time per tank type.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without capacity and head, report 'fall larger than usual for this tank' (compare to the tank's own history) rather than 'leak'.
rules.recommendation: Use per-tank baselines (its own typical daily fall at similar head and temperature) plus expected consumption. Word the alert as 'unexplained drop' with check-float and check-line actions.
rules.phase_note: Needs the phase-3 demand estimate and validation on real tank data. In the meantime the bounded 24 h drop rule (RULE-WAT-03) finds the demo leak.

sources.title: Watering Systems for Serious Graziers
sources.supports: Full-flow floats for rapid refill. Clamp-on floats refill too slowly. 1 gpm = 1,440 gal/day, enough for 50 pairs. Keep backup water sources. Check pipelines for leaks.
sources.checker_note: NRCS Missouri (Columbia, MO), August 2006. Confirmed: 'Use "full flow" float valves ... to allow rapid refill'; clamp-on floats 'do not refill tanks rapidly enough'; 'One gallon of flow per minute output equals 1,440 gallons per day. That's enough water for 50 cow-calf pairs.'; backup water sources; 'Check pipeline routes for leaks'. Not supported: the flow_meter_gal data field cites this document for 'Leak and overflow detection', but it never mentions flow or water meters (only a bucket method for spring flow) and says nothing about stuck-open floats.

sources.title: Tracking and sensor-based detection of livestock water system failure: A case study simulation
sources.publisher: Rangeland Ecology and Management 77:9-16 (Elsevier); record at CQUniversity repository
sources.pub_date: 2021 (Rangeland Ecology & Management 77(1):9-16; accepted 2021-02-24; 2021-07-19 is the repository posting date)
sources.supports: On a 1,096-ha Arizona pasture, water failure was simulated by panelling off the only drinker for 4 h. Movement intensity rose (P = 0.03) and cows stayed near the drinker (P = 0.01). GPS tracking could detect failure remotely. The full text at bioone.org was blocked; I read only the repository abstract.
sources.checker_note: Tobin, Bailey and Trotter, Rangeland Ecology & Management 77(1):9-16, DOI 10.1016/j.rama.2021.02.013. Data from 2018-2019. 'Water system failure was simulated in a 1 096-ha pasture in Arizona' by 'placing metal panels around the only drinker for 4 h (0800−1200)'. Movement intensity was greater (P = 0.03), and 'cows remained closer to water (P = 0.01)'. 'Real-time GPS tracking ... has the potential to remotely detect water system failure'. Metadata error: 2021-07-19 is the date the article was posted to the CQU repository, not the online publication date. The article was accepted 2021-02-24 and is in the July 2021 volume. The bioone full text was blocked for me too (Incapsula).
sources.metadata_note: Checker: the research's 2021-07-19 is the CQU repository posting date, not the online publication date.

sources.title: Reading my water level data and graphs
sources.supports: Units are in, gal or %. Current values are projections 'based on all previous data points, trend predictions'. No accuracy figure. No leak-pattern guidance.
sources.checker_note: September 20, 2023. Units are 'inches (in), gallons (gal) or percentage (%)'. Values 'calculated based on all previous data points, trend predictions'. A dotted projected line is shown. Trend labels Rising/Steady/Falling. No accuracy figure and no mention of leaks.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: storage-days check. For tanks on windmill, solar or otherwise undependable supply, compare storage (gal) with daily herd demand and flag when storage covers fewer than 3 days.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a tank system can ride out a calm or cloudy spell or a pump failure, which drives a haul plan or a move decision.
rules.required_inputs: Storage capacity, supply type, herd daily demand (head x intake at a seasonal high), backup source and haul capacity.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Tanks on windmill, solar or other undependable supply

rules.context_research: Remote Great Plains pastures on wind or solar pumps.
rules.classification_note: Kept at B on the checker's condition (water dispute 6): the 3-day figure is presented as a ranch-set target at the low end of NRCS 614's 'consider (3-5 days)' storage range (Colorado 614, archived: 4 days minimum for undependable sources). Those are design criteria, not alarm levels.
rules.evidence: NRCS 614 national (2023): with windmill, solar or other unreliable power, 'consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3-5 days)', or a battery backup or alternate source. Colorado 614 (2015, archived): minimum 4 days of storage for windmill or undependable sources. Frequently inspected tanks with adequate supply need at least 10% of the daily requirement. Bartlett (GLBGN/MSU, undated): solar storage of at least 3 days without pumping, compressed-air windmill 5-7 days. NRCS Illinois (2004): solar systems typically store up to 5 days.
rules.limitations: These are design criteria, not alarm levels, and state FOTG versions differ. I did not find a South Dakota, North Dakota or Nebraska 614 version (Nebraska showed only a CPPE file in search results, which I did not fetch).
rules.configurable: Yes. Days target per supply type.
rules.missing_data_blocks: No supply type or capacity means no check. Show it as a setup gap.
rules.recommendation: Add as a planning tile (days of storage at current head and forecast heat) rather than a real-time alarm.
rules.phase_note: Belongs to the phase-3 item 'water supply coverage from capacity and head'. Needs storage capacity, supply type and head present.

sources.title: Watering Facility (Code 614) Conservation Practice Standard
sources.supports: 3-5 days of extra storage to consider for windmill or solar. Storage must provide water between replenishments.
sources.checker_note: NRCS CPS Watering Facility Code 614, August 2023. 'To determine the storage volume, use the availability of water, replenishment rate, location, and planned operation.' 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days), a battery backup system, or an alternate water source.' O&M: 'Check for leaks, site erosion, and damage to fences' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' No numeric leak rate. Weak use: it is cited as evidence for the tank_id/pasture_id field, which it does not address, and for tank_shutoff/planned_move_in only through the phrase 'planned operation'.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): 'When windmill, solar, or other potentially unreliable power sources are used, consider supplying additional daily water storage volume (3–5 days)' (Considerations; 'consider', not 'shall'). O&M: 'Check for leaks' and 'Checking the performance of the automatic water level device, if present.' August 2023. Confirmed.

sources.title: Conservation Practice Standard Watering Facility (614), Colorado
sources.supports: Minimum 4 days of storage for undependable sources. 10% of daily requirement for frequently inspected tanks with adequate supply. Automatic controls keep water 2 in below the rim.
sources.checker_note: Colorado CPS 614, October 2015, marked ARCHIVED on every page. Storage for 'tanks supplied by windmill pumps, other undependable sources ... shall be 4 days'. Frequently inspected tanks with adequate supply: 'minimum volume of 10% of the daily water requirement'. 'maintain the water level 2 inches below the top of the tank'.

sources.title: Watering Systems for Grazing Livestock (Ben Bartlett)
sources.publisher: Great Lakes Basin Grazing Network / Michigan State University Extension
sources.supports: Solar storage of at least 3 days, windmill 5-7 days, gravity reservoir 3-7 days. Pumps should run about 4 h/day (12 h max). Design for double the intake.
sources.checker_note: Ben Bartlett DVM (MSU Extension), Great Lakes Basin Grazing Network / MSU Extension, undated. Solar: 'at least three days of non-pumping'. Compressed-air windmill: 'five-to seven-day water supply'. Gravity: 'three-to seven-day period'. 'Pumps should run only about four hours per day, with a maximum of 12 hours'. 'should be able to handle double the intake'. On the supply_type field claim ('have the well tested before summer'), the text only advises testing well yield and draw down with a driller because summer use rises; 'before summer' is a paraphrase.

sources.title: Water Resources Development for Managing Intensive Grazing of Beef
sources.publisher: USDA NRCS Illinois (Illinois Grazing Manual fact sheet)
sources.supports: Solar systems store up to 5 days. Beef needs run from about 9 gal per 1,000 lb in winter to nearly 30 in hot summer. Full-flow floats deliver up to 20 gpm, cheap floats 2-3 gpm.
sources.checker_note: NRCS Illinois, Illinois Grazing Manual, 2004. Solar systems store 'up to five day's supply of water'. About 9 gal per 1,000 lb in winter rising to 'nearly 30 gallons per 1000 lbs. bodyweight per day on hot summer days'. Inexpensive floats 'can only supply 2-3 gallons per minute'; full-flow floats 'can deliver up to 20 gallons per minute'.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: float-fed tank adequacy. Flag when design inflow cannot deliver the herd's daily need within about 4 h, or a tank holds less than 1/4 of daily need for group drinking, or refill takes more than 1 h.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a tank and float are sized for the group placed on it, checked before a move.
rules.required_inputs: Inflow gpm (measured), tank capacity, head and intake, drinking-space length.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Float-fed tanks on pipeline or well supply

rules.context_research: Pipeline or well-fed float tanks, checked when planning a move.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: Bartlett (2006): supply daily needs in 4 h or less of pumping. Group-drinking tanks hold at least 1/4 of daily need, with 5-10% of animals drinking at once. If refill takes more than 1 h, use a larger tank. K-State (2018): at least 10% of the herd at once, 30% where travel is long, 15 in per head. CSU (2021): windmill or solar pumps produce 2-4 gpm. Example from my diagnostic: Cows (180 pairs) need about 4,932 gal/day at 90F. At 3 gpm a supply makes 4,320 gal in 24 h, so it cannot keep up even running continuously (inference from cited figures).
rules.limitations: These are rules of thumb from Midwest and Great Lakes grazing guides. Herds on large Great Plains pastures that travel more than 900 ft drink as a group (Bartlett), which raises peak demand.
rules.configurable: Yes.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a measured inflow, show 'inflow unknown' and do not assert adequacy.
rules.recommendation: Add a pre-move water adequacy check per pasture (tank plus supply versus incoming group).
rules.phase_note: An infrastructure design check that needs design_inflow_gpm and tank volume; not a daily exception.

sources.title: The ABCs of Livestock Watering Systems (Ben Bartlett)
sources.publisher: LPES Small Farms Fact Sheets / MidWest Plan Service
sources.supports: Daily needs in 4 h or less of pumping. Tank at least 1/4 of daily need. 5-10% of the herd drinking at once. Refill in 1 h or less. Worked gpm examples.
sources.checker_note: 'The ABCs of Livestock Watering Systems', Ben Bartlett (MSU), LPES Small Farms Fact Sheets, MidWest Plan Service, Iowa State University, (c) 2006. Quotes: 'the tank should hold at least ¼ of the daily requirement'; 'If the tank cannot be refilled in one hour or less, use a larger tank size'; 'The typical tank float has only a 1/8-inch opening'; 'provides total daily needs in four hours or less of pumping'; 'allow 5% to 10% of the animals to drink at one time'; 'Hot temperatures and dry forage can increase these water needs over fourfold'; 900 ft travel distance. I did not separately confirm the 'worked gpm examples'. This document says nothing about well testing.

sources.title: Calculating Water for Cattle
sources.publisher: Colorado State University Extension, Golden Plains Area
sources.supports: Cattle drink 2-5 gal per visit. Cows lower the level, leaving calves short. Windmill or solar pumps give 2-4 gpm, home wells 3-6 gpm.
sources.checker_note: Scott Stinnett, CSU Extension Golden Plains, June 17, 2021. Formula: π x diameter² ÷ 4 x depth. At about 24 in: 10 ft ≈ 1,000 gal and 12 ft ≈ 1,690 gal. On days over 90F: 'provide 2 gallons of water per 100 pounds of body weight'. Cattle drink '2 gallons to as much as 5 gallons in a single trip'. Windmill/solar pumps 'may provide 2 to 4 gallons per minute'; home wells 3-6 gpm. 'Cows normally drink first and lower the tank water level' (calves). All cited claims match.

sources.title: Water: Questions and Answers
sources.supports: 15 in of trough per head. 10% of the herd at once, 30% for long travel.
sources.checker_note: April 30, 2018. Byline Angie Denton; content by Justin Waggoner. Quotes: '1 to 2 gallons of water per 100 lbs of bodyweight'; 'additional gallon of water for every 10 degree increase in temperature' (above 40F); 'A minimum of 15 inches of linear trough space per head'; 'at least 10% of the animals ... drink ... at once', and 30% for larger pastures with long travel.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: water quality screening by TDS (field EC/TDS meter). Below 3,000 ppm is usually satisfactory. 3,000-5,000 ppm: watch young stock. 5,000-7,000 ppm: not for pregnant or lactating females. 7,000-10,000 ppm: do not use for pregnant or lactating cattle (the source's wording; it does not say 'avoid' for every class). Above 10,000 ppm: not suitable for livestock. If a screen reads above 4,500 ppm, schedule a lab test. Screen surface and shallow sources during drought.
rules.decision_supported: Scheduling a water test, and choosing which water source a class of cattle can use (observation and records, not diagnosis).
rules.required_inputs: Source id and type (well, pond or dugout, pipeline), TDS or EC reading, date, method, class of cattle using the source, drought status.

context.class: All classes; young stock and pregnant or lactating females are the sensitive groups
context.season: Drought and late summer, when salts concentrate
context.geography: Northern Plains surface water and shallow wells
context.management: Field EC/TDS meter screening with lab confirmation

rules.context_research: Northern Plains surface water and shallow wells, especially in drought when salts concentrate.
rules.classification_note: Kept at A for the published TDS bands (NDSU AS1764; SDSU P-00212). Rule wording corrected per checker water dispute 5: AS1764's 7,000-10,000 ppm band says 'Do not use for pregnant or lactating ruminants or horses', not 'avoid'. The drought-screening trigger and the testing interval are ranch choices (C).
rules.evidence: The TDS bands agree across sources. NDSU AS1764 (rev. Jan 2026): under 3,000 ppm usually satisfactory, 5,000-7,000 not for pregnant or lactating, 7,000-10,000 do not use for pregnant or lactating ruminants, over 10,000 possible death. Send to a lab if TDS is over 4,500 or sulfate over 800 on screening. SDSU P-00212 (Nov 2023) gives matching bands. UNL G2060 (2011): 3,000 ppm or less usually satisfactory, 5,000 may cut performance about 10%.
evidence_corrections: AS1764's lab trigger is 'TDS over 4,500 ppm and/or sulfates over 800 ppm'.
rules.limitations: Screening meters need calibration (NDSU WQ1923). TDS does not identify which ion is the problem.
rules.configurable: Partly. The bands are published; the testing interval is a ranch choice.
rules.missing_data_blocks: No reading on record for a surface source in drought should show 'not screened this season', never 'OK'.
rules.recommendation: Add a water-quality log per source, a 'due for screening' task in drought or when a new source is used, and a lab-follow-up flag. No health conclusions.
rules.phase_note: Needs a water-quality test log; not one of the three phase-3 items. Observation, records and escalation only.

sources.title: Livestock Water Quality (AS1764)
sources.supports: TDS bands. Lab triggers (TDS over 4,500, sulfate over 800). Screening with an EC/TDS meter and sulfate strips. Salts concentrate as levels fall in drought.
sources.checker_note: AS1764 'Livestock Water Quality', Meehan, Galbreath and Mostrom, 'Revised January 2026'. TDS table: <3,000 'Usually satisfactory for most livestock'; 3,000-5,000 young stock may be affected; 5,000-7,000 'Should not be consumed by pregnant or lactating females'; 7,000-10,000 'Do not use for pregnant or lactating ruminants or horses' (and swine); >10,000 'May cause brain damage or death'. Lab trigger: 'If TDS levels exceed 4,500 ppm and/or sulfates levels exceed 800 ppm'. Screening with an 'EC or TDS meter and sulfate test strips'; calibration per WQ1923. 'salts in surface water become more concentrated as water levels decline'. Table 2: sulfate <600 ppm on >85% concentrate (diet S 0.3%) and <2,500 ppm on >40% forage (diet S 0.5%). Table 3: 'Nitrate 100', 'Nitrite 33', 'Sulfate 500 to 1,000'. Nitrate is not labelled NO3 vs NO3-N, so 'nitrate-N 100' is not explicit here. Not supported: the labs integration names NDSU VDL, SDSU testing and Midwest Laboratories, but this document names only the 'NDSU Veterinary Diagnostic Lab' (it does mention 'algal toxin determination').

sources.title: Interpretation of Water Analysis for Livestock Suitability (P-00212)
sources.supports: TDS, sulfate and nitrate-N interpretation bands. Field 'quick test' with an EC or TDS meter.
sources.checker_note: P-00212, Robin Salverson, November 2023. The 2004 original was by Thiex and German. TDS bands are <1,000, 1,000-2,999, 3,000-4,999, 5,000-6,999, 7,000-10,000 and >10,000 mg/L; the boundaries match NDSU above 3,000. Sulfate: <1,500 'no serious effects' with mild diarrhea near the limit; 3,500-4,500 not for pregnant or lactating cows; >4,500 not recommended. NO3-N <100 / 100-300 / >300. 'Divide sulfate content by 3 to convert to sulfur content'. Dietary S max 0.4%. Field 'quick test' with an EC or TDS meter.

sources.title: Water Requirements for Beef Cattle (G2060)
sources.supports: TDS 3,000 ppm or less satisfactory. 5,000-7,000 not for pregnant or lactating. Nitrate-N under 100 safe, 100-300 questionable, over 300 unsafe.
sources.checker_note: G2060, Rasby and Walz, March 2011. Source: 1996 NRC 7th rev. ed., derived from Winchester and Morris (J. Anim. Sci. 15(3), Aug 1956). Raw text: 'Lactating Cows4 / 900 11.4 12.6 14.5 16.9 17.9 18.2'. This confirms the 16.2 (NDSU) vs 18.2 (UNL) disagreement is real in the published documents and is not a WebFetch extraction error. The growing rows show '600' twice, which confirms that note. Footnote: 'Water intake is constant up to 40oF.' Other values: TDS '3,000 ppm TDS or less is usually satisfactory'; 5,000 ppm ≈ 10% performance reduction; 5,000-7,000 not for pregnant or lactating; NO3-N <100 safe, 100-300 caution, >300 unsafe; sulfate <500 calves, <1,000 adults.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: sulfate and nitrate screening flags with class and diet context. Sulfate: calves under 500 ppm, adults under 1,000 ppm (UNL and NDSU text), but limits vary with diet. Nitrate under 100 ppm (AS1764 Table 3; the source does not say whether this is NO3 or NO3-N, so record which basis the lab reports; also count feed nitrate).
rules.decision_supported: Whether to schedule lab confirmation and which class may use a source (records only).
rules.required_inputs: Lab or strip results, source, date, class using it, diet type (forage vs concentrate), feed nitrate test if any.

context.class: All classes; calves are more sensitive to sulfate
context.geography: Northern Plains wells and surface water
context.management: Lab water tests; feed sulfur and nitrate also count

rules.context_research: Sulfate-rich Northern Plains groundwater and dugouts.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: The sources disagree on cut-offs. UNL G2060 and BeefWatch: calves under 500, adults under 1,000 ppm. NDSU AS1764 Table 2: under 600 ppm on more than 85% concentrate diets, under 2,500 ppm on more than 40% forage diets with dietary S at or below 0.5%. SDSU P-00212: under 1,500 ppm no harmful effects except mild diarrhea, 3,500-4,500 not for pregnant or lactating, over 4,500 not recommended. Total sulfur from feed plus water matters (SDSU: 0.4% DM).
evidence_corrections: AS1764 does not say whether its nitrate figure is NO3 or NO3-N, so 'nitrate-N 100 ppm' is not explicit in that source.
rules.limitations: Diet and feed sulfur change the safe limit. A dashboard flag must not imply a diagnosis.
rules.configurable: Yes. Choose and cite one reference set.
rules.missing_data_blocks: No diet or class means show the result and the reference ranges side by side without a pass or fail.
rules.recommendation: Show results against cited ranges and flag 'discuss with nutritionist or veterinarian' above the lower limit.
rules.phase_note: Needs lab results entered by hand. A flag must not imply a diagnosis.

sources.title: Livestock Water Quality (AS1764)
sources.supports: Diet-dependent sulfate limits. Nitrate 100 ppm, nitrite 33 ppm safe upper limits (NO3 vs NO3-N basis not stated).
sources.checker_note: AS1764 'Livestock Water Quality', Meehan, Galbreath and Mostrom, 'Revised January 2026'. TDS table: <3,000 'Usually satisfactory for most livestock'; 3,000-5,000 young stock may be affected; 5,000-7,000 'Should not be consumed by pregnant or lactating females'; 7,000-10,000 'Do not use for pregnant or lactating ruminants or horses' (and swine); >10,000 'May cause brain damage or death'. Lab trigger: 'If TDS levels exceed 4,500 ppm and/or sulfates levels exceed 800 ppm'. Screening with an 'EC or TDS meter and sulfate test strips'; calibration per WQ1923. 'salts in surface water become more concentrated as water levels decline'. Table 2: sulfate <600 ppm on >85% concentrate (diet S 0.3%) and <2,500 ppm on >40% forage (diet S 0.5%). Table 3: 'Nitrate 100', 'Nitrite 33', 'Sulfate 500 to 1,000'. Nitrate is not labelled NO3 vs NO3-N, so 'nitrate-N 100' is not explicit here. Not supported: the labs integration names NDSU VDL, SDSU testing and Midwest Laboratories, but this document names only the 'NDSU Veterinary Diagnostic Lab' (it does mention 'algal toxin determination').

sources.title: Interpretation of Water Analysis for Livestock Suitability (P-00212)
sources.supports: Sulfate bands up to over 4,500 ppm. Divide sulfate by 3 for sulfur.
sources.checker_note: P-00212, Robin Salverson, November 2023. The 2004 original was by Thiex and German. TDS bands are <1,000, 1,000-2,999, 3,000-4,999, 5,000-6,999, 7,000-10,000 and >10,000 mg/L; the boundaries match NDSU above 3,000. Sulfate: <1,500 'no serious effects' with mild diarrhea near the limit; 3,500-4,500 not for pregnant or lactating cows; >4,500 not recommended. NO3-N <100 / 100-300 / >300. 'Divide sulfate content by 3 to convert to sulfur content'. Dietary S max 0.4%. Field 'quick test' with an EC or TDS meter.

sources.title: Water Requirements for Beef Cattle
sources.supports: Sulfate: calves under 500 ppm, adults under 1,000 ppm. Nitrate-N under 100 ppm.
sources.checker_note: Troy Walz, July 2, 2020. Sulfate: 'upper limit for calves is less than 500 ppm' and 'For adult cattle ... less than 1,000 ppm'. 'A safe level of nitrate nitrogen (NO3N) ... is less than 100 ppm.' Intake runs from 1 gal per 100 lb in cold weather to nearly 2 gal in the hottest weather. No TDS guidance.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) observation and escalation. If scum, blue, green, red or yellow colour, or wind-blown accumulation is seen on a pond, dugout or stagnant tank in hot, sunny, calm weather (late summer to early autumn), log it. Then move cattle to an alternate or windward water point, collect a 500 ml or larger sample (gloves; cool, not frozen), and contact a veterinarian. Do not move dead stock until a vet is consulted.
rules.decision_supported: Restricting access to a water source, and lab and vet escalation (observation only).
rules.required_inputs: Source id and type, observation (none, suspect, bloom), photo, date, weather, cattle using the source, sample sent (y/n), lab, vet contacted.

context.season: Hot, sunny, calm weather, late summer to early fall
context.geography: Ponds, dugouts and stagnant tanks
context.management: Visual observation with a fixed escalation path (restrict access, sample, call the veterinarian)

rules.context_research: Surface water (ponds, dugouts) and stagnant tanks, late summer and early autumn.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research A).
rules.evidence: NDSU V1136 (rev. June 2026) and UNL BeefWatch (2021) agree. Blooms are fed by nitrogen and phosphorus with hot, sunny weather. Numbers can double in a day or less. Wind concentrates them on the downwind side. Presence 'does not mean the water is toxic'. Sample at least 500 ml from surface and depth, keep cool, wear gloves. Contact a veterinarian. Use alternate water and the windward side.
rules.limitations: Toxicity cannot be judged by eye. Lab turnaround matters. A level sensor gives no quality signal.
rules.configurable: Partly. Which sources are surface water, and lab contacts.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a recent observation on a surface source in late summer, show 'not observed', not 'safe'.
rules.recommendation: Add as a manual observation type with a fixed escalation path (restrict access, sample, vet). Exclude treatment instructions.
rules.phase_note: Needs an observation log. Observation and escalation only; no treatment instructions.

sources.title: Cyanobacteria Poisoning (Blue-green Algae) (V1136)
sources.supports: Bloom conditions, visual signs, sampling protocol, management actions, contact a veterinarian.
sources.checker_note: V1136, 'Revised June 2026', original 1997 (Stoltenow). Quotes: blooms from nitrogen and phosphorus with 'hot, sunny days'; 'doubling in one day or less'; gentle winds concentrate it 'on the leeward (downwind) side'; 'commonly occur in late summer and early autumn'; 'the presence of the bacteria does not mean the water is toxic'; 'at least 500 ml', surface and deeper, 'kept cool but not frozen', 'wear gloves'; 'avoid moving dead stock until a veterinarian has been consulted'; alternate water and fencing; 'Force the cattle to the windward side'.

sources.title: Blue-Green Algae Impacts on Cattle
sources.supports: Same observation and sampling guidance. Fence off downwind corners. Pump from depth into a tank.
sources.checker_note: Amy Timmerman, July 7, 2021. Hot, sunny days plus nutrients; 'doubling in a day or less'; 'at least 500 milliliters'; keep cool, do not freeze, wear gloves; necropsy by a veterinarian. 'If wind concentrates the bacteria on one corner ... fence that corner off.' 'Pump water from the center of the water body well below the surface to a water tank.' Alternate water sources. On toxicity it says 'not all species are harmful'.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: sensor trust band and calibration record. Store each device's stated accuracy and the sensor offset or usable-bottom setting. Mark readings within the accuracy band of a threshold as 'near threshold, verify'. Do not re-judge history when the offset changes.
rules.decision_supported: How far to trust a reading before sending someone.
rules.required_inputs: device_model, stated accuracy, offset_in and the date it was set, tank shape and dimensions.

context.class: Any cattle on the tank's pasture (demo groups: Cows 180 cow-calf pairs, Heifers 45 first-calf heifers, Yearlings 150 yearling steers)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Remote level sensors on stock tanks (demo: 8 tanks, one tank per pasture, a reading every 6 h); vendor-stated accuracy and offsets

rules.context_research: Pressure-transducer and ultrasonic tank sensors.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker water dispute 1: the only numeric accuracy is LoneStar's vendor statement 'accurate to about 10%'; Ranchbot, Farmbot, MLA, USU and NMSU give none, and no independent accuracy trial was found. The 'near threshold, verify' band is a design choice.
rules.evidence: Vendor claims only. LoneStar says 'accurate to about 10%' (temperature, barometric pressure and sediment affect it). Ranchbot and Farmbot give no numeric accuracy and display projected values ('based on all previous data points, trend predictions'). The Ranchbot offset is 'not applied retrospectively'. Tank shape is needed to turn level into gallons (Ranchbot shape and volume article, 2024; Farmbot shows a dash for volume until total volume is entered). Independent evaluations I found report no accuracy metrics: USU (spikes, one faulty unit), MLA producer and vendor reports (no accuracy data), NMSU LoRaWAN test (no accuracy).
evidence_corrections: MLA 2021 report: 'MLA has its own product interest' is not supported; MLA appears only as funder and publisher, and the report gives no accuracy or uptime data.
Ranchbot's tank-shape settings offer no rectangular option.
rules.limitations: I found no independent accuracy trial for livestock tank sensors.
rules.configurable: Yes.
rules.missing_data_blocks: With no accuracy on record, label readings as 'vendor accuracy unknown'.

rules.context_research: Cow-calf and grazing operations with remote tank sensors. The source is a BQA cow-calf assessment guide, not a Northern Plains study.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. rules.evidence: SOURCE: a sample 'Water Tank Protocol' template in the BQA Cow-Calf Assessment guide reads '("X" crew) will monitor water tank function and cleanliness daily by visually inspecting the tanks and reporting any problems immediately to (the operation's manager)'; 'daily' and the cleaning interval ('at least every (two weeks)') are fill-in values. The guide notes 'Water is the most important nutrient for general animal well-being.' OBSERVED: the current T6 first step already says 'Check the tank by eye today, then the sensor battery and signal', but no data field records that an eyes-on check happened.

rules.limitations: The assessment guide is undated (FY26 file). Daily checking may be impractical on large Plains pastures in some seasons, where frequency is a ranch decision informed by weather, stocking and sensor reliability.

rules.rule: CURRENT: Serious when an open stay's days in pasture (as_of date minus in_date) is more than the pasture's planned_graze_days (exceptions.js, grazing block of findExceptions: over = g.days - g.planned; over > 0 gives 'serious'). The threshold is hard-coded; RULES has no setting for it.
rules.decision_supported: Move the group now, or check the grass and record a new move date.
rules.required_inputs: moves.csv (group, pasture_id, in_date, empty out_date), pastures.csv planned_graze_days, meta.csv as_of. No forage, residual, growth-stage, herd-size or water input is used.

context.class: Any grazing group (demo: Cows, Heifers, Yearlings)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Rotational grazing on 8 pastures with a planned stay length per pasture

rules.context_research: Any rotational system with a written plan. A planned day count is a legitimate scheduling tool. It is a weak proxy for plant impact because the forage a group removes depends on herd size and animal size (AU), production that year (driven mostly by April to June rain), and growth rate (fast vs slow).
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). Planned stay length is the ranch's plan; extension sources say moves should follow plant growth and use, not a fixed count.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (ran `node docs/audit/diagnostics/grazing.rest.research.mjs` and `node docs/audit/diagnostics/grazing.forage.research.mjs`): on the committed data the rule raises exactly one grazing row: "[serious] Yearlings in Sand Hills | Day 24 of a 21-day plan (3 days over)". The plan is per pasture, not per stay or herd: "P4 Lone Tree: one planned 14-d stay = Heifers 22 AUM, Yearlings 48 AUM (x2.2)" and "P2 Windmill: one planned 18-d stay = Cows 123 AUM, Yearlings 62 AUM (x2.0)" (AUE values assumed from NDSU R1810). Closed stays also deviate without being recorded as a problem: "Cows (180 hd) in P6 Cedar Draw 2026-07-31..2026-08-22: 22 d vs plan 18 d (+4)". GUIDANCE: NRCS SD Range Tech Note 9 (Apr 2017) p.4: "Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates." and "Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules." SDSU MC-04340: "movement to the next pasture should follow plant growth – not the calendar." UNL G1908: move livestock when a predetermined criterion such as a stubble height is reached. CARM (Augustine et al. 2020) used a maximum days-in-pasture limit only alongside minimum-biomass thresholds and cattle-behaviour checks; the limit was dropped in 2015 and set to 14–21 days by 2018. CPS 528 (June 2025) asks for monitoring that 'documents decisions based upon ecological triggers and thresholds'.
rules.limitations: Elapsed days do not measure the plants. The same 14-day plan removes about 2.2x more forage with 150 yearlings than with 45 heifers. A dry year gives less forage for the same days (TR 1734-3: light use in a drought year can look like heavy use in a wet year). During fast growth, a long stay lets cattle regraze regrowth before the plant recovers (SD TN9 p.3). One day over is rated 'serious' no matter what the forage looks like, which overstates urgency when forage is ample and misses overuse when the pasture runs short before the planned date. Moves are dates with no time of day, so a move on the morning of the planned day still counts that day.
rules.configurable: Partly. planned_graze_days is editable per pasture in pastures.csv. The 'any day over is serious' threshold is hard-coded in findExceptions and is not in RULES, so a ranch cannot tune it without code changes.
rules.missing_data_blocks: With no residual or stubble, utilization or forage-condition observation, the dashboard can say 'past the planned date' but must not imply overgrazing or 'grass is fine'. When a group's head count or average weight changed after the plan was written (for example, groups combined), the planned days are no longer comparable.
rules.recommendation: Keep it as a plan-deviation check, but: (1) store a planned_out_date on each stay in moves.csv instead of using a per-pasture day count, so plans can differ by herd size. (2) Make the default severity 'warning: past planned move date; check key-species stubble and water'. Escalate to serious only with corroborating observations, such as stubble below the pasture's target, utilization above the target, the water source failing, or no forage check during the stay. (3) Put the escalation thresholds in RULES. (4) Show one row per stay listing every reason (days, stubble, rest, water), in line with the README's no-noise principle. (5) In the README and rules table, describe it as a ranch planning choice, not an agronomic standard.
rules.phase_note: Keep it (the yearlings on day 24 of 21 must still be found). An open stay in an unknown pasture, or a group with more than one open stay, becomes a data issue (CAN'T TELL), not a grazing row. Label planned_graze_days as the ranch's plan (demo values). The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Prescribed Grazing, Range Technical Note No. 9 (South Dakota Technical Guide, Section I, Notice SD-424)
sources.supports: p.4: 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing schedules. p.3: keep grazing periods as short as practical to minimise grazing of regrowth before recovery.
sources.checker_note: Fetched with WebFetch; curl gave 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Metadata is correct: 'Prescribed Grazing', Range Technical Note No. 9, April 2017, running header 'SOUTH DAKOTA TECHNICAL GUIDE NOTICE SD-424'. VERIFIED: p.4 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' and 'Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules.' p.3 'Keeping the grazing periods as short as practical, especially during periods of fast plant growth, will minimize the opportunity ... to graze plant regrowth prior to plant recovery.' p.3, once-over use ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed only one time'): rangeland 'minimum of 45 consecutive days of rest during the growing season', pasture 30. p.3, 2+ grazings ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed two or more times during a growing season'): 'Each pasture will be deferred for a minimum of 90 days during the growing season.' The p.4 Table 1 range values match the research: 20-30%* West fast 40, slow 60; East 35/55. 40-50%: West 50/70, East 45/65. Footnote: 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage.' Note: 'Under drought conditions, recovery periods may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Utilization limits match: 50% seasonal and 30% temporal (p.4), 65% browse and 60% dormant season (p.6). Table 3 (p.6, titled 'Minimum Height of Pasture Species') gives end stubble WWG 4, CWG 3, switchgrass 8, big & sand bluestem 6, KBG 2, sideoats 2, and begin heights WWG 6-10 etc., all as cited. Riparian 'residual heights of 4 to 8 inches is commonly cited as adequate' (Section IV, p.7). App. B p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' Phase I removes 10% in the first month; Phase II removes 20-40% and says 'Routinely monitor conditions such as soil moisture and plant growth on a weekly basis'; Phase III says 'measure remaining forage in all pastures', 'combine remaining herds into one herd', with 30%+ removal on p.16. All verified. MISREAD: the research says '>1 mile to water = very large field needing herding or water relocation'. The source says 'A very large field would roughly be where the distance to water is greater than one mile' ('could be considerably larger on smooth terrain'). Its point is that continuous season-long use gives adequate recovery only on very large fields where livestock are herded or redistributed by changing water. It does not say every field over 1 mile needs herding. The page number for this passage came back inconsistently from two fetches (p.2 and p.3).

sources.title: Adaptive, Multipaddock Rotational Grazing Management: A Ranch-Scale Assessment of Effects on Vegetation and Livestock Performance in Semiarid Rangeland. Rangeland Ecology & Management 73:796-810, doi:10.1016/j.rama.2020.07.005
sources.publisher: Elsevier / Society for Range Management (author PDF hosted by USDA ARS)
sources.url: https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/51815/67. 2020 REM - CARM - adaptive multipaddock rotational grazing - vegetation and livestock responses.pdf
sources.data_years: 2013 pretreatment; 2014-2018 treatment; Central Plains Experimental Range, Nunn CO
sources.supports: Move timing used forage biomass thresholds (e.g. 300 lb/ac loamy in 2014, 450 lb/ac 2016-18), cattle behaviour checks 3 days/week, and a max-days cap (dropped 2015, 14-21 d by 2018). Adaptive rotation gave 12-16% lower cattle gain (abstract; the Results give 11.7-16.2%) than continuous grazing at the same stocking rate, with little vegetation benefit.
sources.checker_note: Augustine, Derner, Fernandez-Gimenez, Porensky, Wilmer, Briske & CARM Stakeholder Group. REM 73:796-810, 2020, doi 10.1016/j.rama.2020.07.005. 2013 pretreatment, 2014-2018 treatment, CPER near Nunn CO. Biomass thresholds: loamy 300 lb/ac in 2014-15 and 450 in 2016-18 (mixed 400/500, sandy 450/550). Max days: varied by site in 2014, 'dropped entirely' in 2015, 24 d in 2016, 21 d in 2017, 14 d early and 21 d mid-late season in 2018, so '14-21 d by 2018' is correct. Methods: 'cattle were moved when a threshold was met in vegetation biomass, cattle behavior, or a maximum number of grazing days'. Behaviour was checked '3 d/wk', including 'whether any cattle displayed signs of attempting to leave the pasture', and was an explicit move criterion (App. B 'Yes' 2014-2018). Same stocking rate: 'the same total number of steers grazed in the CARM and TRM pastures'. Abstract: 'a 12–16% reduction in total cattle weight gain relative to continuous grazing'. Vegetation: 'little supporting evidence for grazing management effects on C3 graminoid abundance or production'. Claim (rule 2) that it says nothing on move lead time: no lead-time statement surfaced, but absence was not exhaustively checked.

sources.title: Switchgrass, Big Bluestem, and Indiangrass for Grazing and Hay (NebGuide G1908)
sources.supports: Move livestock when a predetermined criterion such as recommended stubble height or readiness of another pasture is reached. Big bluestem/indiangrass: stubble of half the original height or 4-6 in. Note: the guide calls these 'native warm-season grasses' and recommends certified cultivars, so it fits seeded native warm-season pasture rather than native range.
sources.checker_note: 'Switchgrass, Big Bluestem, and Indiangrass for Grazing and Hay', G1908, R.B. Mitchell (USDA-ARS) and B.E. Anderson, 'Issued December 2008' (date correct). VERIFIED: under rotational stocking, livestock graze until a benchmark such as target stubble height or readiness of another pasture is reached, then 'Livestock then are moved to the next pasture.' Big bluestem and indiangrass: graze no more than 2-3 weeks to about one-half the original height, or alternatively 'to a stubble height of 4 to 6 inches' (needs longer rest). Switchgrass: 4-6 in stubble then 30-45 d rest, or keep 8-16 in. CORRECTION to the research note 'covers warm-season tame pasture, not native range': the guide calls these 'native warm-season grasses'. It recommends certified cultivars, which implies seeded stands, but it does not call them tame. 'Seeded native warm-season pasture' is more accurate.

sources.title: Grazing Management (Code 528) Conservation Practice Standard, 528-CPS-1
sources.supports: General Criteria: 'Develop and implement a monitoring strategy that supports adaptive management and documents decisions based upon ecological triggers and thresholds...'; 'Manage livestock numbers and grazing periods to adjust the intensity, frequency, timing, duration, and distribution'.
sources.checker_note: Cover and footer: 'GRAZING MANAGEMENT', 'CODE 528', 'June 2025'. General Criteria, verbatim: 'Develop and implement a monitoring strategy that supports adaptive management and documents decisions based upon ecological triggers and thresholds to optimize the conservation outcome.' 'Manage livestock numbers and grazing periods to adjust the intensity, frequency, timing, duration, and distribution...' 'Provide adequate quantity, quality, and distribution of drinking water for animals during periods of occupancy.' 'Provide desired plants sufficient recovery time from grazing/browsing to meet planned objectives.' 'Deferment or rest should be planned for critical periods of plant or animal needs.' PARTLY: 'Implement longer rest periods before perennial forage dormant seasons to extend root growth' is NOT a General Criterion. It sits under 'Additional Criteria to Reduce Runoff and Compaction and Enhance or Maintain Key Soil Health Components...'. The rest rule quotes it next to the general criteria without saying it applies only to that purpose. The CPS gives no support for 'planned_next_pasture' (data field) beyond the general water and monitoring criteria; that link is loose.

rules.rule: CURRENT: Warning when a planned move is 2 days away or less (RULES.graceDays = 2; over >= -2).
rules.decision_supported: Line up the move (crew, gates, trailer or horseback, water at the next pasture).
rules.required_inputs: Same as the over-plan rule: in_date, planned_graze_days, as_of.

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Rotational grazing on 8 pastures with a planned stay length per pasture

rules.context_research: Logistics lead time for moving cattle. It depends on crew size, distance, terrain and how the move is done. It is not an agronomic threshold.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D). No extension or NRCS source sets a lead time for move reminders.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED: on the committed data the rule fires on no stay. Cows are on day 18 of 21 in P7 and Heifers on day 11 of 14 in P4 (3 days left each), so neither is within 2 days (diagnostic section B). I found no extension or NRCS source that sets a lead time for move reminders. CARM staff checked cattle and forage 3 days a week (Augustine et al. 2020), which shows how often monitoring was done, not how much warning a move needs.
rules.limitations: It does not check that the destination is ready: whether it has had its minimum rest, whether its tank level and sensor are OK, or whether the key species is at grazing height. A move that is 'due' into an unrested pasture produces no signal. As an exception row it competes with real problems, even though it is a routine scheduled task.
rules.configurable: Yes, through RULES.graceDays, but the value is a demonstration setting with no source behind it.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a planned destination pasture on the stay, the dashboard cannot check readiness and should say 'destination not planned' rather than 'ready'.
rules.recommendation: Move this from the exception list to an 'upcoming moves' panel or task list. Add a planned_next_pasture field and show destination readiness: rest days elapsed vs that pasture's minimum, current tank level and sensor status, and the latest key-species height. Keep it as a warning exception only when the destination fails a readiness check (see the rest and water rules). Label graceDays as a ranch preference.
rules.phase_note: Label 2 days as a demo setting. It raises nothing on the demo data. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

rules.rule: UNUSED DATA -> PROPOSED: Rest/recovery check. pastures.csv carries min_rest_days (30-60 d), but no shipped code reads it. Proposed check: rest = days between the last out_date by ANY group and the next in_date in the same pasture, counting growing-season days only, compared with a recovery minimum that depends on growth rate (fast/slow) and region.
rules.decision_supported: Before a move: don't send cattle into a pasture that has not recovered, or record why you are doing it anyway. After the fact: record and review re-entries made short of the plan.
rules.required_inputs: Stays per pasture across all groups (in/out dates). A per-pasture recovery minimum for fast and for slow growth (min_rest_fast_days, min_rest_slow_days). A growth-stage observation, or a date-based proxy marked as an assumption. Growing-season start and end dates. Optional: temporal utilization, drought status, and an override reason recorded by the manager.

context.season: Growing season; rest needs differ between fast-growth (May-June) and slow-growth (July-August) periods
context.geography: Northern Plains native range and tame pasture
context.management: Rotational grazing on 8 pastures with a planned stay length per pasture; pastures.csv already carries min_rest_days (30-60 d) that no code reads

rules.context_research: Applies when paddocks are grazed 2+ times per growing season. For once-over use, SD TN9 sets a separate minimum of 45 consecutive days' rest during the growing season on rangeland. Recovery minimums differ by region (West vs East River SD; western vs eastern ND), growth rate (vegetative pre-boot is fast; boot onward is slow), utilization level, and drought (90+ d). Rest during dormancy does not count as recovery.
rules.classification_note: Kept at B. Checker grazing dispute 3: the CPS 528 line on longer rest before dormancy sits under a purpose-specific soil-health criterion, not general guidance; and recovery minimums tied to utilization depend on use ceilings that SD TN9 (30% temporal) and NDSU R1780 (about 50% per period) set differently.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED: `grazing.rest.research.mjs` prints 'exceptions.js: occurrences of "min_rest_days" = 0' and 'app.js: occurrences of "min_rest_days" = 0', and 'total re-entries shorter than min_rest_days or overlapping: 13'. `grazing.forage.research.mjs` prints 're-entries: 15', 'short under data min_rest_days (synthetic): 13 of 15', 'short under NDSU R1780 western ND range: 14 of 15', 'short under SD TN9 West River range 20-30%: 13 of 15'. For current stays: 'Cows in P7 South Divide since 2026-09-12 ... entered after 6 d rest (previous: Yearlings out 2026-09-06); pasture min_rest_days=60 -> 54 d SHORT ... dashboard grazing rows for this stay: none' and 'Heifers in P4 Lone Tree since 2026-09-19 ... entered after 34 d rest ... min_rest_days=45 -> 11 d SHORT ... dashboard grazing rows for this stay: none'. GUIDANCE: SD TN9 Table 1 (range, 20-30% temporal use, the level it recommends for multiple grazings): West River 40 d fast / 60 d slow; East River 35 / 55. At 40-50% use: West 50/70, East 45/65. Drought: 'may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Each pasture grazed 2+ times is deferred at least 90 days during the growing season. NDSU R1780 (rev. Oct 2024), rangeland: fast growth (May/June) 45 d western ND / 30 d eastern; slow growth (July/Aug) 65 / 45. CPS 528: 'Provide desired plants sufficient recovery time from grazing/browsing to meet planned objectives' and, under a purpose-specific soil-health criterion rather than the General Criteria, 'Implement longer rest periods before perennial forage dormant seasons to extend root growth.'
evidence_corrections: Manske (NDSU DREC): a 1999 research report on 1984-1994 data; its rotation implies rest of about 30-60 days, not 'about 30 days'.
rules.limitations: Published minimums are planning guides for one state or sub-region, not validated universal thresholds. They depend on utilization level, which the data do not record. The script's fast/slow split by calendar month is an assumption; SD TN9 defines it by growth stage. A September re-entry may be a deliberate late-season or dormant-season plan (dormant-season grazing has its own 60% utilization limit in SD TN9). The fictional generator plans each group independently, so 13 of 15 historical re-entries break the data's own minimums and 2 stays overlap. That is a generator artefact, not a planted problem.
rules.configurable: Must be. The minimums should be per pasture and per growth rate, with region-appropriate defaults (state NRCS FOTG technical notes), and editable. The override reason should be a recorded field.
rules.missing_data_blocks: No growth-stage observation: label the minimum used as a 'calendar proxy'. No out_date for the previous stay, or an overlapping stay: report a data problem, not a rest violation. Outside the growing season: do not count the days as recovery and do not flag. Never report 'rested' when records for a pasture are incomplete.
rules.recommendation: Add it in two parts. (a) PROSPECTIVE (most useful): warning when a group's planned next pasture will not have reached its recovery minimum by the planned entry date. The action: pick another pasture, or record why the re-entry is planned. (b) RETROSPECTIVE: one warning per stay that began short of the minimum, giving rest days vs minimum and the growth period. Suppress it when an override reason is recorded (planned dormant-season use, targeted grazing of invasive cool-season grass, drought herd consolidation). Escalate to serious only when the short rest happened during fast growth AND a key-species stubble or utilization reading breaks its target, not on days alone. Replace the single min_rest_days with min_rest_fast_days and min_rest_slow_days. Before shipping, change the fictional generator so the planned rotation honours rest (or plants exactly one violation); otherwise the README's 'exactly the 10 problems that were planted' claim and its test will fail on data the project generated itself.
rules.phase_note: Phase-2 default 'rest-period checks using min_rest_days'. The demo generator produces 13 of 15 short re-entries (an artefact; Cows in P7 after 6 days against 60, Heifers in P4 after 34 against 45), so scripts/generate_data.py and the tests must change in the same step or the check adds new alarms.

sources.title: Prescribed Grazing, Range Technical Note No. 9
sources.supports: p.3: once-over rangeland >= 45 consecutive days rest in the growing season (pasture 30). 90-day growing-season deferral for 2+ grazings. p.4 Table 1: recovery minimums by utilization, West/East River, fast/slow. 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage'. Drought: 90+ days.
sources.checker_note: Fetched with WebFetch; curl gave 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Metadata is correct: 'Prescribed Grazing', Range Technical Note No. 9, April 2017, running header 'SOUTH DAKOTA TECHNICAL GUIDE NOTICE SD-424'. VERIFIED: p.4 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' and 'Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules.' p.3 'Keeping the grazing periods as short as practical, especially during periods of fast plant growth, will minimize the opportunity ... to graze plant regrowth prior to plant recovery.' p.3, once-over use ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed only one time'): rangeland 'minimum of 45 consecutive days of rest during the growing season', pasture 30. p.3, 2+ grazings ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed two or more times during a growing season'): 'Each pasture will be deferred for a minimum of 90 days during the growing season.' The p.4 Table 1 range values match the research: 20-30%* West fast 40, slow 60; East 35/55. 40-50%: West 50/70, East 45/65. Footnote: 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage.' Note: 'Under drought conditions, recovery periods may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Utilization limits match: 50% seasonal and 30% temporal (p.4), 65% browse and 60% dormant season (p.6). Table 3 (p.6, titled 'Minimum Height of Pasture Species') gives end stubble WWG 4, CWG 3, switchgrass 8, big & sand bluestem 6, KBG 2, sideoats 2, and begin heights WWG 6-10 etc., all as cited. Riparian 'residual heights of 4 to 8 inches is commonly cited as adequate' (Section IV, p.7). App. B p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' Phase I removes 10% in the first month; Phase II removes 20-40% and says 'Routinely monitor conditions such as soil moisture and plant growth on a weekly basis'; Phase III says 'measure remaining forage in all pastures', 'combine remaining herds into one herd', with 30%+ removal on p.16. All verified. MISREAD: the research says '>1 mile to water = very large field needing herding or water relocation'. The source says 'A very large field would roughly be where the distance to water is greater than one mile' ('could be considerably larger on smooth terrain'). Its point is that continuous season-long use gives adequate recovery only on very large fields where livestock are herded or redistributed by changing water. It does not say every field over 1 mile needs herding. The page number for this passage came back inconsistently from two fetches (p.2 and p.3).

sources.title: The North Dakota Grazing Monitoring Stick: A Way to Measure Range and Pasture Utilization (R1780)
sources.supports: Rangeland recovery: fast growth (May/June) 45 d western ND, 30 d eastern; slow growth (July/August) 65 d western, 45 d eastern. Introduced pasture 25/15 fast, 35/25 slow.
sources.checker_note: R1780, Meehan, Sedivec, Printz. 'Revised October 2024'; no original date shown, so the research is correct. Table 1 recovery (min days): rangeland fast (May/June) 45 western ND / 30 eastern; slow (July/August) 65 / 45. Introduced pasture 25/15 fast, 35/25 slow. All match. Measure before turnout and during grazing to prevent overuse; 'Final utilization levels should be evaluated within three days of livestock removal.' 'You should take a minimum of 30 measurements for each key species across a pasture.' Avoid water sources, salt sites and gates. Removal % = (1 - grazed/ungrazed) x 100. WWG: 75% height removal is about 58% by weight (Table 3). Table 5 classes: slight-moderate <40, full 40-60, close 60-80, severe >80. Rule of thumb about 50% by weight. Native cool-season reaches 3.5-leaf mid-late May or early June. One extra point the research did not use: the document also suggests targeting about 50% weight use per grazing period, which is looser than SD TN9's 30% temporal limit. The two sources disagree on the per-stay ceiling.

sources.title: Grazing Management (Code 528) Conservation Practice Standard
sources.supports: 'Provide desired plants sufficient recovery time from grazing/browsing to meet planned objectives.' 'Manage livestock numbers and grazing periods to adjust the intensity, frequency, timing, duration, and distribution...' 'Provide adequate quantity, quality, and distribution of drinking water for animals during periods of occupancy.' 'Provide desired plants sufficient recovery time from grazing/browsing to meet planned objectives.' 'Deferment or rest should be planned for critical periods of plant or animal needs.' sources.title: Grazing Management for Rangeland
sources.publisher: NDSU Dickinson Research Extension Center (L. Manske)
sources.supports: Twice-over rotation in western ND: first rotation June 1-July 15, 15 d per pasture (3 pastures); second rotation 30 d per pasture to mid-October. Inferred rest between a pasture's first and second use is about 30-60 d (about 30, 45 and 60 d for the three pastures if the order repeats; the second-rotation order was not confirmed). An example of fixed calendars used deliberately within a growth-stage rationale (3rd leaf to flowering).
sources.checker_note: 'GRAZING MANAGEMENT FOR RANGELAND', Llewellyn L. Manske, NDSU Dickinson Research Extension Center. METADATA: the document is listed under '1999 Research Reports', the study ran 1984-1994, and citations span 1988-1998. The research's data_years 'not stated in fetched text' is wrong (should be 1984-1994), and pub_date can be given as a 1999 DREC research report. VERIFIED: three pastures, each 'grazed for 15 days between 1 June and 15 July', then 30 days each from mid-July to mid-October. The rationale is the 'third-leaf stage and flowering phenophase'. PARTLY WRONG INFERENCE: 'about 30 d between a pasture's first and second use' holds only for the first pasture, if the order repeats. My arithmetic: P1 out Jun 15, in Jul 16 = 30 d; P2 out Jun 30, in Aug 15 = 45 d; P3 out Jul 15, in Sep 14 = 60 d. Rest ranges about 30-60 d. The order of the second rotation was not confirmed in the fetch.

Use stubble height (warning near the ranch's target; serious below it with cattle still in) or, as an alternative or companion, utilization (% of current-year growth removed by weight) per grazing period and per season.
rules.decision_supported: [grazing research rule 4] Move now, or not yet. This replaces elapsed days as the main move trigger. | [grazing research rule 5] Whether a stay or a season's use stayed within the plan, and whether the stocking rate needs adjusting next season.
rules.required_inputs: [grazing research rule 4] Per pasture: key species and a target residual height (inches). Observations: date, pasture, species, mean height, number of readings (NDSU recommends at least 30 per key species), observer, and optionally the ungrazed reference height. | [grazing research rule 5] Utilization estimate per pasture and key species, with the method (grazing stick height-weight, ocular, paired plot), date, and whether it is temporal (one period) or seasonal.

context.management: Rotational grazing on 8 pastures with a planned stay length per pasture; grazing-stick or ocular residual measurements

rules.context_research: [grazing research rule 4] Northern mixed-grass and tallgrass range and tame pasture. The targets are species-specific: SD TN9 Table 3 minimum stubble at end of grazing is western wheatgrass 4 in, crested wheatgrass 3, switchgrass 8, big and sand bluestem 6, Kentucky bluegrass 2, sideoats grama 2. Riparian residual is commonly 4-8 in. | [grazing research rule 5] SD TN9: seasonal use on desirable rangeland grasses should not exceed 50% by weight of current-year growth. Temporal use (per grazing period) should not exceed 30%. Browse up to 65%. Dormant-season grazing of grasses up to 60%. NDSU R1780 degree-of-use classes: slight-moderate <40%, full 40-60%, close 60-80%, severe >80%.
rules.classification_research: grazing R4: B-context-dependent + grazing R5: B-context-dependent
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (both research rules B). Targets come from state NRCS technical notes and extension protocols and must be set per pasture.
rules.evidence: [grazing research rule 4] SD TN9 Table 3 (stubble minimums and start heights, e.g. begin western wheatgrass at 6-10 in). NDSU R1780: measure before turnout, during the grazing period 'to prevent overuse', and within 3 days of livestock removal; at least 30 measurements per key species; avoid water, salt and gates; percent removal = [1 - grazed/ungrazed height] x 100; height-weight table, e.g. 75% height removal on western wheatgrass is about 58% by weight. UNL G1908 moves on a stubble target. Interagency TR 1734-3: residual measurement 'may be preferable' to utilization because remaining plant material drives regrowth. Derner et al. 2022: CARM moves on residual-biomass thresholds (visual obstruction) read before entry, weekly, and at exit. OBSERVED: the repo has no stubble, residual or forage observation field at all. | [grazing research rule 5] SD TN9 p.4 quotes: seasonal '...should not remove more than 50 percent by weight of the total current year's growth.' Temporal '...should not remove more than 30 percent by weight...'. NDSU R1810: 'Harvest efficiency includes the "take half, leave half" concept of forage disappearance within the pasture' (25% harvest efficiency for season-long native range). SD Grassland Coalition Range 101 (May 2021): 50% utilization under continuous season-long use gave about 25% harvest efficiency, with 29% lost to trampling, wildlife, insects and senescence. TR 1734-3: seasonal values 'cannot simply be added together' because of regrowth; utilization should not be used alone to set stocking rates.
evidence_corrections: UNL G1908 covers native warm-season grasses, not tame pasture.
Use ceilings differ: SD TN9 caps seasonal use at 50% and temporal use at 30%, while NDSU R1780 suggests about 50% per grazing period.
rules.limitations: [grazing research rule 4] The targets are site-, species- and season-specific, and some are pasture rather than range values. A reading is only as good as the sampling (key areas, enough readings). Stubble says nothing about weight removed without species height-weight curves. | [grazing research rule 5] 'Take half, leave half' is a rule of thumb for season-long native range, not a per-stay target. For multiple grazings the temporal ceiling is lower (30%). Ocular estimates vary between observers. Utilization measured mid-season is confounded by regrowth.
rules.configurable: [grazing research rule 4] Yes. Key species and target height must be per pasture and set by the ranch, with defaults from the state NRCS FOTG. | [grazing research rule 5] Yes. Temporal and seasonal ceilings per pasture.
rules.missing_data_blocks: [grazing research rule 4] No reading during an occupied stay: do not say 'OK'. Show 'no forage check since <date>' (see the stale-observation rule). Fewer readings than the ranch's minimum: show the value as low confidence and do not escalate to serious. | [grazing research rule 5] No utilization or stubble data: the dashboard must not report 'within take-half-leave-half'.

sources.title: Prescribed Grazing, Range Technical Note No. 9 (Table 3)
sources.supports: Minimum stubble heights at end of grazing by species, and start-grazing heights. Riparian residual 4-8 in (Section IV). | p.4 utilization limits: 50% seasonal, 30% temporal, 65% browse, 60% dormant-season grasses.
sources.checker_note: Fetched with WebFetch; curl gave 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Metadata is correct: 'Prescribed Grazing', Range Technical Note No. 9, April 2017, running header 'SOUTH DAKOTA TECHNICAL GUIDE NOTICE SD-424'. VERIFIED: p.4 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' and 'Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules.' p.3 'Keeping the grazing periods as short as practical, especially during periods of fast plant growth, will minimize the opportunity ... to graze plant regrowth prior to plant recovery.' p.3, once-over use ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed only one time'): rangeland 'minimum of 45 consecutive days of rest during the growing season', pasture 30. p.3, 2+ grazings ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed two or more times during a growing season'): 'Each pasture will be deferred for a minimum of 90 days during the growing season.' The p.4 Table 1 range values match the research: 20-30%* West fast 40, slow 60; East 35/55. 40-50%: West 50/70, East 45/65. Footnote: 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage.' Note: 'Under drought conditions, recovery periods may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Utilization limits match: 50% seasonal and 30% temporal (p.4), 65% browse and 60% dormant season (p.6). Table 3 (p.6, titled 'Minimum Height of Pasture Species') gives end stubble WWG 4, CWG 3, switchgrass 8, big & sand bluestem 6, KBG 2, sideoats 2, and begin heights WWG 6-10 etc., all as cited. Riparian 'residual heights of 4 to 8 inches is commonly cited as adequate' (Section IV, p.7). App. B p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' Phase I removes 10% in the first month; Phase II removes 20-40% and says 'Routinely monitor conditions such as soil moisture and plant growth on a weekly basis'; Phase III says 'measure remaining forage in all pastures', 'combine remaining herds into one herd', with 30%+ removal on p.16. All verified. MISREAD: the research says '>1 mile to water = very large field needing herding or water relocation'. The source says 'A very large field would roughly be where the distance to water is greater than one mile' ('could be considerably larger on smooth terrain'). Its point is that continuous season-long use gives adequate recovery only on very large fields where livestock are herded or redistributed by changing water. It does not say every field over 1 mile needs herding. The page number for this passage came back inconsistently from two fetches (p.2 and p.3).

sources.title: The North Dakota Grazing Monitoring Stick (R1780)
sources.supports: Field protocol (timing, at least 30 readings per key species, avoid water/salt/gates), percent-removal formula, height-weight tables by species, start/end heights for introduced species. | Degree-of-use classes and the about-50%-by-weight general rule for key species.
sources.checker_note: R1780, Meehan, Sedivec, Printz. 'Revised October 2024'; no original date shown, so the research is correct. Table 1 recovery (min days): rangeland fast (May/June) 45 western ND / 30 eastern; slow (July/August) 65 / 45. Introduced pasture 25/15 fast, 35/25 slow. All match. Measure before turnout and during grazing to prevent overuse; 'Final utilization levels should be evaluated within three days of livestock removal.' 'You should take a minimum of 30 measurements for each key species across a pasture.' Avoid water sources, salt sites and gates. Removal % = (1 - grazed/ungrazed) x 100. WWG: 75% height removal is about 58% by weight (Table 3). Table 5 classes: slight-moderate <40, full 40-60, close 60-80, severe >80. Rule of thumb about 50% by weight. Native cool-season reaches 3.5-leaf mid-late May or early June. One extra point the research did not use: the document also suggests targeting about 50% weight use per grazing period, which is looser than SD TN9's 30% temporal limit. The two sources disagree on the per-stay ceiling.

sources.title: Utilization Studies and Residual Measurements, Interagency Technical Reference 1734-3
sources.publisher: BLM, USDA Forest Service, USDA NRCS Grazing Land Technology Institute, Cooperative Extension Service (copy hosted by University of Arizona Extension)
sources.supports: Definitions of utilization, residual measurement, key species and key area; residual may be preferable to utilization; utilization data should not be used alone; seasonal utilization cannot simply be summed; weather changes interpretation.
sources.checker_note: 'Utilization Studies and Residual Measurements', Interagency Technical Reference 1734-3 (supersedes BLM TR 4400-3). By BLM, USDA Forest Service, NRCS Grazing Land Technology Institute and Cooperative Extension Service. 1996, 'Revised in 1997, 1999'. VERIFIED: residual or stubble 'may be preferable because it is the plant biomass remaining that will have an important impact on plant health, potential regrowth'. Utilization/residual data 'should not be used alone to determine stocking rates'. Seasonal values 'cannot simply be added together to get total utilization for the year'. 'Light grazing use during a drought year can appear to be the same as heavy use' in a wetter year. Key species and key area definitions are present.

sources.title: Adaptive grazing management in semiarid rangelands: An outcome-driven focus. Rangelands 44(1):111-118, doi:10.1016/j.rala.2021.02.004
sources.publisher: Elsevier / Society for Range Management (USDA ARS-hosted PDF)
sources.data_years: case studies (CARM, Rancho Largo, Red Canyon); years not summarised
sources.supports: Residual-biomass thresholds (visual obstruction) read before entry, weekly, and at exit as move triggers. Red Canyon uses stubble height for riparian removal. 'Short-term observations and monitoring procedures should be simple, quick, and based on consistent methods'.
sources.checker_note: Derner, Budd, Grissom, Kachergis, Augustine, Wilmer, Scasta, Ritten. Rangelands 44(1):111-118, 2022, doi 10.1016/j.rala.2021.02.004. Case studies: Rancho Largo (CO), Red Canyon Ranch (TNC, WY), CARM (CPER, CO). VERIFIED: 'residual biomass thresholds for ecological sites using visual obstruction readings' are a move benchmark, read 'before cattle entry into each pasture and weekly' and at exit. Red Canyon uses 'stubble height measurements' plus judgement to time removal from riparian areas (no threshold value given). Verbatim: 'Short-term observations and monitoring procedures should be simple, quick, and based on consistent methods.' Selection of 'less desirable plants' is 'an early indicator' of unmet nutritional needs. NOT SUPPORTED AS WORDED: 'weight gain indicates whether forage quality is adequate'. The article says gains will decline unless higher-quality forage is provided by moving, and cattle weighing is one way to track the effect of rotation decisions. That is close, but the article does not state it as a diagnostic.

sources.title: Determining Carrying Capacity and Stocking Rates for Range and Pasture in North Dakota (R1810)
sources.supports: Harvest efficiency 25% for season-long native range, 12.5% wet meadow, 30% tame; harvest efficiency includes 'take half, leave half'.
sources.checker_note: R1810, Meehan, Sedivec, Printz, Brummer. Published November 2018, reviewed April 2024, page modified January 16, 2025, all as stated. AU = 'a 1,000-pound cow with a 6-month-old or younger calf'. 'Average consumption of an AU for one month is 913 pounds of air-dried forage.' AUE: 1.00, 1.07, 1.15, yearling (600-800 lb) 0.70, mature bull 1.40. Harvest efficiency: season-long native 25%, wet meadow 12.5%, tame 30%; it 'includes the take half, leave half concept'. Example 1: 100 x 1.15 x 5.5 = 632.5 AUM, as quoted. The example itself uses bulls at 1.50 AUE, which conflicts with the 1.40 in its own Table 1; this does not affect the research. Drought: 'early adjustments of the stocking rate will need to occur'.

sources.title: Range 101: Efficiencies of Rotational Grazing
sources.data_years: cites an NDSU long-term comparison and a 1986 Nebraska report; years not given
sources.supports: About 25% harvest efficiency at 50% utilization under continuous grazing (from Smart's 2010 REM paper, cited on the page; the 29% loss figure comes from a separate NDSU comparison). Planning values: 30% harvest efficiency for simple rotation and 40% for intensive rotation; 35% appears only in an eight-paddock example.
sources.checker_note: Sandy Smart byline, South Dakota Grassland Coalition, 'May 2021'. Page published and modified 2023-10-26, so metadata is correct. CONFLATION: the '25% harvest efficiency at 50% utilization' comes from Smart's 2010 REM paper (63:397-406). The '29% loss through trampling, wildlife, insects, and senescence' comes from a separate NDSU long-term comparison. The research presents them as one finding. Planning values: simple rotation '30% harvest efficiency'; intensive rotation 'plan for a 40% harvest efficiency'. The 35% appears only in an eight-paddock example ('we could safely plan for 35%'), so '35-40% intensive' is a loose merge. Cited studies also include the 2010 and 2013 REM papers and Nebraska EC 86-113-C (1986). data_years omits the 2010 paper, which is the actual source of the 25% figure.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Derive planned graze days from forage demand (AU-days) instead of a fixed per-pasture day count: planned days = (acres x usable forage lb/ac x harvest efficiency) / (head x AUE x daily forage per AU).
rules.decision_supported: Writing the move plan, and re-planning when herd size, animal weight or forage estimates change.
rules.required_inputs: Acres; a forage production or standing-crop estimate (lb/ac, from ecological site description, clipping, or RAP/Grass-Cast as context); harvest efficiency; group head and average weight or class to get AUE; forage per AUM.

context.class: Any grazing group; animal-unit equivalents by class and weight
context.geography: Site- and year-specific forage production
context.management: Stocking plan from forage demand

rules.context_research: General stocking-rate method used by NRCS and extension. Every input value is site- and year-specific.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from A. Checker grazing dispute 1: the AU/AUM/harvest-efficiency method is general extension practice (A), but every constant it needs is not general (913 vs 780 lb per AUM; harvest efficiency 25%, 30-35% or 40% by source; site- and year-specific production). Any computed planned-days figure must be shown as B, not as supported general guidance.
rules.evidence: NDSU R1810: AU = 1,000-lb cow with calf up to 6 months; 913 lb air-dry forage per AUM; AUE table (1,000-lb cow+calf 1.00, 1,100 lb 1.07, 1,200 lb 1.15, yearling 600-800 lb 0.70, mature bull 1.40); worked example 100 cows x 1.15 x 5.5 months = 632.5 AUM. UNL EC127: 1 AUM about 780 lb air-dry forage; common Sandhills rate 0.75 AUM/ac; harvest efficiency about 25% continuous, 30-35% properly managed rotation. The two sources use different forage-per-AUM figures (913 vs 780 lb), which shows the constants are conventions. OBSERVED (`grazing.forage.research.mjs`, assumed AUE): 'season to as_of: 1433 AUM on 4300 ac = 0.33 AUM/ac'. One planned 14-d stay in P4 means 22 AUM for Heifers vs 48 AUM for Yearlings (x2.2).
rules.limitations: The data hold no forage production, so the dashboard cannot compute this today. AUE values are class averages; yearlings averaged 847 lb by Sep 15, above the 600-800 lb band, so 0.70 understates late-season demand. 0.33 AUM/ac falls between the two published context figures I saw (0.25 AUM/ac western ND SCS 1983 figure in an NDSU report; 0.75 Sandhills). That validates nothing; carrying capacity depends on the ecological site and the year.
rules.configurable: Yes. Every constant (AUE, lb/AUM, harvest efficiency) should be a visible setting, because published values differ (913 vs 780 lb/AUM).
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a forage estimate, show planned days as 'manager plan' and do not claim they match carrying capacity.
rules.recommendation: Short term: store planned_out_date per stay and group head/average weight, and show AU-days per stay next to the plan so differences between herds are visible. Longer term: optional forage-budget inputs. In a portfolio piece, being explicit about this is more credible than implying the per-pasture day count is agronomically derived.
rules.phase_note: Needs forage production and harvest-efficiency inputs the demo lacks.
