sources.title: Grazing Systems for Nebraska Sandhills Rangeland (EC127)
sources.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension (Schacht, Volesky, Bauer, Stephenson)
sources.supports: 0.75 AUM/ac Sandhills; 1 AUM about 780 lb; harvest efficiency 25% continuous vs 30-35% rotation; deferred-rotation grazing periods 30-45 d; short-duration 3-10 d; 8-pasture short-duration gave no vegetation or animal-performance advantage over 4-pasture deferred rotation.
sources.checker_note: 'Grazing Systems for Nebraska Sandhills Rangeland', EC127, Schacht, Volesky, Bauer, Stephenson, (c) 2011. Verbatim: 'common stocking rates used in the Sandhills (0.75 AUM/acre)'; AUM 'is equivalent to about 780 lb of air-dry forage'; continuous 'a harvest efficiency of 25 percent'; rotation 'a harvest efficiency of 30 to 35 percent'; deferred rotation 'for 30 to 45 days'; short-duration '(3 to 10 days)'. Barta Brothers 1999-2008: 'there are no vegetation productivity and animal performance improvements with SDG'. Heifer gains were about 1.8 lb/d in both systems. All claims match.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Cattle behaviour and performance as a move signal (manual note: herd walking fence, bunching at gates or water, selecting less-preferred plants; plus a gain trend), giving a 'check forage now' warning.
rules.decision_supported: Check the pasture or move early; link a low-gain exception to the forage situation.
rules.required_inputs: Dated behaviour observation (categorical) per group; the existing gain data (weights.csv).

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Manual behaviour notes plus gain trend

rules.context_research: Used as a formal move benchmark in CARM (shortgrass steppe, yearling steers). K-State MF3232 describes a traditional Flint Hills practice of removing stockers in early fall once gains fall below 1 lb/head/day; it does not recommend it as a rule.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker grazing dispute 2: K-State MF3232 describes traditional practice (stockers 'removed in early fall when weight gains had declined to less than 1 pound per head per day'), not a recommendation, and Derner et al. 2022 does not say gain 'indicates whether forage quality is adequate'. Only the CARM behaviour trigger (Augustine et al. 2020) is directly supported. As written, the gain-threshold element is a ranch choice.
rules.evidence: Augustine et al. 2020: CARM staff checked herd distribution and attempts to leave the pasture 3 days/week as a move criterion. Derner et al. 2022: selection of less-desirable plants is an early indicator of unmet nutritional needs, and weighing cattle is one way to track the effect of rotation decisions (the article does not say gain shows whether forage quality is adequate). K-State MF3232 (Feb 2016) describes the traditional practice of removing stockers in early fall once gains had declined below 1 lb/head/day (a description, not a recommendation); moving stockers within the season to rested areas can cut gain by 'as much as 30 to 40 pounds per animal'.
evidence_corrections: K-State MF3232 describes removal below 1 lb/head/day as traditional Flint Hills practice; it does not recommend it (grazing checker).
Derner et al. 2022 does not state that weight gain shows whether forage quality is adequate (grazing checker).
rules.limitations: Behaviour is subjective and confounded by weather, flies and water. The K-State thresholds apply to Flint Hills stocker systems and do not transfer to cow-calf herds or northern mixed-grass.
rules.configurable: Yes. Categories and the escalation rule are ranch choices.
rules.missing_data_blocks: An absent behaviour note means unknown, not normal.
rules.recommendation: Optional quick-entry field (one tap, few categories). Use it only to add a 'check forage' reason to an existing grazing row or to raise a warning, never a serious, on its own.
rules.phase_note: Needs an observation log; revisit after the phase-3 forage observations exist.

sources.title: Summer Grazing Strategies for Stocker Cattle in the Kansas Flint Hills (MF3232)
sources.publisher: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service (Owensby, Fick)
sources.supports: Describes traditional practice, not a recommendation: stockers were 'removed in early fall when weight gains had declined to less than 1 pound per head per day'; about 4 acres/steer is the moderate season-long rate; in-season rotation to rested areas reduces stocker gains; continuous grazing called the most economically efficient system in the Flint Hills.
sources.checker_note: MF3232, Clenton Owensby and Walter Fick, February 2016 (title, authors and date correct). OVERSTATED: 'remove stockers when gains fall below 1 lb/head/day' is not a recommendation. The document describes traditional practice: stockers were 'removed in early fall when weight gains had declined to less than 1 pound per head per day.' Rule 10's context, 'K-State uses a gain threshold for season removal', overstates this. Gain loss: 'Gains may be reduced as much as 30 to 40 pounds per animal' for systems that 'move animals from one grazed area to an area not previously grazed during the same season'. Moderate rate 'about 4 acres per steer'. 'In the Flint Hills, the most economically efficient, sustainable grazing system is continuous grazing.' DATA YEARS INCORRECT: the tables are 9-, 10-, 8- and 10-year averages (Table 5 uses 2003-2013 market values), not just '10-year and 8-year'.
sources.metadata_note: Checker: data years were given as '10-year and 8-year' only.

rules.rule: PROPOSED (season start): Range readiness. Warning when a planned first entry into a native pasture comes before its key cool-season species reaches about the 3.5-leaf stage (tame cool-season: 3-leaf), or before the ranch's height trigger.
rules.decision_supported: Delay turnout or start on tame pasture first.
rules.required_inputs: Per pasture: key species and native/tame; planned turn-in date; leaf-stage or height observation; optional growing degree days.

context.geography: Northern Plains native cool-season range and tame pasture
context.management: Growth-stage observations before first entry

rules.context_research: Northern Great Plains spring turnout. In NW South Dakota native range is generally ready around end of May/early June and tame grass in early May (SDSU). At SDSU Cottonwood, green needlegrass readiness averaged May 29 (earliest May 15). It does not apply to the demo's September as_of, but it belongs in a season-long tool.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: SDSU 'Reading the Range' (Apr 13, 2022): native cool-season grasses such as western wheatgrass and green needlegrass 'should not be grazed until they reach the 3.5-leaf stage'; tame at 3-leaf. SDSU Grazing Readiness Map (updated Apr 8, 2022; page timestamp Oct 4, 2024): growing degree days to 3.5-leaf are crested wheatgrass 516, western wheatgrass 1,170, green needlegrass 1,209, blue grama 1,296 (USDA-ARS Mandan; PRISM 40-yr); keep yearly turn-in records by pasture. NDSU R1780: native cool-season 3.5-leaf stage mid-late May or early June.
rules.limitations: GDD-based dates are averages; turnout varies by about a month between years.
rules.configurable: Yes.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a readiness observation, show the planned date as unverified.
rules.recommendation: Lower priority for this demo (the data start June 1). Mention it in the README roadmap.
rules.phase_note: Needs growth-stage observations; the demo season starts after turnout.

sources.title: South Dakota Grazing Readiness Spring Turnout Map
sources.supports: GDD thresholds for 3- and 3.5-leaf stages; Cottonwood average readiness May 29; keep turn-in records.
sources.checker_note: Jameson Brennan, Hector Menendez, Krista Ehlert (with Ken Olson). Visible 'Updated April 08, 2022'; metadata update time 2024-10-04. GDD to 3.5-leaf: crested wheatgrass 516, western wheatgrass 1,170, green needlegrass 1,209, blue grama 1,296. Requirements come from USDA-ARS Mandan work. The tool uses the 'PRISM 40-year dataset'; the research's 'climate normals' is a slight relabel. Cottonwood green needlegrass average May 29, earliest May 15 (latest June 7 in text vs June 8 in caption). 'by recording turn in dates every year, producers can begin to see trends'.

sources.title: Reading the Range: Range readiness, grazing timing and drought considerations
sources.supports: 3.5-leaf rule for native cool-season; calendar dates are rules of thumb.
sources.checker_note: Krista Ehlert, originally by Jessalyn Bachler; 'updated April 13, 2022'. 'Research has demonstrated that precipitation received during these months [April, May, June] accurately predicts annual forage production in the central and northern Great Plains (Smart et al. 2020)'. The research's word 'strongly' is a paraphrase; the source says 'accurately'. The reference list gives 2021, an in-text/reference mismatch in the source. Native cool-season grasses 'should not be grazed until they reach the 3.5-leaf stage'; tame grasses are ready at three-leaf. NW SD native turnout is 'generally around the end of May or beginning of June', tame 'beginning of May'. 'general rules of thumb'. Inadequate spring moisture means turnout will be later. Overgrazed pastures 'need adequate time (up to a year) to recover'.

rules.rule: CURRENT: Group 'serious' when the mean of per-animal ADG since the last weigh-in is < 80% of the group's fixed target (exceptions.js: g.adg < g.target * R.adgSerious, adgSerious 0.8). Action text: 'Check forage quality and mineral; look for a health problem in the group'.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a grazing group needs a look at forage, supplement/mineral, water, health observations or weighing conditions before the next move, sale or supplement decision.
rules.required_inputs: Paired weights for the same animals over the same interval; weight basis (full / overnight-shrunk / pencil-shrunk) and gather time for both weigh-ins; interval length; period-specific expected ADG (not a whole-season target); inventory head to judge coverage; pasture/forage and precipitation context.

context.class: Growing cattle judged on ADG (demo: Yearlings target 2.0 lb/d, Heifers 1.0 lb/d)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15)

rules.context_research: Yearling steers and heifers on native range or cool-season pasture in the Northern/Central Great Plains, May-October. Gains fall in late summer as forage matures, and they vary a lot from year to year with precipitation.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). Gains normally decline late in the season, so a fixed 80% test fires in normal years without a period-specific expectation.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (node docs/audit/diagnostics/gain.evidence.research.mjs): 'Heifers: inventory 45, weighed 45 (100%), distinct intervals 1 [2026-07-20..2026-09-15], 57 d; mean ADG 0.44 ... group serious < 0.80'; 'Yearlings: ... mean ADG 1.94 ... group serious < 1.60'. Published period gains vs this threshold, from the same run: 'Yearlings 1.30 vs serious < 1.60: would be SERIOUS | [G02] 1994 season-long steers, late period 15 Jul-8 Sep (precip 44% of normal)'; 'Yearlings 1.46 ... would be SERIOUS | [G02] 1995 ... late period 4 Aug-26 Sep (precip 104% of normal)'; 'Yearlings 2.36 ... no group flag | [G02] 1994 season-long steers, whole season'; 'Yearlings 1.51 ... would be SERIOUS | [W22] HPAL crested wheatgrass, unsupplemented'. Grings et al. 2002 attribute the low late-season gains to forage quality that 'had substantially declined'. Currie et al. 1989 (daily automatic weights, 1986-87): predicted live weight peaked in late July to early August and declined through the end of the September grazing period in 1986. Manual weighings from 1983-87 showed lower gain in the second half of summer every year. UNL BeefWatch 2022: 'Forage quality and yearling rate of gain decline throughout the summer, particularly in cool season grasses.' Gillespie et al. 2014 (Sandhills): unsupplemented yearling heifers gained 1.17 lb/d in 2011 and 0.73 lb/d in the 2012 drought. Diet CP fell from 9.5% in May to 6.3% in August. Weighing-condition error, from the run: '[D14] Jun-Aug vs Sep overnight shrink gap (8.9% vs 7.1%) on a 780-lb yearling (lb) = 14.0 ... 57 d 0.25'; '[W12] mean full-weight offset, pasture steers (lb) = 37.0 ... 57 d 0.65'. Watson et al. 2013: 'handling cattle in a similar manner when weighing is more important than limiting intakes to decrease variance between weights'.
rules.limitations: A fixed whole-season target applied to a late-summer interval (Jul 20-Sep 15 in the shipped data) flags normal seasonal decline as 'serious'. In Grings 2002 it would have fired in a near-normal precipitation year (1995). The 80% cut-off has no published basis. Nothing records whether both weigh-ins were taken under the same conditions, and a one-sided fill shift of 14-37 lb moves a 57-day group ADG by 0.25-0.65 lb/d. The mean of per-animal ADGs is not checked for mixed intervals or coverage (other auditors cover these code defects). The action text never says to check the weighing conditions.
rules.configurable: Yes. RULES.adgSerious and groups.csv target_adg_lbs are plain values. The 80% share should stay configurable because it is a management tolerance, but the target it multiplies should become period-specific (see the proposed period-expectation rule).
rules.missing_data_blocks: Do not give a confident group verdict when the weight basis or gather time of either weigh-in is unknown or differs between them, the interval is shorter than the ranch's minimum (see the interval rule), fewer than the configured share of inventory head have matched pairs, animals in the group have different intervals, or no period-specific expectation exists. Show 'gain not assessable' with the reason rather than silence or 'serious'.
rules.recommendation: Keep the rule but present it as a ranch-set tolerance against a period-specific expected ADG, preferably from the ranch's own past weigh-ins for that pasture and season. Show the ADG with the interval, coverage and weighing basis. Downgrade to 'below expected - verify' when weigh conditions differ or are unknown. Add 'confirm both weigh-ins used the same gather/shrink routine' to the action text. Do not describe 80% as an industry standard.

rules.rule: CURRENT: Individual 'warning' when an animal's ADG between its last two weigh-ins is < 50% of the group target (RULES.animalShare 0.5). Suppressed when the group is already serious. Action text: 'Pull and check these animals at the next gather'.
rules.decision_supported: Which individual animals to look at closely at the next gather (observation, records, escalation to the herd veterinarian when observations warrant).
rules.required_inputs: At least two (preferably three or more) weights per animal over an adequate span; weight basis and gather time; animal ID that is stable across weigh-ins (visual tag + EID); class and lactation status; observation notes.

context.class: Growing cattle judged on ADG (demo: Yearlings target 2.0 lb/d, Heifers 1.0 lb/d)

rules.context_research: All weighed classes. The noise problem is worst for low-target classes (first-calf heifers at 1.0 lb/d) and for short intervals.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C). The research's sensitivity sweep (assumed noise levels) estimated about 2 false individual flags per 150 yearlings per weigh-in at the demo's 57-day interval; BIF test standards require at least 70 days for individual ADG.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (gain.evidence.research.mjs): 'Gap between target and the individual threshold: yearlings 1.00 lb/d, heifers 0.50 lb/d.' Individual worst cases at the shipped 57-d interval: '[W12] individual full vs limit-fed weight, high end (lb) 99 lb -> ... 57d 1.74'; '[W13] 2-day full-fed re-weigh difference, low end (-14 kg) -31 lb -> ... 57d -0.54'. Shipped data: 'Heifers ... animals under: 32' (of 45) and 'Yearlings ... animals under: 6'. The earlier sensitivity sweep (node docs/audit/diagnostics/gain.noise.research.mjs, assumed noise levels) printed 'interval 57 d, noise 2% BW: mean false individual flags per weigh-in = 2.0 of 150' and 'interval 28 d, noise 2% BW: ... 15.1 of 150'. BIF feed-efficiency guidelines (2019): 'a minimum of a 70-d test period is required to accurately compute average daily gain for individual animals', with two start and two end weights on separate days. Archer et al. 1997: a 70-d test with weights every 2 weeks was optimal for growth rate.
rules.limitations: A single full weight at each end of a 57-day interval can carry individual errors comparable to, or larger than, the 1.0 lb/d (yearling) or 0.5 lb/d (heifer) gap between target and threshold. Some flagged animals will be on target. The fixed 50% share has no published basis. Hiding individuals when the group is flagged also hides any animal that is actually losing weight (covered by another auditor as a design limit). 'Pull' implies sorting and handling. For range cattle a lower-cost first step is to observe and record at the next gather.
rules.configurable: Yes (RULES.animalShare). Also make these configurable: minimum interval, minimum number of weights, and whether lactating classes are included at all.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Do not list an individual as slow when the interval is under the configured minimum (BIF uses 70 d for individual ADG under controlled test conditions), when the animal has fewer than two valid weights or a weight is blank or implausible, when weigh conditions differ between the two weigh-ins, or for lactating first-calf heifers (use BCS instead).
rules.recommendation: Reword as 'Observe at next gather' and require persistence: slow in two consecutive intervals, or a regression over 3 or more weights spanning at least about 70 d. Alternatively rank the bottom X% within the group (relative to herd-mates weighed under the same conditions) rather than a fixed share of a fixed target. Record what was observed. Escalate to the herd veterinarian per the ranch's health plan. No diagnosis or treatment is implied by the list.
rules.phase_note: Use the minimum-interval gate (RULE-GAIN-07) and reword the action to observe, record and escalate (RULE-HLTH-11). The six planted slow yearlings must still appear: the demo has three weigh-ins and a 57-day last interval, so choose and test the phase-1 default with that in mind. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

rules.rule: CURRENT: Yearling steer target ADG = 2.0 lb/d, applied to any interval (groups.csv).
rules.decision_supported: Expected performance benchmark for yearlings on summer grass, used to judge group and individual gain.
rules.required_inputs: Forage type (native range vs. improved/introduced cool-season pasture), supplementation, grazing period dates, stocking rate, precipitation/forage outlook, ranch history for the pasture.

context.season: Whole grazing season vs shorter intervals
context.geography: Northern Great Plains
context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15)

rules.context_research: Northern/Central Plains native range, roughly mid-May to early October. Published season-long gains in many years fall around 1.9-2.6 lb/d, but late-season and drought-year gains fall well below.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker gain dispute 3: 2.0 lb/d is reasonable as a season-average figure (Grings whole-season 2.36-2.62; Cheng 1.90-2.51 lb/d), which is B. Applying a season figure to any sub-season interval has no support, and the research's own sources show late-period gains of 1.30-1.46 lb/d. The rule as implemented is the demo's simplification, so the stricter class D applies; the season-average value alone is B.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (gain.evidence.research.mjs, kg x 2.2046): Grings 2002 whole-season 2.62 / 2.36 / 2.45 lb/d (1993-95), but late periods 2.45 / 1.30 / 1.46. Cheng et al. 2022 (CPER, Colorado, 2014-18): traditional management 0.86-1.14 kg/d = 1.90-2.51 lb/d, adaptive rotation 0.74-1.00 kg/d = 1.63-2.20 lb/d. HPAL crested wheatgrass unsupplemented 1.51 lb/d. Sandhills spayed yearling heifers 1.17 / 0.73 lb/d. Reeves et al. 2013 (Cheyenne WY, 1982-2011) found cattle not grazed in 1989, 2000 and 2002 because of drought. Reeves et al. 2014 (Mandan ND, 1936-2005) report that seasonal weather explained up to 74% (R2 0.44-0.74) of variation in steer beef production per hectare (not per-head ADG).
rules.limitations: 2.0 lb/d is inside the published season-long range for good years. Applied flat to a single late-summer interval, it overstates expectations. It also ignores forage type, supplementation and year. Steer data are not directly transferable to heifers.
rules.configurable: Yes. It should be set per period (early/late season) and per pasture/forage type, ideally from the ranch's own records.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without the period dates and forage/pasture context, label the comparison 'against a season-average target' rather than treating a shortfall as a problem.
rules.recommendation: Replace the single target with an expected-ADG table by period (for example turnout-mid July and mid July-removal) and pasture type. Seed it with the ranch's own history and show the source of each expectation. A flat 2.0 is acceptable for the fictional demo only if labelled as a season-average illustration.
rules.phase_note: Label 2.0 lb/d as a demo season-average target. The gates in RULE-GAIN-06 and -07 limit misuse; period-specific expectations (RULE-GAIN-08) are deferred. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

rules.decision_supported: Whether young lactating cows are being fed well enough to keep growing and rebreed.
rules.required_inputs: BCS (1-9) at the standard scoring times; calving date and lactation status; pregnancy diagnosis; optional weight paired with BCS at weaning.

context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15)

rules.context_research: 2-year-old cows nursing their first calf on summer range, often during or just after the breeding season. The UNL BCS guide puts them at about 85% of mature weight at calving.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D). No source sets 1.0 lb/d for first-calf heifers; the supported measure is body condition (about BCS 6 at calving).
rules.evidence: No extension or research source located in this pass sets a summer ADG target for lactating first-calf heifers. The standard monitoring tool is BCS: UNL (2020) and SDSU (2022) both target BCS 6 for first-calf heifers (5 for mature cows). Published weight change of lactating young cows on Plains range, from gain.evidence.research.mjs: 'Heifers -0.15 vs serious < 0.80: would be SERIOUS | [L18] Sandhills 2-yr-old primiparous cows, ~5 Aug-pregnancy dx, unsupplemented'; 'Heifers 0.18 ... [L18] same, supplemented'. Pregnancy rate did not differ (75% vs 81%, P = 0.41; Lansford et al. 2018). Lactating cows (pairs) on native range at NDSU Dickinson 1983-86 gained 0.25-0.82 lb/d (mean 0.59). That class is not identical to first-calf heifers. Shipped data: 'Heifers ... mean ADG 0.44 ... group serious < 0.80' and 'animals under: 32'.
rules.limitations: With a 1.0 lb/d target, the rule flags weight changes that published Plains studies report as typical for lactating young cows (about -0.15 to +0.8 lb/d). An experienced ranch reader would see the planted 'heifers gaining well under target' alert as a likely false alarm, which hurts the portfolio's credibility. The individual threshold (0.5 lb/d) is inside weighing noise (see the individual rule).
rules.configurable: Yes. Better: make 'judged on ADG' a per-class switch and judge this class on BCS.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without BCS, calving date and lactation status, do not issue a nutrition verdict on first-calf heifers from weights alone.
rules.recommendation: Set the first-calf heifer ADG target to 'not judged', like cows. Add BCS records with target BCS 6 at calving (configurable) and score at weaning, about 90 d pre-calving, at calving and at breeding start. Keep any weights as context, paired with BCS. If the demo must show a heifer alert, plant it as BCS below target before calving.
rules.phase_note: Label 1.0 lb/d as a demo setting with no source. The BCS-based replacement is RULE-CTX-12 (deferred). The planted heifer problem must still be found. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Effect of Supplementation during the Breeding Season on a May-calving Herd in the Nebraska Sandhills
sources.supports: 2-yr-old primiparous cows (n = 135) at Gudmundsen Sandhills Lab. ADG from prebreeding to pregnancy diagnosis was -0.15 lb/d unsupplemented and 0.18 supplemented. Pregnancy 75% vs 81% (P = 0.41).

sources.title: Complementary Rotation Grazing System in Western North Dakota (Project 1906; file named 'Pasture Management for Western North Dakota')
sources.supports: Table 4: cow ADG on native range was 0.82, 0.25, 0.50 and 0.78 lb/d (mean 0.59) while nursing calves. That native range was a three-pasture twice-over rotation. sources.checker_note: 'Complementary Rotation Grazing System in Western North Dakota', Project 1906, by Manske, Conlon & Nelson. Publisher and date not stated; data run through 1986. rules.rule: CURRENT: Cows (cow-calf pairs) target 0.0, so the gain rules skip them ('if (!g.target) continue'). No other cow condition measure exists.
rules.decision_supported: Whether mature cows need nutritional attention ahead of calving or breeding.
rules.required_inputs: BCS (1-9) by cow or by sampled group, date, scorer; optional cow weight at weaning paired with BCS.

context.season: All year; key points at weaning and before calving
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: No condition records in the demo

rules.context_research: Mature beef cows on Plains range. Weight swings with gut fill, pregnancy and lactation, so condition is tracked by BCS.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from A. Checker gain dispute 0: only the narrow point 'do not judge mature cows on ADG' is general guidance. The supported practice is to monitor cows by body condition score (UNL, SDSU, Angus AHIR), and the current rule does neither: it silently skips 180 head. rules.evidence: OBSERVED (gain.evidence.research.mjs): 'Cows: inventory 180, target 0 -> skipped by 'if (!g.target) continue'; weights.csv rows for Cows: 0; no BCS field exists in any CSV.' Extension sources monitor cows by BCS (UNL 2020; SDSU 2022). Breed-association recording pairs cow weight with BCS around weaning: Angus AHIR says 'Dams must be weighed 45 days before or after weaning a calf' and 'Dams should be scored 45 days before or after weaning'.
rules.limitations: Not judging cows on ADG is the supported practice. But the dashboard then has no cow condition signal at all, and 'target 0' reads as 'no gain expected' rather than 'judged on BCS'.
rules.configurable: Yes. Make it an explicit per-class 'metric: ADG | BCS | none' setting instead of overloading target 0.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a recent BCS (for example none since weaning, or none within ~90 d of calving), show 'condition not recorded', not 'no exceptions'.
rules.recommendation: Add a bcs.csv (group or tag, date, score, scorer). Add a rule that flags a group when its median or share-below-target BCS misses a ranch-set target at the standard scoring times (default 5 for mature cows, 6 for first-calf heifers).
rules.phase_note: Copy only: say on the page that cows are not monitored by the gain rules and that no body condition records exist. The BCS module is deferred (RULE-CTX-12).

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Weigh-condition consistency gate. Every weigh-in records its weight basis (full, overnight-shrunk, pencil shrink %), gather/weigh time and hours off feed/water. ADG is only compared across weigh-ins with the same basis and routine, or after a stated adjustment.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a change in weight reflects tissue gain or a change in gut fill and handling.
rules.required_inputs: weight_basis, pencil_shrink_pct, gather_time/weigh_time, hours_off_feed_water, handling notes per weigh session.

context.class: Growing cattle judged on ADG (demo: Yearlings target 2.0 lb/d, Heifers 1.0 lb/d)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15); full or shrunk weights

rules.context_research: All classes. Matters most for short intervals, lush versus mature forage, and lactating cows.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from A. Checker gain dispute 4: weighing under consistent conditions is well supported (A), but the gate behaviour (withholding serious and individual flags when the basis is unknown or differs) and the session metadata schema are design choices (C).
rules.evidence: Watson et al. 2013: 'handling cattle in a similar manner when weighing is more important than limiting intakes to decrease variance between weights'. Heitschmidt 1982 (Texas Experimental Ranch keyword, mature cows): early-morning weights were ~2.5% below late-morning weights, and cows lost 3.5% in the first 3 h, then ~1% every 3 h. OSU ANSI-3257: cattle gathered at 6 a.m. shrank 6.2% by 3 p.m. versus 3.3% when gathered at 9 a.m. Mississippi State P2577: ~1%/h for the first 3-4 h without feed and water, then ~0.25%/h; '2 percent to 4 percent pencil shrink' is common in sales. Derner et al. 2014: summer overnight shrink 8.8-9.0% vs 7.1% in September at CPER (its main finding was that shrink was insensitive to environmental variables, which sits uneasily with Derner 2016). Derner et al. 2016: shrink increased with air temperature and NDVI. OBSERVED consistency check: '[W12] pasture heifers, mean full-vs-limit-fed difference 10.2 lb over 20 d -> 0.51 lb/d (report states 0.51)'.
evidence_corrections: Derner et al. 2014 found overnight shrink 'insensitive to environmental variables'; the research does not reconcile this with its Derner 2016 citation.
Watson 2012 (Nebraska Beef Report) states its data years: four weighing events, October 2009 to May 2011.
rules.limitations: Most of the shrink rates come from shipping/sale contexts or from other regions (Texas, Mississippi, Oklahoma). Magnitudes vary with forage, weather and handling, so no single pencil-shrink value applies to every weigh-in.
rules.configurable: Yes. The ranch picks a standard routine and an optional pencil shrink.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If the basis is unknown for either weigh-in, or differs between them, mark ADG 'unverified' and do not raise group-serious or individual flags from it.
rules.recommendation: Add weigh-session metadata. Show a 'weighing conditions differ' note beside any ADG.
rules.phase_note: Add weight_basis per weigh session. The demo must record a basis (for example 'full') for every session so the planted gain problems still show. Comparisons across different or unknown bases become CAN'T TELL for serious and individual flags. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Diurnal Variation in Weight and Rates of Shrink of Range Cows and Calves (J. Range Manage. 35:717-720)
sources.publisher: Society for Range Management (Rangelands Gateway / Univ. of Arizona repository)
sources.supports: Early vs late morning cow weights differ by ~2.5%. Shrink rates over time.
sources.checker_note: Heitschmidt, J. Range Manage. 35(6):717-720 (1982). Verbatim: 'Early morning weights of mature Hereford/Angus crossbred cows were approximately 2.5% less than late morning weights'; 'Rate of weight loss was approximately 1% every 3 hours after an initial 3 hour loss of 3.5%.' Suckling calf weights did not differ between early and late morning. Location appears only in keywords (Texas Experimental Ranch, Rolling Plains). Study years are not stated. Applying the figure to young cows is the research's own labelled extrapolation.

sources.title: Managing Shrink and Weighing Conditions in Beef Cattle (ANSI-3257)
sources.supports: Gather-time effect (6.2% vs 3.3%), ~1%/h then 0.25%/h, ~0.5% per 30 min of corral movement, and a 2-3% shrink assumption for cattle near the scales.
sources.checker_note: 'Managing Shrink and Weighing Conditions in Beef Cattle' by Barnes, Smith & Lalman, OSU Extension, undated (footer 0607). Table 4: shrink to 3 p.m. was 6.2% for a 6 a.m. gather vs 3.3% for a 9 a.m. gather. 'Cattle will lose approximately 1% of their body weight per hour for the first three to four hours and then .25% an hour for the next eight to ten hours.' 'for every 30 minutes ... moved around in a corral, expect an additional .5% weight loss.' 'one can probably assume 2-3% shrink from actual pasture weight.' Cited studies run from 1972 (Self and Gay) to 1997 (Coffey et al.).

sources.title: Understanding and Managing Cattle Shrink (P2577)
sources.supports: Fill vs tissue shrink, hourly shrink rates, and the common 2-4% pencil shrink.
sources.checker_note: P2577 'Understanding and Managing Cattle Shrink' by Jane Parish & Justin Rhinehart, reviewed by Brandi Karisch; code POD-12-23, no explicit date. Verbatim: 'cattle shrink about 1 percent per hour for the first 3 to 4 hours and then roughly 0.25 percent per hour for the next 8 to 10 hours.' 'Many board sales and private treaty contracts are based on a 2 percent to 4 percent pencil shrink.' The page distinguishes fill from tissue shrink.

sources.title: Estimating Overnight Weight Loss of Corralled Yearling Steers in Semiarid Rangeland (Rangelands 38(3):101-104)
sources.data_years: four consecutive years (not named on page)
sources.supports: Percent overnight shrink rose with air temperature and NDVI. A prediction equation 'can provide temporal weight gain data within a grazing season'.
sources.checker_note: Derner, Reeves, Mortenson, West, Irisarri & Durante, Rangelands 38(3):101-104 (2016), doi 10.1016/j.rala.2016.02.004. Shrink 'was influenced positively by air temperature and NDVI values, but not relative humidity'. Steers were weighed 'for four consecutive years'. A prediction equation 'can provide temporal weight gain data within a grazing season'. No location on the page (keyword 'shortgrass steppe'). See the Derner 2014 note on the apparent tension between the two.

sources.title: Do Environmental Variables Influence Overnight Weight Loss of Yearling Steers in Semiarid Rangelands
sources.supports: 8.8-9.0% (Jun-Aug) vs 7.1% (Sep) overnight shrink.
sources.checker_note: Derner, Mortenson & West, SRM annual meeting abstract, Orlando 2014. CPER, Nunn CO; 2009-2012 summers; 16 weighings (Jun/Jul/Aug/Sep x 4 yr). Overnight shrink was 8.8-9.0% for June-August combined and 7.1% for September (confirmed). Caveat the research does not mention: this abstract's main finding is that 'Overnight shrink in yearlings was insensitive to environmental variables', which sits awkwardly beside the research's use of Derner 2016 (shrink rose with temperature and NDVI).

sources.title: Impacts of a limit-feeding procedure on variation and accuracy of cattle weights
sources.publisher: American Society of Animal Science (UNL Digital Commons)
sources.supports: Similar handling matters more than limit feeding.
sources.checker_note: Watson, Nuttelman, Klopfenstein, Lomas & Erickson, J. Anim. Sci. 91:5507-5517 (2013), doi 10.2527/jas2013-6349; 18 experiments. Abstract: 'Differences between 2 d of FFW were -14 to +34 kg in the 10 experiments measuring FFW on 2 consecutive d'. 'Differences between LFW and FFW ADG were -0.29 to +0.31 kg/d.' The full-text PDF (viewcontent.cgi?article=1802) confirms both are INDIVIDUAL-animal ranges: Results give -13.6 to +34.1 kg (mean 4.6 kg) and ADG 'ranged between -0.292 and +0.313 kg/d for individual animals' (mean 0.082 kg/d). The 10 two-day experiments were at Kansas State. The quoted sentence is accurate but truncated. In full: 'handling cattle in a similar manner when weighing is more important than limiting intakes to decrease variance between weights' (i.e., about variance).

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Minimum interval / number of weights before ADG is judged. Individual ADG needs at least about 70 d, or a regression on 3 or more weights. Group ADG needs an interval long enough that a plausible one-sided weighing error stays under a chosen share of the expectation.
rules.decision_supported: Whether an ADG figure is precise enough to act on.
rules.required_inputs: Weigh dates; count of weights per animal; ranch-chosen tolerance; an estimate of the weighing error for its routine.

context.class: Growing cattle judged on ADG (demo: Yearlings target 2.0 lb/d, Heifers 1.0 lb/d)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15)

rules.context_research: All weighed classes, on any scale.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker gain dispute 5: the 70-day individual default comes from controlled-diet test standards (BIF 2019; Archer 1997), an extrapolation to pasture (B). The group minimum is the author's arithmetic on a ranch-chosen tolerance (C). The bundled rule takes the stricter class C.
rules.evidence: BIF 2019: 70-d minimum for individual ADG with paired start and end weights on separate days. Archer 1997: 70 d with 2-week weights is optimal. OBSERVED (gain.evidence.research.mjs) minimum days for error within 10% / 20% of target: '[D14] ... yearlings(2.0): 10% 71 d, 20% 36 d | heifers(1.0): 10% 141 d, 20% 71 d'; '[W12] mean full-weight offset, pasture steers (lb) yearlings(2.0): 10% 185 d, 20% 93 d'. Error rows at 57 d: 0.18, 0.25, 0.48 and 0.65 lb/d for the four error sources. Augustine et al. 2022 (CPER) used ~53-60-d intervals with weights corrected for estimated overnight shrink.
evidence_corrections: Citation critic (critic-rules, 2026-10-16), WebFetch re-read of the BIF guidelines: 'a minimum of a 70-d test period is required to accurately compute average daily gain for individual animals', with animals weighed twice on separate days at the start and end; regression 'may enhance the accuracy of measured rate of gain somewhat'. BIF uses regression inside a test of at least 70 days. It does not say a regression on 3 or more weights over a shorter span replaces the 70-day minimum, so the 'or a regression' path should still span at least the minimum. BIF tests also require ad libitum feed, unlike pasture.
rules.limitations: The error magnitudes used come from published studies under other conditions. A ranch should estimate its own, for example from repeat weights of the same animals. BIF test conditions (controlled diet) are stricter than pasture conditions.
rules.configurable: Yes: minimum days, minimum weights per animal, tolerance.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Below the minimum, show ADG as 'provisional' and raise no flag.
rules.recommendation: Add RULES.minIntervalDaysIndividual (default 70) and RULES.minIntervalDaysGroup (ranch-set; the README must state the basis). Prefer regression when 3 or more weights exist.
rules.phase_note: Lead default 'gain minimum interval'. Make the minimum a labelled setting and check it against the demo's 57-day last interval and three weigh-ins so the planted heifer and six-yearling problems remain. The demo weigh-ins (2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15) span 106 days, so a 70-day individual default is met only by a method that uses all three weigh-ins; an ADG from the last 57-day interval alone falls under it (not tested in this audit). The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Beef Improvement Federation Guidelines for Feed Efficiency Testing as of March 26th, 2019
sources.publisher: Beef Improvement Federation (vendor-hosted copy, C-Lock Inc.)
sources.url: https://docs.c-lockinc.com/Document - Beef Improvement Federation Guidelines for FE Testing.pdf
sources.supports: 70-d minimum for individual ADG.
sources.checker_note: Title: 'Beef Improvement Federation Guidelines for Feed Efficiency Testing as of March 26th, 2019'. Verbatim: 'a minimum of a 70-d test period is required to accurately compute average daily gain for individual animals'; 'At a minimum animals should be weighed twice (on separate days) at the beginning and at the end of the test period'; regression 'may enhance the accuracy of measured rate of gain somewhat.' The document names no author or host. It is a vendor-hosted copy (C-Lock), as the research says. The guideline is for controlled feed-efficiency tests, not pasture monitoring. As the evidence_url for weights.tag it only indirectly supports per-animal pairing; it says nothing about tag uniqueness.
sources.critic_recheck: Re-read 2026-10-16 (critic-rules, WebFetch): 'a minimum of a 70-d test period is required to accurately compute average daily gain for individual animals'; weigh twice on separate days at start and end; regression 'may enhance the accuracy ... somewhat'; ad libitum feed required. Confirmed; the 70 d is a controlled-feeding test length.

sources.title: Optimum postweaning test for measurement of growth rate, feed intake, and feed efficiency in British breed cattle
sources.publisher: American Society of Animal Science (University of Adelaide repository)
sources.supports: 70-d test, fortnightly weights.
sources.checker_note: Archer, Arthur, Herd, Parnell & Pitchford, J. Anim. Sci. 75(8):2024-2032 (1997). Abstract: 'a 35-d test was sufficient for measurement of feed intake'; 'a 70-d test was required to measure growth rate, feed conversion, and residual feed intake'; 'minimal loss in accuracy when weights are collected every 2 wk instead of weekly'; 5-wk intervals 'caused a decline in the accuracy'. Data: 760 progeny of 78 sires (postweaning tests; years not stated). Supports the weights.date (interval) field.

sources.title: Can measurements of foraging behaviour predict variation in weight gains of free-ranging cattle? (Animal Production Science)
sources.supports: Rangeland research practice: interval ADG over ~53-60 d, weights corrected for estimated overnight shrink.
sources.checker_note: Augustine, Raynor, Kearney & Derner, Animal Production Science 2022 (doi 10.1071/AN21560; volume not shown in the PDF), CPER, 2019-2020. Steers were weighed '53 days before the end of the 2019 grazing season, 59 days after the start of the 2020 grazing season, and 60 days prior to the end of the 2020 season'. They were weighed 'without overnight restriction' and 'corrected for estimated overnight shrinkage following Derner et al. (2016)'. Individual ADG SD and range are not reported.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Period-specific expected ADG. The expectation used by the group rule depends on season segment, forage type, supplementation and the current year's forage outlook.
rules.decision_supported: Separating a management or health problem from normal seasonal and weather-driven decline.
rules.required_inputs: Expected ADG by period and pasture (ranch history); supplementation flag; Grass-Cast or drought status as context.

context.class: Growing cattle judged on ADG (demo: Yearlings target 2.0 lb/d, Heifers 1.0 lb/d)
context.season: Early, mid and late season segments; supplemented or not
context.geography: Northern Great Plains; year-to-year forage variation
context.management: Group weigh-ins on a chute scale (demo: 2026-06-01, 2026-07-20, 2026-09-15)

rules.context_research: Northern/Central Plains summer grazing.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: Grings 2002 late-period values (1.30, 1.46 lb/d in 1994 and 1995) versus whole-season values (2.36-2.62). Currie 1989 found a decline from late July to September. Gillespie 2014 found a 1.17 vs 0.73 lb/d year effect. Reeves 2014: weather explains R2 0.44-0.74 of beef production per hectare (not per-head ADG). The Grass-Cast About page says it is 'updated every two weeks' at 10 km x 10 km, is experimental, and should not be the 'sole source for making management decisions'.
rules.limitations: Ranch-specific history is needed. Public forecasts are experimental and county or grid scale, so they cannot set a herd's expected ADG by themselves.
rules.configurable: Yes.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If no period expectation exists, compare only to the ranch's own prior years for the same period, or report the ADG without a verdict.
rules.recommendation: Replace groups.csv target_adg_lbs with an expectations table (group, pasture or forage type, start_date, end_date, expected_adg, source).
rules.phase_note: Needs a gain_expectations table built for a real ranch; the demo cannot validate it. It is the main accuracy follow-up for the gain rules.

sources.title: About Our Maps (Grass-Cast)
sources.publisher: Grass-Cast (USDA-ARS, National Drought Mitigation Center, Colorado State Univ., Univ. of Arizona)
sources.supports: Experimental, 10 km grid, updated every two weeks. Does not account for local management or species. Not to be used as a sole decision source.
sources.checker_note: Verbatim: 'is updated every two weeks'. Cell size is '10 km x 10km'. 'This new experimental grassland forecast'. 'Producers should not rely on Grass-Cast as a sole source for making management decisions'. It 'does not directly account for local management practices' and 'cannot tell the difference between desirable forage species and undesirable species'. Forecasts are percent change vs the cell's '38-year average' under three MJJA precipitation scenarios. White or gray cells mean no forecast. Partners: CSU, USDA, NDMC (UNL), Univ. of Arizona. The page is undated.

sources.title: Growth patterns of yearling steers determined from daily live weights
sources.supports: Gains lower in the second half of summer every year.
sources.checker_note: Currie, Volesky, Adams & Knapp, J. Range Manage. 42(5):393-396, issued 1989-09-01. Abstract: 'Forty steers were monitored during each summer grazing period of 1986 and 1987.' 'In 1986, predicted live weight of the steers peaked in late July to early August and then decreased through to the end of the grazing period in September.' In 1987 the pattern was similar, but 'the late summer decrease was not as great as in 1986.' Manual weighing showed 'a lower rate of gain ... in the second half than in the first half of the summer grazing period every year from 1983 through 1987.' The abstract also notes 'substantial within-day live weight variability among steers.' No location appears on the page (confirmed). The abstract has a '1996 and 1987' typo.

sources.title: Intensive-early stocking for yearling cattle in the Northern Great Plains
sources.supports: Late-period vs whole-season ADG.
sources.checker_note: Grings, Heitschmidt, Short & Haferkamp, J. Range Manage. 55(2):135-138, March 2002, Fort Keogh (Miles City MT), 1993-1995. Table 6 'ADG after IES period' (season-long steers): 1993 1.11, 1994 0.59, 1995 0.66 kg/d. Table 1 dates: IES removed 17 Sep 1993 / 15 Jul 1994 / 4 Aug 1995; SS removed 4 Oct / 8 Sep / 26 Sep, so the late periods are as the research states. Whole-season SS ADG was 1.19, 1.07 and 1.11 kg/d. Precipitation: 'May through August 1993 was about 169% of normal'; 'Precipitation in 1994 was 44% of normal'; 1995 'close (104%) to the average'. Quote: 'forage quality had substantially declined in 1994 and 1995 ... and associated gains of season-long stocking steers were reduced in the second half of the grazing season.' 1993 IES ran to 17 Sep because forage was 'visibly above average'. All conversions in the diagnostic (x2.2046 gives 2.45/1.30/1.46 and 2.62/2.36/2.45 lb/d) match.

rules.rule: PROPOSED (class not in current data): Replacement heifer target-weight rule. Required ADG = (target % of mature BW x mature BW - current BW) / days to breeding start. Flag when the projected breeding weight falls short of the ranch's target.
rules.decision_supported: Whether developing heifers will reach the ranch's chosen breeding weight in time.
rules.required_inputs: Mature cow weight estimate (own cows, weighed with BCS), target % (ranch choice), breeding start date, current weights.

context.class: Replacement heifers (a class not in the demo data)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)

rules.context_research: Yearling replacement heifers in winter and spring development, before a spring or summer breeding season.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: SDSU (Grussing, updated 2021-10-25): '55 - 65% of mature weight by breeding'. Worked example: a 1,400-lb mature cow and 60% gives an 840-lb target. A 600-lb heifer then needs 240 lb over 151 d (the article states 1.5 lb/d; 240/151 = 1.59). UNL BeefWatch 2024: GSL data 2005-2019 (1,434 heifers and cows) at 50-70% of mature BW. Heifers at 60-70% had higher initial and 2-yr-old pregnancy rates, with no effect at ages 3-5. UNL G2215 (2013): lower-input systems target 50-57% vs the traditional 60-65%. SDSU (Ricardo, updated 2026-07-10): about 65% at breeding and 80% by calving historically; lower-input 50-55% with ADG ~1.0-1.5 lb/d. MU G2091 (2021): 65% traditional; 1.5 lb/d during development.
rules.limitations: The target % is a ranch trade-off between cost and reproduction. Mature-weight estimates are uncertain.
rules.configurable: Yes: target %, mature weight, breeding date.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without a mature-weight estimate and a breeding date, no projection.
rules.recommendation: Optional future feature. The repo's 'Heifers' group is first-calf heifers, so do not relabel it as replacements.

rules.context_research: Portable load-bar scales at ranch working facilities.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker gain dispute 1: no cited source recommends zeroing plus a known-weight check every session for ranch scales. 9 CFR 201.72 covers trade weighing only, PAMI 654 is 1991 equipment evidence, and the Gallagher manual is a vendor statement.
rules.evidence: PAMI Evaluation Report 654 (July 1991) tested four livestock scales. One read 2% low to 1% high in final tests (about 2% high, or 20 lb on a 1,000-lb animal, initially). Re-zeroing was needed every ~15-50 cattle depending on model. Cold could cause a ~0.4% low reading. 9 CFR 201.72 requires scales used in trade under the Packers and Stockyards Act to be tested at least twice each calendar year, at least 120 days apart. The Gallagher load bar manual (vendor; Ed. 12, Mar 2014) states the product is 'not certified for trade use' and that uneven mounting 'may result in weighing errors'. The Tru-Test indicator info sheet (vendor; REV 12192023) gives no accuracy figure.
rules.limitations: PAMI tested 1991-era equipment. Current scales may perform differently, and no current independent test was located. 9 CFR 201.72 covers trade weighing, not ranch performance weighing.
rules.configurable: Yes: check-weight tolerance.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If no check is recorded for a session, mark its ADGs 'scale not checked' (informational, not blocking).
rules.recommendation: Add session metadata. Do not import vendor-computed ADG without the underlying weights.

sources.title: Livestock Scales (Evaluation Report 654)

Four scales: Elias, Paul, Prairie Systems, Senstek. Elias initially 'read about 2% higher' (about 20 lb on 1,000 lb) and in final tests 2% lower to 1% higher. Re-zeroing was needed about every 20 (Elias), 50 (Paul) and 15 (Prairie Systems, Senstek) cattle. Senstek: 'cold temperatures could cause the displayed weight to read about 0.4% lower'.

rules.context_research: Treats every task type, cattle class and season the same way. One date per row; there is no window, no source for the date and no task type.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D). The demo booster is 105 days after the first dose, against the label's usual 2-4 week window, so 'Schedule it this week' does not fit the case.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (node docs/audit/diagnostics/health.schedule.research.mjs): 'serious | Yearlings: Booster vaccine | Overdue by 15 days (due 2026-09-15) | action: "Schedule it this week"'. OBSERVED: 'Booster: last_done 2026-06-02 -> next_due 2026-09-15 = 105 days apart'. SOURCES: the BQA National Manual says 'almost all products recommend a second vaccination two (2) to four (4) weeks after the initial vaccination' and 'Follow all FDA/USDA/EPA guidelines and label directions'. UC Davis (Maas 2008) says booster needs are reviewed by USDA at licensing and 'will therefore, be on the label and should be followed', and that without the timed second dose the vaccine 'will probably not stimulate an effective immune response'. INFERENCE: lateness that matters for a label-driven booster is lateness against the label or vet window, not against a ranch-entered date. A 105-day gap does not fit the 2-4 week primary-series pattern. Either the row is a different kind of revaccination or the date is not from a label, and the data cannot show which.
rules.limitations: No task type, so a missed observation check and a missed label booster window get the same severity and the same action. No window_end or schedule_source, so 'Overdue' cannot say whether the label window is gone. The status match is exact: healthbudget.repro.mjs H-01 OBSERVED that status 'Open', 'OPEN' and 'open ' all give '(no alerts)' on a task 15 days late. 'Schedule it this week' implies a late booster can simply be given, which is a label and veterinarian question. None of the fetched sources gives a general rule on whether a late dose still counts.
rules.configurable: Partly. Keep an overdue flag. Severity and wording should depend on task_type and schedule_source (product_label / vet_plan / ranch_plan) rather than being one global rule.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without window_end and schedule_source the dashboard must not word a vaccination row as if the window is still usable. Without task_type it must not reuse vaccination wording for observation checks.
rules.recommendation: Compute overdue against window_end rather than a single next_due. For vaccination or parasite tasks whose window came from the label or vet plan and has passed: 'The window on the [label/vet plan] closed N days ago. Check the label and ask your veterinarian how to proceed before scheduling.' For ranch-plan tasks: 'Past the planned date. Reschedule with [responsible].' For observation tasks: 'No check recorded since [date]. Look the group over on the next pasture check and record what you see.' The rules table and README should say the threshold is a demonstration setting.
rules.phase_note: Normalise status first (RULE-HLTH-03). Keep the overdue booster found. Reword the action to scheduling plus 'check the label or your veterinarian's plan for the booster window', and label the severity as a demo setting. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Beef Quality Assurance National Manual (bqa_manual_final.pdf)
sources.publisher: Beef Quality Assurance program (the PDF names no publisher; 'Funded by Beef Farmers and Ranchers'; NCBA is the Beef Checkoff contractor)
sources.pub_date: undated (no date in the PDF; newest data cited are the 2016 NBQA, a 2018 footnote and a 1998-2017 series). Likely superseded: NCBA announced an updated manual on 2024-12-19 (2025-01-06 is a trade-press reprint date), and bqa.org now links a 2026 edition that could not be fetched.
sources.data_years: newest data cited: 2016 National Beef Quality Audit; a 1998-2017 series
sources.supports: Sec. 4.4 Vaccinations (p.47 per fetch): 'almost all products recommend a second vaccination two (2) to four (4) weeks after the initial vaccination'. p.42: 'Follow all FDA/USDA/EPA guidelines and label directions for each product.' p.44: booster vaccinations follow the herd health plan.
sources.checker_note: I fetched it three times. Every quoted claim was found. Sec 4.4 (pp.46-47): 'To establish immunity, almost all products recommend a second vaccination two (2) to four (4) weeks after the initial vaccination.' p.42 (also p.11): 'Follow all FDA/USDA/EPA guidelines and label directions for each product.' Sec 6.2 (pp.14-15) lists the individual record items, and group treatments record 'Group or lot identification' plus the same items. p.15: 'Keep records for a minimum of two years or longer as required by laws/regulations'. Ch.2 Temperature Conditions (pp.26-27): 'work them before the temperature humidity index (THI) reaches 84', 'Avoid handling cattle when the risk of heat stress is high', and 'Work cattle more prone to heat stress first, earlier in the day'. p.48: 'A VCPR cannot exist based solely on phone, video, or other telemedical interactions.' p.45: vaccines 'have either a 21 or 60 day withdrawal time'. p.42: VFD records are kept two years. Sec 4.3: 'Booster vaccinations as indicated in the herd health plan', 'Always read and follow label directions' and 'Keep records of all products administered including date, animal identification, product used, serial number, amount administered, route...'. Sec 4.5 (titled 'Judicious Use of Antimicrobials', not VCPR): protocols 'define when to quit treating and seek professional help'. Small drifts: the processing map (Sec 1.7.2, p.10) records 'where each injection was given', which is not 'how much'. The research cites the field guide for the withdrawal and sale point, but the manual gives stronger support: 'Verify withdrawal on any animals being sold' and 'Employ strict adherence to pre-harvest withdrawal periods'. METADATA PROBLEM: the PDF names no publisher. It shows only 'Funded by Beef Farmers and Ranchers'. NCBA's own release confirms that NCBA is a contractor to the Beef Checkoff. Its newest data are the 2016 NBQA, a 2018 'Unpublished' footnote and data for '1998 to 2017', which points to an edition from about 2019. NCBA announced an updated manual on 2024-12-19. The research's 2025-01-06 date is that of the trade-press reprints. bqa.org/resources/manuals now links bqa-national-manual-2026.pdf and does NOT link bqa_manual_final.pdf. The cited file is therefore very likely a superseded edition. My two fetches of the 2026 manual both failed with CLIENT_ERROR, so I could not confirm that the 2-4 week, THI 84, record-item, retention and VCPR wording is still in the current edition.
sources.metadata_note: Checker: likely superseded. bqa.org now links 2026 editions (NCBA announced an updated manual 2024-12-19); the 2026 manual could not be fetched, so claims are not re-verified against the current edition.

sources.checker_note: 'Booster Vaccines' by John Maas, DVM (UC Davis Extension Veterinarian), UCD Vet Views column in California Cattlemen's Magazine, October 2008. All three phrases appear verbatim: USDA 'will determine if the data meets their approval requirements. This will include the need for booster doses if appropriate'; 'The need for booster doses will therefore, be on the label and should be followed'; 'the vaccine will probably not stimulate an effective immune response'; and 'The best source of vaccine information is from your cattle veterinarian.'

rules.context_research: The same 7-day lead applies to every task. Vet-dependent work (pregnancy check), crew and gather work (boosters) and pasture observation (eye checks) all get one horizon and one action.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D).
rules.evidence: OBSERVED: 'warning | Cows: Pinkeye check | Due in 3 days (2026-10-03) | action: "Plan it with the next gather"'. OBSERVED (healthbudget.repro.mjs HB-C3): due in 7 days gives a warning and due in 8 days gives nothing. The code comment reads 'health task due within a week' and cites no source. SOURCES: NDSU 2025 says to check cattle closely in pasture for early pinkeye signs and that dust and crowding (tail switching) irritate eyes. That describes observation in place, not gathering. NDSU 2020 ties pregnancy-check timing to the breeding season and says to consult the veterinarian on method. SDSU 2020 notes the difficulty of getting cattle back off pasture for boosters, which argues for matching tasks to gathers well ahead.
rules.limitations: One horizon does not fit vet booking or a crew gather. The 'next gather' wording is wrong for observation tasks. No responsible person is shown, so nobody owns the warning.
rules.configurable: Yes. Lead time should be a per-task-type setting (for example observation 0 days, gather tasks about 7 days, vet-dependent tasks longer). Values are a ranch choice and should be labelled as such.

rules.recommendation: Warn when window_start is within the task type's lead time. Use action text by type: observation 'Look the group over on the next pasture check…'; gather task 'Plan it with the next gather ([responsible])'; vet-dependent 'Confirm the date with your veterinarian and plan the gather.' Label 7 days as a demonstration setting in the rules table.

sources.title: Summer brings raised pinkeye concerns in cowherds
sources.publisher: NDSU Agriculture Communication (J. Galbreath, L. Quail)
sources.supports: Check cattle closely in pasture and drylot for early signs. Dust and crowding (tail switching) irritate eyes. Treatment decisions are made 'in consultation with their veterinarian'.
sources.checker_note: Dated July 2, 2025, NDSU Agriculture Communication. Galbreath and Quail are the quoted sources, not bylined authors. Verbatim: 'closely checking cattle in pasture and dry lot environments'; 'The first signs of pinkeye occur 12 to 72 hours after exposure.'; 'This progression can take place over just a few days'; irritants include 'blowing dust, ultraviolet light and physical trauma from grazing coarse forages or tail switching when crowded'; medications and dosing chosen 'in consultation with their veterinarian'; 'Records of affected cattle should be kept so that any potential retained breeding stock can be evaluated.' Early signs are watery eyes or face staining, then squinting, then a cloudy spot. This supports in-pasture observation. It does not describe gathering cattle for the check.

sources.title: Consider Pregnancy Testing Beef Cattle Early
sources.publisher: NDSU Agriculture Communication (J. Block, K. Hoppe, G. Stokka)

Verbatim: 'as early as 30 to 45 days after the end of the breeding season'. Ultrasound about 30 d post-breeding, palpation 1-2 weeks later, blood tests 25-30 d post-breeding and 60-90 d post-calving. An additional pregnancy check before winter feeding programs begin.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: For vaccination and parasite-control tasks, evaluate against a window (window_start..window_end) recorded from the product label or the veterinarian's plan, with schedule_source stored. Warning when window_start is within the lead time. Serious when window_end has passed, with an escalate-to-vet action.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a booster or revaccination can still be done inside its label or vet window, or needs veterinarian input first.
rules.required_inputs: task_type, window_start, window_end, schedule_source, product name (record only), as_of, responsible.

context.class: Groups on a vaccination or parasite-control program
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Window recorded from the product label or the veterinarian's plan

rules.context_research: All classes. Windows are product-specific and come from the label or the herd veterinarian. The dashboard never computes them.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker health dispute 5: the window concept is supported (BQA 2-4 weeks; BCRC 'at least 3 weeks apart'), but making a missed window_end 'serious' with an escalate-to-vet action is not sourced; it is a reasonable design choice.
rules.evidence: BQA Manual: 'Always read and follow label directions'; almost all products recommend the second dose 2-4 weeks after the first. BQA Field Guide: boosters given when the label calls for them. BCRC/University of Calgary clostridial guideline: 'Vaccines should always be given according to label instructions' and 'Specific recommendations for your operation should be discussed with your veterinarian.' UC Davis 2008: booster need is on the label. OBSERVED with SYNTHETIC window values: 'Yearlings: Booster vaccine | window 2026-06-16..2026-06-30 (product_label) … -> serious: label window passed | "Window from the product label closed 92 days ago. Check the label and ask your veterinarian how to proceed before scheduling."'
rules.limitations: The window values in the fictional data would themselves be synthetic and must be labelled so. No fetched source gives a general rule for what happens after a missed booster (restart or not). That is left to the label and the veterinarian, and the dashboard must not decide it.
rules.configurable: Yes. Window dates are data, not code. Lead time per task type is a ranch setting.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If window_end or schedule_source is missing on a vaccination task, show 'Window not recorded. Check the label or vet plan' instead of a confident overdue or OK.
rules.recommendation: Add window_start, window_end and schedule_source to the health schedule. Keep next_due only as a planned date inside the window. Never print a dose or product instruction.
rules.phase_note: Needs window_start, window_end and schedule_source fields; not in the phase lists.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: In fly season, each pastured group gets a recurring eye and condition observation. Warn when a group has no recorded check in N days (N is a ranch setting). When an observation records animals with watery eyes, squinting or a cloudy eye, show 'N head with eye signs recorded. Call your veterinarian' and schedule a recheck within a few days. The current one-off 'Pinkeye check' row and its 'Plan it with the next gather' action become this.
rules.decision_supported: Early detection and timely veterinarian contact for eye problems during face-fly season, without the dashboard diagnosing.
rules.required_inputs: observation records (date, group, observer, head_with_signs, sign codes), fly-season start/end dates (ranch-entered), optional fly counts.

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Recurring group observations recorded by the crew

rules.context_research: Pastured cow-calf and yearling groups, summer into early fall in the Northern and Central Plains. Face flies peak late July to early September (UNL), and populations peak in late summer (NDSU 2024).
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker health dispute 4: the default 'any head with eye signs: call your veterinarian' is a ranch or veterinarian choice; sources say to act promptly and treat in consultation with the veterinarian, and the N-day interval is a ranch setting.
rules.evidence: NDSU 2025: early signs are 'watery eyes or face staining from excess tear production', squinting, and a cloudy spot. 'The first signs of pinkeye occur 12 to 72 hours after exposure.' Progression 'can take place over just a few days'. Treat in consultation with the veterinarian. 'Records of affected cattle should be kept so that any potential retained breeding stock can be evaluated.' OSU VTMD-9128: 'Pinkeye rarely affects just one animal, but spreads throughout the herd'. Keep current health records. UNL 2021: act on tearing, squinting and blinking 'immediately'. Fly tags work best applied near fly season. UNL 2023: face flies peak late July, August and early September, and aggregate to overwinter as day length falls below 12.5 h. NDSU 2024: tags when flies near the economic threshold, which the article gives as '200 flies per animal'. Remove tags when no longer effective. OBSERVED (computed, astronomy only): day length 2026-09-30 is Pierre SD 11.83 h, North Platte NE 11.86 h, Bismarck ND 11.81 h, all under 12.5 h. INFERENCE: the committed Oct 3 'Pinkeye check' falls at the tail of face-fly season. That is plausible (an NDSU release dated 2017-09-25 reported pinkeye 'infecting cattle in some herds') but it is an observation job, not a gather job.
evidence_corrections: The NDSU 2024 fly article's 200-fly threshold names no species; the research called it 'horn flies per animal'.
OSU VTMD-9128 says pinkeye 'can range from a few cases up to 80 percent of the herd'; it does not say 80% are affected at the peak of an outbreak.
rules.limitations: Recheck interval and N are management choices. Season dates vary by year and location. The day-length cue is a seasonal indicator, not a fly count. Eye signs can have causes other than pinkeye (UNL 2023 notes face-fly lesions 'mimic the symptoms of bovine pinkeye'), so the dashboard must record signs, not name a disease.
rules.configurable: Yes: fly-season dates, observation interval, and the head count that triggers 'call your veterinarian' (default: any).
rules.missing_data_blocks: No observation records means the dashboard shows 'No eye check recorded since [date]' rather than implying the group is clear.
rules.recommendation: Replace the dated 'Pinkeye check' task with an observation log and a fly-season window. Wording: 'Look the group over on the next pasture check; record animals with watery eyes, squinting or a cloudy eye and call your veterinarian if you see any.' Add an end-of-season 'fly tag removal' task (NDSU 2024) instead of a 'done' fly tag row whose next_due has passed (H-05).
rules.phase_note: Needs an observation log. Observation and escalation wording only; no diagnosis.

sources.title: Summer brings raised pinkeye concerns in cowherds
sources.supports: Signs to observe, 12-72 h onset, progression over a few days, keep records of affected cattle, involve the veterinarian, check cattle closely in pasture.
sources.checker_note: Dated July 2, 2025, NDSU Agriculture Communication. Galbreath and Quail are the quoted sources, not bylined authors. Verbatim: 'closely checking cattle in pasture and dry lot environments'; 'The first signs of pinkeye occur 12 to 72 hours after exposure.'; 'This progression can take place over just a few days'; irritants include 'blowing dust, ultraviolet light and physical trauma from grazing coarse forages or tail switching when crowded'; medications and dosing chosen 'in consultation with their veterinarian'; 'Records of affected cattle should be kept so that any potential retained breeding stock can be evaluated.' Early signs are watery eyes or face staining, then squinting, then a cloudy spot. This supports in-pasture observation. It does not describe gathering cattle for the check.

sources.title: Pinkeye (VTMD-9128)
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Extension (Boileau, Lalman, Whitworth)
sources.supports: 'excessive tearing and squinting are the initial clinical signs'. It rarely affects one animal. Infection 'can range from a few cases up to 80 percent of the herd', with cases usually peaking in the 3rd-4th week of an outbreak. Incubation 2-3 days. Maintain health records.
sources.checker_note: VTMD-9128, October 2016. The byline spells 'Bioleau' and the bio spells 'Boileau'. The co-authors are Lalman and Whitworth. Verbatim: 'excessive tearing and squinting are the initial clinical signs' and 'Pinkeye rarely affects just one animal, but spreads throughout the herd.' Incubation is usually 2-3 days (up to 3 weeks in experimental trials). Keep current health records to 'identify cattle that repeatedly become infected'. Paraphrase drift: the source says infection 'can range from a few cases up to 80 percent of the herd', with cases usually peaking in the 3rd-4th week of an outbreak. It does not say 80% of the herd is affected 'at the peak of an outbreak'.

sources.title: Do not let Pinkeye Decrease Efficiencies in Summer Grazing
sources.supports: Act on early signs immediately. Season rises in spring, peaks in summer and declines in fall. Fly-tag timing relative to routine processing. Discuss vaccine timing with the veterinarian well in advance.
sources.checker_note: By Connor Biehler, August 1, 2021. Verbatim: 'address symptoms (tearing, squinting, and blinking) immediately'; 'The occurrence of pinkeye increases in the spring and peaks in the summer months before decreasing in the fall.' On tags, the optimal time 'usually falls after vaccinating and de-horning', and that work typically happens about 60 days before fly season. Vaccine timing 'should be discussed well in advance with your veterinarian.'

sources.title: Face Flies on Pastured Cattle
sources.supports: Face flies peak late July to early September and aggregate to overwinter when day length is under 12.5 h. Face-fly lesions mimic pinkeye.
sources.checker_note: By Dave Boxler, June 1, 2023. Verbatim: 'populations usually peak in late July, August, and early September'; once 'day length falls below 12.5 hours, both sexes aggregate on sunny sides'; 'serious ocular lesions that mimic the symptoms of bovine pinkeye' (from 1-5 face flies per eye per day).

sources.title: Controlling flies on cattle requires proper timing
sources.publisher: NDSU Extension and Ag Research News (Stokka, Tobin, Hoppe)
sources.supports: Horn and face flies are not present at turnout. Tags go in when populations near the threshold, typically mid-June to July. Threshold given as 200 flies per animal (no species named). Remove tags when no longer effective. Scout and monitor.
sources.checker_note: May 22, 2024, with Stokka, Tobin and Hoppe as sources. Supported: horn and face flies 'typically are not present at pasture turnout'. Tags go in near the economic threshold, typically mid-June to July. 'When fly counts reach 200 flies per animal, the economic threshold has been reached.' Remove tags 'when they no longer provide effective fly control'. Scout and monitor. Face flies 'tend to peak in late summer'. Over-specified: the data_fields entry fly_count_per_animal says 'horn flies per animal', but the article names no species for the 200 figure.

sources.title: Pinkeye Infecting Some N.D. Cattle
sources.supports: Pinkeye was reported in ND herds at the end of September 2017. Signs include teary eyes, squinting and aversion to light. 'Producers should contact their veterinarian or the VDL'.
sources.checker_note: The URL and breadcrumb give Sept. 25, 2017 and the footer gives Sept. 27, 2017. Sources are Stokka, Webb and Dyer. Verbatim: 'pinkeye has been infecting cattle in some herds'; 'Symptoms of pinkeye include teary eyes', 'squinting and aversion to bright light'; 'Producers should contact their veterinarian or the VDL'.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: A health task can be marked done only with a BQA-style completion record: date, group or animal ID, product and lot/serial (product tasks), route and location, withdrawal clear date, person administering, and head count worked. Missing items show as 'record incomplete'.
rules.decision_supported: Whether the ranch can show what was done, to which animals, by whom, and when they clear withdrawal (BQA compliance and marketing).
rules.required_inputs: done_date, group/animal_id, product, lot_serial, route_location, withdrawal_clear_date, done_by, head_done.

context.class: Any group or animal receiving a product
context.geography: US beef operations following BQA
context.management: Completion records for scheduled health tasks

rules.context_research: Every product given to cattle. Observation-only tasks need date, observer and findings only.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from A. Checker health dispute 2: the BQA product-record items are A (manual Sec 6.2), but head_done (from the KS-BQA form), blocking 'done' until the record is complete, and the minimum record for observation tasks are design choices. BQA is voluntary; only VFD and extralabel records are legal requirements. Evidence-currency caveat (health dispute 7): the cited BQA manual is likely superseded by the 2026 edition.
rules.evidence: BQA Manual, Record Keeping (p.15 per fetch): treatment records must include 'Individual animal identification', 'Date treated', 'Product administered and manufacturer's lot/serial number', 'Dosage', 'Route and location of administration', 'Earliest date animal will have cleared the withdrawal period', 'Name of individual administering the treatment'. Group treatments need a group or lot ID plus the same items. Kansas BQA Processing/Treatment Map form includes 'No. of Head', 'Lot or Serial #', 'Route of Admin', 'Withdrawal Time (WD)' and 'Crew Initials'. OBSERVED (health.research.mjs): 'health.csv columns: group, task, last_done, next_due, status', with lot/serial, route and location, withdrawal clear date, person, head count, window and schedule source all MISSING.
rules.limitations: The dashboard needs only some of these to make decisions (date, head count, withdrawal clear date, person). Dose, route and lot are for the record, and the page should not display them as instructions.
rules.configurable: No for the BQA fields. Yes for which fields the page displays.
rules.missing_data_blocks: A 'done' status without done_date and head_done should not count as complete. Show 'record incomplete'.
rules.recommendation: Add an append-only health_records.csv. Keep health.csv as the schedule. The dashboard reads both. Record dose and route but do not surface them in exception text.
rules.phase_note: Shared records are deferred. Dose and route stay in the record system and are never shown as instructions.
