rules.rule: PROPOSED: Serious when a recorded withdrawal clear date falls after the group's planned ship or sale date. Action: 'Do not ship before [clear date]. Talk with your veterinarian.'
rules.decision_supported: Marketing timing that avoids residues: whether a group can leave on its planned date.
rules.required_inputs: withdrawal_clear_date per completion record (from the label, or from the veterinarian for extralabel use), planned_ship_date per group.

context.class: Any animal or group with a recorded withdrawal
context.geography: US
context.management: Withdrawal clear dates from the label or the veterinarian; planned ship dates

rules.context_research: Any class marketed or culled, especially fall-shipped yearlings and cull cows.
rules.classification_note: Kept at A for the principle (do not ship before the recorded withdrawal clear date). Evidence-currency caveat (health dispute 7): the cited BQA manual is likely superseded and was not re-verified against the 2026 edition.
rules.evidence: BQA Manual: records must include the 'Earliest date animal will have cleared the withdrawal period'. Most vaccines have a 21- or 60-day withdrawal (p.45 per fetch). BQA Field Guide: consult pharmaceutical, veterinary or screening experts on high-risk animals before sale. FDA: extralabel use requires a VCPR. FARAD (AABP 2021) answers withdrawal-interval requests from veterinarians. OBSERVED with SYNTHETIC values: 'withdrawal 21 d -> clear 2026-10-23; planned ship 2026-10-15 -> CONFLICT: ship date is before the withdrawal clear date'.
rules.limitations: The dashboard must use the clear date recorded from the label or the vet. It must not compute withdrawal for extralabel use. groups.csv has no planned ship date today.
rules.configurable: No for the rule. Lead time for the warning before a ship date is configurable.
rules.missing_data_blocks: A product task without a withdrawal_clear_date should block a 'clear to ship' reading. Show 'withdrawal not recorded'.
rules.recommendation: Add planned_ship_date to groups and withdrawal_clear_date to completion records. Flag conflicts as serious.
rules.phase_note: Needs withdrawal_clear_date and planned_ship_date records. The dashboard never computes a withdrawal.

sources.supports: Withdrawal clear date is a required record item. Vaccines carry 21- or 60-day withdrawals.
sources.checker_note: I fetched it three times. Every quoted claim was found. Sec 4.4 (pp.46-47): 'To establish immunity, almost all products recommend a second vaccination two (2) to four (4) weeks after the initial vaccination.' p.42 (also p.11): 'Follow all FDA/USDA/EPA guidelines and label directions for each product.' Sec 6.2 (pp.14-15) lists the individual record items, and group treatments record 'Group or lot identification' plus the same items. p.15: 'Keep records for a minimum of two years or longer as required by laws/regulations'. Ch.2 Temperature Conditions (pp.26-27): 'work them before the temperature humidity index (THI) reaches 84', 'Avoid handling cattle when the risk of heat stress is high', and 'Work cattle more prone to heat stress first, earlier in the day'. p.48: 'A VCPR cannot exist based solely on phone, video, or other telemedical interactions.' p.45: vaccines 'have either a 21 or 60 day withdrawal time'. p.42: VFD records are kept two years. Sec 4.3: 'Booster vaccinations as indicated in the herd health plan', 'Always read and follow label directions' and 'Keep records of all products administered including date, animal identification, product used, serial number, amount administered, route...'. Sec 4.5 (titled 'Judicious Use of Antimicrobials', not VCPR): protocols 'define when to quit treating and seek professional help'. Small drifts: the processing map (Sec 1.7.2, p.10) records 'where each injection was given', which is not 'how much'. The research cites the field guide for the withdrawal and sale point, but the manual gives stronger support: 'Verify withdrawal on any animals being sold' and 'Employ strict adherence to pre-harvest withdrawal periods'. METADATA PROBLEM: the PDF names no publisher. It shows only 'Funded by Beef Farmers and Ranchers'. NCBA's own release confirms that NCBA is a contractor to the Beef Checkoff. Its newest data are the 2016 NBQA, a 2018 'Unpublished' footnote and data for '1998 to 2017', which points to an edition from about 2019. NCBA announced an updated manual on 2024-12-19. The research's 2025-01-06 date is that of the trade-press reprints. bqa.org/resources/manuals now links bqa-national-manual-2026.pdf and does NOT link bqa_manual_final.pdf. The cited file is therefore very likely a superseded edition. rules.rule: PROPOSED: Low-stress timing for sensitive groups. When a handling task is planned for females in early pregnancy (inside a configurable number of days after bull turn-in), show a note: 'Early-pregnant females: keep handling, transport and heat stress low. Confirm timing with your veterinarian.' Pregnancy-check windows are derived from breeding-season dates.
rules.decision_supported: Whether to combine, delay or move a gather for bred heifers or cows. When to book the pregnancy check.
rules.required_inputs: bull_in_date, bull_out_date per group, planned task dates, vet-chosen method.

context.season: Within a set number of days after bull turn-in
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Handling tasks planned against breeding dates

rules.context_research: Bred heifers and cows. Northern Plains spring-calving herds that breed in summer.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: NDSU 2020: 'producers should minimize handling, transportation, and heat stress' for cows in early pregnancy. Pregnancy testing 'as early as 30 to 45 days after the end of the breeding season'. Consult the veterinarian on method. UW-Madison Extension summary of peer-reviewed work: Reinhardt, Busby & Corah 2009 J. Anim. Sci. 87:3030 (more than 20,000 cattle, 2002-2006) linked excitable disposition with lower ADG and carcass merit. Dewell et al. 2019 Bovine Practitioner: low-stress-handled cattle gained 2.92 vs 2.70 lb/d. These are associations or single trials, cited second-hand.
rules.limitations: The days-after-turn-in cut-off is a ranch and vet choice. The peer-reviewed results come from feeder and feedlot settings and were read through an extension summary, not the papers.
rules.configurable: Yes (days after turn-in, which groups).
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without breeding dates the dashboard cannot derive the preg-check window or flag early pregnancy. Show 'breeding dates not recorded'.
rules.recommendation: Add bull_in and bull_out to groups. Derive a suggested preg-check window (end of breeding plus a vet-set offset) and show it as 'confirm with your veterinarian'.
rules.phase_note: Needs breeding dates (deferred breeding module).

sources.title: Consider Pregnancy Testing Beef Cattle Early
sources.supports: Minimize handling, transport and heat stress in early pregnancy. Timing of methods after breeding. A follow-up check before winter feeding.
sources.checker_note: By Block, Hoppe and Stokka, NDSU Ag Communication. The URL and breadcrumb give July 6, 2020 and the dateline gives July 9, 2020, as the research says. Verbatim: 'as early as 30 to 45 days after the end of the breeding season'. Ultrasound about 30 d post-breeding, palpation 1-2 weeks later, blood tests 25-30 d post-breeding and 60-90 d post-calving. 'Producers should consult their veterinarian' on method. 'producers should minimize handling, transportation and heat stress' (the source has no comma before 'and'). An additional pregnancy check before winter feeding programs begin.

sources.title: Cattle handling and stockmanship influence on animal performance
sources.publisher: University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of Extension (B. Halfman)
sources.pub_date: undated (image uploaded 2022-07; not confirmed as article date)
sources.data_years: cites Reinhardt et al. 2009 (data 2002-2006), Dewell et al. 2019, Woiwode et al. 2016
sources.supports: Summarises peer-reviewed evidence that calm handling and disposition are associated with gain and carcass merit.
sources.checker_note: By Bill Halfman, UW-Madison Extension, 'originally published in the Wisconsin Agriculturist'. No article date is given, as the research said. Reinhardt, Busby & Corah 2009, JAS 87:3030-3042: 'over 20,000 head' in the Tri-County Steer Futurity, 2002-2006. More excitable cattle had lower gain, HCW, quality grade and marbling. Steer ADG was 3.6/3.5/3.3 lb/d by disposition score. Dewell et al. 2019, Bov Pract 53(1):71-80: abruptly weaned feeder cattle gained '2.92 lb/day vs 2.70 lb/day (P=0.01)' from day 19 to 95. Woiwode 2016 is given with no numbers, and the reference list spells it 'Woide'. All of this is feedlot or feeder data, as the research's limitation says.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Escalate-to-veterinarian triggers from observation records. (a) Any death without a known cause gives 'Call your veterinarian about a necropsy'. (b) Abortions or late pregnancy losses above the herd's own baseline give 'Call your veterinarian'. (c) Signs recorded in more than one animal of a group, or the same sign recurring, give 'Call your veterinarian'. Reportable diseases are left to the veterinarian, who reports to the state.
rules.decision_supported: When the manager should bring in the herd veterinarian, worded as observations, not diagnoses.
rules.required_inputs: death records (date, group, ID, found-dead flag), abortion and loss records, herd baseline loss rate from past years, observation sign counts, herd vet contact.

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Loss and observation records; herd veterinarian

rules.context_research: All classes and seasons. Baselines come from the herd's own records.
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B. Checker health dispute 3: triggers (a) necropsy on an unexplained death (eXtension) and (b) losses above the herd's baseline (UNL 2023) stay B, but trigger (c) 'signs recorded in more than one animal of a group' has no source as a call-the-veterinarian threshold. The bundled rule takes the stricter class C.
rules.evidence: eXtension Beef Cattle: 'it is very important that any time an animal dies a necropsy is performed'. Without necropsy clues 'more animals may die'. UNL 2023 (Hille, Steffen): about 2-2.5% mid-to-late-term abortions expected in an average Nebraska herd. Published thresholds range from about 2% to 8%, so set your own from past records. 'If in doubt, call and discuss the situation with your veterinarian.' Keep the carcass cool until the veterinarian or lab can examine it, and obtain the placenta when possible. Record breeding, pregnancy and birth dates. SD ARSD 12:68:03:09: reportable diseases are reported 'immediately by telephone, fax, or writing' by licensed accredited veterinarians and diagnostic labs, not by producers. OSU and NDSU: pinkeye spreads through a herd within days.
evidence_corrections: UNL 2023 (abortions): the source says to keep the carcass cool until the veterinarian or lab examines it and to obtain the placenta when possible; it does not say to keep the placenta cool.
rules.limitations: Thresholds for (b) and (c) are herd-specific and set with the veterinarian. The dashboard must not name a disease. The 'every death' necropsy guidance is strong, and some ranches will use judgment on cost.
rules.configurable: Yes (baseline rate, sign-count trigger). The 'call your veterinarian' wording should stay fixed.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without past-year loss records there is no baseline. Show raw counts and 'set a baseline with your veterinarian' instead of 'normal'.
rules.recommendation: Add deaths.csv or loss records and observation logs. The only action the dashboard gives on a health finding is 'record it and call your veterinarian'.
rules.phase_note: Needs loss and observation records. Wording stays observational; the veterinarian handles any state reporting.

sources.title: What is causing my cattle to die suddenly?
sources.supports: Necropsy any time an animal dies. A veterinarian combines necropsy with history to reach a diagnosis.
sources.checker_note: Verbatim: 'it is very important that any time an animal dies a necropsy is performed' and 'Meanwhile, more animals may die.' A veterinarian uses 'the necropsy findings along with history' to diagnose. No author, publisher or date appears in the content. The eXtension attribution comes from the domain only.

sources.title: Investigating the cause of cattle abortions: When to involve your veterinarian and what happens next
sources.publisher: Nebraska Extension BeefWatch (M. Hille, D. Steffen)
sources.supports: Baseline about 2-2.5% in Nebraska. Thresholds from 2-8%. Use the herd's own records. Call the vet when in doubt. What to save and record.
sources.checker_note: By Hille and Steffen, November 1, 2023. Verbatim: 'we suggest a 2-2.5% rate of mid to late term abortions to be expected for the average herd in Nebraska'; thresholds 'range widely from ~2% - 8%'; 'You will need to develop a threshold for concern based on past experiences'; 'If in doubt, call and discuss the situation with your veterinarian'; record 'breeding dates, pregnancy dates, and birth dates'. Paraphrase drift: the source says 'Keep the carcass cool until it can be examined by your veterinarian or shipped to the diagnostic lab' and to obtain the placenta when possible. It does not explicitly say to keep the placenta cool.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: wording rule for every Health row and for gain follow-ups. Describe what is scheduled or what was observed, and who to call. Never state a diagnosis, cause, drug, dose or treatment. For slow-gaining animals: list them, observe them at the next gather, record what was seen, and refer to the herd veterinarian under the ranch's health plan. Reword the current Gain action 'look for a health problem in the group' the same way.
rules.decision_supported: [health research rule 11] Keeping the dashboard inside the manager's role (observe, schedule, record, escalate) and the veterinarian's role (diagnose, prescribe). | [gain research rule 11] Who to look at, and how the observation is recorded.
rules.required_inputs: [health research rule 11] Action strings in exceptions.js and the rules table in app.js. | [gain research rule 11] Tag, date, observation note, observer, whether escalated.

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Dashboard copy for health and gain rows

rules.context_research: [health research rule 11] All Health and Gain rows. | [gain research rule 11] All classes.
rules.classification_research: health R11: A-supported-general + gain R11: A-supported-general
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from A (both research rules). Checker health dispute 0: 21 CFR 530.3 defines when a VCPR exists for extralabel drug use; it does not govern what a producer or tool may say, and extension sources teach producers to recognise signs. Only the narrow sub-rule 'prescription, extralabel and VFD decisions need a VCPR' is A. Checker gain dispute 2: record-keeping is A, but 'observe at the next gather instead of pulling' is a management choice. The rule stays a fixed project scope rule (not configurable).
rules.evidence: [health research rule 11] 21 CFR 530.3(i): a valid VCPR is one in which 'A veterinarian has assumed the responsibility for making medical judgments regarding the health of (an) animal(s) and the need for medical treatment', with 'sufficient knowledge of the animal(s) … to initiate at least a general or preliminary diagnosis'. BQA Manual: 'A valid VCPR is required for all prescription medications, extra-label use of non-prescription medications,' (VFD feeds per field guide). FDA: a VCPR cannot be established by telemedicine alone. OBSERVED: current Health actions 'Schedule it this week' and 'Plan it with the next gather' contain no diagnosis words (health.research.mjs section 4 'ok'). The Gain action 'Check forage quality and mineral; look for a health problem in the group' was flagged NOTE because it asks the manager to find a health problem. | [gain research rule 11] Merck Veterinary Manual (reviewed 2023-07): screening relies on 'regular observation of the herd'. Records are 'essential to monitor the incidence of disease ... and impact of disease on performance' and should be 'analyzed on a regular basis'.
rules.limitations: [health research rule 11] Task names such as 'Pinkeye check' name a disease as the target of an observation, which is acceptable as a schedule label. Exception text about findings should list signs, not conditions. | [gain research rule 11] A low ADG alone is not evidence of disease, because weighing noise and forage effects are larger in many cases (see the individual rule).
rules.configurable: [health research rule 11] No. | [gain research rule 11] Yes (the action text).
rules.missing_data_blocks: [health research rule 11] n/a | [gain research rule 11] Not applicable. This rule only routes to observation.
rules.recommendation: [health research rule 11] Use templates. Scheduled: '[Task] for [group]: due [window]. Owner: [responsible].' Observed: '[N] head in [group] with [signs] recorded [date]. Call your veterinarian.' Gain: 'Check forage and mineral; watch the group for illness or lameness and call your veterinarian if you see any.' | [gain research rule 11] Change 'Pull and check' to 'Look at these animals at the next gather and record what you see'. Link to a health observation record.
rules.phase_note: Lead default 'honest rule copy'. Applies to all health and gain row text from phase 1 on.

sources.title: 21 CFR 530.3 Definitions (paragraph (i) veterinarian-client-patient relationship)
sources.publisher: Cornell Legal Information Institute (reproducing the Code of Federal Regulations)
sources.supports: The three VCPR conditions. Medical judgments and diagnosis rest with the veterinarian. Requires recent examination or timely premises visits.
sources.checker_note: Paragraph (i) conditions are confirmed. (1) The veterinarian 'has assumed the responsibility for making medical judgments regarding the health of (an) animal(s)' and the need for treatment. The relationship 'can exist only when the veterinarian has recently seen and is personally acquainted with the keeping and care' of the animals, through examination and/or 'medically appropriate and timely visits to the premises'. The page is undated. Note that 530.3 is the definitions section for Part 530 (extralabel drug use), which matters for the wording-rule classification below.

sources.supports: Observation and records practice.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Herd veterinarian and VCPR currency. Store the herd veterinarian's name and contact and the date of the vet's last visit to the premises. Show an info row when no visit is recorded within a ranch-set period. Escalation text uses the stored contact.
rules.decision_supported: Whether the ranch has a working vet relationship to escalate to and to authorize prescription, extralabel or VFD products.
rules.required_inputs: vet_name, vet_phone, last_vet_premises_visit, state.

context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Herd veterinarian contact and last premises visit

rules.context_research: All operations. What counts as 'timely' is defined by the state.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C).
rules.evidence: 21 CFR 530.3(i): the relationship 'can exist only when the veterinarian has recently seen and is personally acquainted with the keeping and care of the animal(s)… by medically appropriate and timely visits to the premises'. AVMA page: states may define 'timely', and the AVMA Model Act definition differs from the federal one. NAHMS Beef 2017 Report 2: 80.7% of cow-calf operations used a veterinarian for their cattle in 2017 (large operations 98.4%), so about 1 in 5 did not. The dashboard should not assume one.
rules.limitations: The dashboard cannot judge whether a VCPR is legally valid. It can only show the recorded facts.
rules.configurable: Yes (reminder period).
rules.missing_data_blocks: No vet contact recorded means escalation rows say 'Call your veterinarian (no contact recorded)'.
rules.recommendation: Add a small config entry. Never present a VCPR as 'valid'. Present it as 'last vet visit recorded [date]'.

sources.title: 21 CFR 530.3 Definitions

rules.rule: CURRENT: Serious when a category is more than 10% over budget, season to date (exceptions.js RULES.budgetSerious = 0.10; budgetStatus sums every row in budget.csv per category, pct = (actual - budget) / budget).

rules.context_research: Any operation. The fictional ranch runs mixed cow-calf and yearling stocker groups (groups.csv: 180 cow-calf pairs, 45 first-calf heifers, 150 yearling steers), and the season shown is Jun-Sep 2026.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research D). Today the rule sums every row in budget.csv, so future plan rows dilute the total and a zero budget gives 'Infinity%'.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (node docs/audit/diagnostics/budget.materiality.research.mjs): committed data gives 'Fuel budget 9600 actual 11640 cur pct 21.3% -> current: serious' and 'Repairs budget 7200 actual 9000 cur pct 25.0% -> current: serious'. Scenario S2: 'Ear tags budget 200 actual 230 cur pct 15.0% -> current: serious', 'Labor budget 36000 actual 38700 cur pct 7.5% -> current: warning', 'Feed (big) budget 90000 actual 92700 cur pct 3.0% -> current: -'. OBSERVED (node docs/audit/diagnostics/healthbudget.repro.mjs): BU-01 'serious | Hay | Infinity% over season to date ($500)'; BU-06 adding Oct/Nov plan rows with actual 0 gives 'Fuel 11640/14400 = -19.2%; Repairs 9000/10800 = -16.7%; (no alerts)'. EXTERNAL: no extension, agency or peer-reviewed source found that sets 10% for ranch budget categories. Institutional variance policies that use 10% pair it with a dollar test (UW MAA: '+/- 10% or more AND +/- $5,000 or more'). Others use different percentages joined by OR (U Alberta: 5% or $100,000 unfavorable). GFOA speaks only of 'significant' variances and gives no number.
rules.limitations: Percent-only: it ignores scale, so a $30 overrun on a small line outranks a $2,700 overrun on a large one. It compares against the full-season straight-line sum of whatever rows are in the file, not the plan to date. Division by zero produces Infinity or NaN. Future plan rows dilute the result. rules.configurable: Yes. RULES.budgetSerious is a single constant, but on its own it cannot express a dollar materiality test.
rules.missing_data_blocks: A closed month with no actual for a category; a zero or blank budget (percent is undefined); plan rows after as_of; an unknown cash or accrual basis. Each should stop a confident serious call for that category.
rules.recommendation: Keep 10% only as a labelled demonstration setting inside the combined percent-and-dollar rule below. Compute it over closed months only, and label it in the UI and README as a ranch-chosen setting, not a validated standard.
rules.phase_note: Count closed months only (RULE-BUD-05), exclude rows after as_of, and judge a zero budget in dollars (RULE-BUD-06). Fuel and repairs (planted) must still be found. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Combined percent-and-dollar materiality per category over closed months (V = actual - plan to date; p = V / plan). Serious if p >= seriousPct AND V >= seriousUsd. Warning if p >= warnPct AND V >= warnUsd. Large-dollar override: warning if V >= largeUsd whatever p is. Dollar floors are either fixed dollars or a share of the total season-to-date operating budget, so they scale with ranch size. Demo values used in the diagnostic: warnPct 5%, seriousPct 10%, warnUsd $500, seriousUsd $1,000, largeUsd $2,500, unbudgetedUsd $250.
rules.decision_supported: Which category overruns deserve the manager's time this month, ranked by both relative and absolute size.

rules.context_research: Any cow-calf or stocker operation. Dollar floors must be set by each ranch for its scale. The fictional ranch's season-to-date total budget is $88,400 (Jun-Sep).
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B; every number is D. Checker budget dispute 0: no ranch, extension or agency source recommends a combined percent-and-dollar trigger for monthly category monitoring. The structural support is two non-agricultural examples that disagree (UW recharge centers: AND, on hold; U Alberta year-end: OR) plus an audit analogy. The large-dollar override and 'share of total season budget' floors have no source.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (budget.materiality.research.mjs, proposed rule with demo values): committed data unchanged in outcome, 'Fuel ... proposed ...: serious 21.3% and $2040 over' and 'Repairs ...: serious 25.0% and $1800 over'. S2: 'Ear tags ... proposed: -' (15%/$30 no longer serious); 'Labor ... warning 7.5% and $2700 over'; 'Feed (big) ... warning $2700 over (only 3.0%)'. OBSERVED (budget.fuel.pricevolume.research.mjs): 'Fuel over $ 2040 21.3% of category 2.31% of total budget'; 'Repairs over $ 1800 25.0% of category 2.04% of total budget'. EXTERNAL: two non-agricultural institutional examples combine percent and dollar tests, and they disagree: UW (a recharge-center rate review, now on hold) uses AND (10% and $5,000); U Alberta (year-end variances that trigger funding plans) uses OR (5% or $100,000). PCAOB AS 2105 treats materiality as quantitative plus qualitative. Extension budgets show category sizes differ by an order of magnitude (UNL 2026 400-cow budget: feed $801/cow vs fuel and energy $35/cow, repairs $38/cow; ND Farm Management Education 2020: feed and grazing $412/cow vs fuel $18.73/cow), so a single percent band treats very different dollar stakes alike.
evidence_corrections: The UW page's real title is 'Recharge Center Variance Analysis *ON HOLD'; it reviews recharge-center rates, not general budget-vs-actual.
U Alberta's thresholds trigger year-end funding or carry-forward plans, not monthly alerts or variance explanations.
'Combined percent and dollar tests are a common institutional design' is not supported: two examples do not show that.
rules.limitations: No ranch, extension or agency source recommends a combined percent-and-dollar trigger for monthly category monitoring, so the structure is a management design choice (C). The specific numbers are demonstration settings (D): no ranch-specific study validating any percent or dollar pair was found. AND vs OR and the override amount are management choices. Qualitative triggers (e.g., a vet-and-health underspend reflecting missed scheduled work) are not captured by numbers alone.
rules.configurable: Yes, and it must be: the dollar floors depend on ranch scale and the owner's tolerance. Per-category overrides are useful (e.g., labor vs ear tags).
rules.missing_data_blocks: Missing actual for any closed month in the category; no budget entered (route to the unbudgeted rule); thresholds not configured (show variance but no severity); basis unknown (show a label).
rules.recommendation: Adopt this as the budget rule, with the thresholds in RULES clearly labelled as demonstration settings and editable. Show both percent and dollars in every alert text. Offer 'share of total season budget' as the default way to scale dollar floors (e.g., warn at 0.5% of total, serious at 1%, both D-class demo values).
rules.phase_note: Lead default 'combined percent + dollar materiality labelled demo'. Demo values (warn 5% and $500, serious 10% and $1,000, large $2,500, unbudgeted $250) are labelled as demo settings. Fuel ($2,040, 21.3% over) and repairs ($1,800, 25% over) must still be found. rules.rule: PROPOSED: Compare season-to-date actual against a monthly phased plan through the same month (which months count as closed is set by RULE-BUD-05, class C), not against a straight-line or full-season total.
rules.decision_supported: Whether spending is ahead of plan or only ahead of a flat average, e.g., a planned early-season overhaul or winter feed purchases.
rules.required_inputs: A budget amount per category per month entered as the ranch expects to spend it (phased); actual per month; books-closed-through month.

context.season: Season to date (demo: monthly rows June-September 2026)
context.geography: Northern Plains rangeland (the Example Ranch data are fictional)
context.management: Monthly phased budget by category; actuals entered when the month's books close

rules.context_research: All ranches. Ranch spending is seasonal: winter feeding (SE Wyoming budget Jan 1-Apr 30; NW Wyoming Nov 15-Apr 15), calving (Mar 20-May 20 in SE WY), and fall calf sales for spring-calving herds with Aug-Sep cash pressure.
rules.classification_note: Kept at A: several extension budgeting sources support comparing actuals with a monthly phased plan. Checker caveat: GFOA lists seasonality only as a revenue-review item, not in its 'basis of comparison' list. Citation critic (critic-rules, 2026-10-16): the A covers comparing actual with a monthly phased plan over the same months; the closed-month cut-off is RULE-BUD-05 (C) and does not inherit A.
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (budget.materiality.research.mjs S3): the same June actual of $4,300 against a straight-line plan gives 'Repairs budget 1800 actual 4300 cur pct 138.9% -> current: serious', and against a phased plan (4,200 in June) gives 'cur pct 2.4% -> current: -'. EXTERNAL: cash-flow budgets are built in monthly, bi-monthly or quarterly columns and used to monitor actual against plan (OSU AGEC-751; UNL CropWatch 2018: 'a cash flow budget as a monitor and control'). ISU (Edwards): review the cash-flow budget during the year using monthly bank statements. GFOA lists previous-year actuals, averages of prior-year actuals and projections or forecasts as bases of comparison (seasonality appears only as a revenue-review item). Tennessee Comptroller recommends monthly budget-to-actual reports. Wyoming enterprise budgets' operations calendars show activities concentrated in specific months.
rules.limitations: Extension enterprise budgets are annual (UNL 2026 is Jan-Dec; the Wyoming budgets have calendars but no monthly dollars), so the monthly phasing must come from the ranch's own records or prior-year actuals. The committed fictional data uses a flat monthly plan, so phasing cannot be demonstrated on it without a change.
rules.configurable: Yes: phasing is data, entered per month; a fallback can phase by prior-year actual shares.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If only an annual budget exists, the dashboard should say 'plan not phased; comparison uses straight-line' rather than present the percent as authoritative.
rules.recommendation: Treat budget.csv as the phased plan and document that each month's budget is the expected spend in that month. Show a 'plan to date' column. Add an optional prior-year actual column to help phase.
rules.phase_note: budget.csv already has monthly rows; document that each month's budget is the planned spend for that month and compare through the same closed month. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.supports: 'Review your cash-flow budget from time to time during the year'; 'Monthly bank statements and canceled checks are a good source of cash-flow information'; 'You may even need to prepare a revised budget for the remainder of the year.'
sources.checker_note: Progressive Dairy (AgProud), 2010-11-12, by William Edwards (Iowa State University). It ends with 'Excerpts from Ag Decision Maker, Iowa State University Extension Service.' The quotes appear in a 'Monitoring cash flows' section after Step 12: 'Review your cash-flow budget from time to time during the year.' 'Prices and costs may differ from your estimates, or production plans may change.' 'Monthly bank statements and canceled checks are a good source of cash-flow information...' 'You may even need to prepare a revised budget for the remainder of the year.' The bank-statement context is checking actuals against the budget during the year. Two claims go beyond the text: that 'the month must be complete', and that statements are THE source used to compare actual against budget. The research labels the first as implied; the source does not state either. This affects the closed-month rule; the reforecast rule's claim is fully supported.

Supported: 'analyze and articulate why deviations occurred in order to move towards resolution'; 'Identify who is responsible for resolving variances'; 'Is it anticipated for any identified variance to continue'; frequency 'should be agreed upon at all levels of the organization, but may vary for different program areas'; and 'any significant variances' with no number given. Partly or not supported: (a) the phasing rule says the bases of comparison include seasonality. rules.rule: PROPOSED: Count only closed months (on or before a books-closed-through month) and show a data-completeness row when a closed month has no actual for a category. Never treat a blank as $0 and never let future plan rows dilute the season total.
rules.decision_supported: Whether the variance shown is trustworthy enough to act on.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Zero-budget or unbudgeted spending is judged in dollars only ('$X spent with no budget'), with a configurable dollar trigger. It is never shown as a percent.
rules.decision_supported: Whether unplanned spending (e.g., emergency hay or a new category) needs a budget line or a reforecast.
rules.required_inputs: Actual by category and month; an explicit budget of 0 vs a missing budget; the unbudgetedUsd threshold.

rules.context_research: All ranches. Common in drought (unplanned feed), after breakdowns, or with new categories.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research C).
rules.evidence: OBSERVED: BU-01 'serious | Hay | Infinity% over season to date ($500)'; BU-02 zero/zero gives 'pct=NaN'; budget.materiality.research.mjs S4 'Hay (unplanned) budget 0 actual 1800 cur pct Infinity -> current: serious | proposed ...: warning unbudgeted spend $1800'. EXTERNAL: percent variance is undefined at a zero base (arithmetic). Institutional policies carry a dollar-only alternative trigger (U Alberta '$100,000' OR clause).
rules.limitations: Whether unbudgeted spend is a warning or serious depends on the amount and on whether it was authorized. The dashboard cannot know authorization without a reforecast or note field.
rules.configurable: Yes (unbudgetedUsd; optionally a serious level).
rules.missing_data_blocks: A missing budget cell (vs an explicit 0) should produce 'no budget entered', not an unbudgeted-spend alert.
rules.recommendation: Branch on budget <= 0 before computing percent. Alert text shows dollars only. Suggest adding a budget line or reforecast.
rules.phase_note: Lead default 'zero-budget handling'. Show '$X spent with no budget' against a labelled dollar trigger; never a percent. The 10 planted problems must still be found, with no new false alarms, after this change.

sources.title: Budget Variance Accountability Procedure
sources.supports: A dollar-amount trigger that operates regardless of the percentage ($100,000 unfavorable, joined by OR to 5%), for year-end variances that trigger a funding plan, not monthly alerts.
sources.checker_note: These checks cover the threshold claims in the 10% rule, the warning rule, the combined rule and the zero-budget rule. Verbatim: unfavorable 'exceeds 5% of the responsibility level's revised budget or $100,000' (s.1.d.ii); favorable 'exceeds 5% of the responsibility level's revised budget or $500,000' (s.1.c.i). The joining word is OR, as claimed. Missing context: both apply to the YEAR-END variance ('finalized following the completion of the external audit'), not to in-year monitoring alerts. Crossing either one requires a funding plan (unfavorable) or a carry-forward use plan (favorable), not a variance explanation. Calling this 'the basis for a large-dollar override' in monthly alerts is the researcher's inference. Metadata is correct: approved 2006-07-17, editorial amendments 2025-05-20, Office of Resource Planning. The direct curl download was refused by the proxy ('curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'), so I read the file through WebFetch only.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Credits, refunds and rebates (warranty refunds, returned supplies, patronage or fuel-tax credits) are entered as separate signed rows with an entry_type. Net spend is used for variance, but gross spend and credits are shown separately. The period a credit lands in follows the declared accounting basis. Amounts use a plain minus sign ('-300'), not accounting parentheses.
rules.decision_supported: Whether an apparent improvement is real savings or a timing artefact of a refund.
rules.required_inputs: entry_type (expense | refund | credit | rebate | tax_credit); signed amount; related month (accrual) or received month (cash); basis.

sources.title: Instructions for Form 4136 and Schedule A (2025)
sources.supports: Farm-use gasoline must have been used 'on a farm for farming purposes' during the period of claim, and the credit is claimed for a period. It is a separate claim, not a supplier credit.
sources.checker_note: Page title: 'Instructions for Form 4136 and Schedule A (2025)', last reviewed or updated 30-Apr-2026. Verbatim: 'For line 1b, the gasoline must have been used during the period of claim on a farm for farming purposes (type of use 1).' 'The ultimate purchaser of the gasoline is the only person eligible to make this claim.' 'Form 4136 can't be used by ultimate vendors to make gasoline claims.' Form 4136 is an annual credit; Form 8849 handles periodic refunds. This supports the claim that the credit is a separate claim, not a supplier credit. Metadata problem: the research title leaves out the edition year (2025), and the research pairs these 2025 instructions with rates from the 2024 form. The rates should be confirmed against the edition actually cited.

sources.title: Farm Accrual Adjustments to a Cash Basis Income Statement
sources.supports: Cash statements exclude unpaid expenses and mistime prepaid ones. Adjust for changes in accounts payable, prepaid expenses and supplies inventory.
sources.checker_note: 'Farm Accrual Adjustments to a Cash-basis Income Statement', Miguel Antonio Saviroff (former Extension Educator). The page is a video with transcript, has no date (only a © 2026 footer), and is correctly marked undated. Supported: 'any expenses that were not paid during the period are excluded from this statement'; prepaid timing ('Cash was spent during the previous accounting period, but this was used for production during the current year'); adjustments for payables, 'prepaid expenses and unused supplies'. Feed appears only in a closing list of inventory adjustments. As the evidence_url for budget.entry_type, it supports only the prepaid and payable kinds. It says nothing about refund, credit, rebate, tax_credit or capital entry types.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: Declare the accounting basis (cash or accrual-adjusted) on the page. For operational monitoring prefer accrual-adjusted actuals (expense in the month the input was received or used), or at minimum flag prepaid and year-end purchases so they are not read as overruns.
rules.decision_supported: Whether a variance reflects operations or only payment timing (prepaying feed, paying a quarter's fuel bill late).
rules.required_inputs: meta.basis; optional prepaid and payable adjustments per category and month; entry_type for prepayments.

rules.context_research: Most farms file taxes on cash basis. Cash-basis ranches often prepay inputs near year-end, within limits (50% of other deductible farm expenses), which creates spending spikes unrelated to use.
rules.classification_note: Unchanged (research B).
rules.evidence: EXTERNAL: OSU AGEC-753 says FFSC recommends 'accrual adjusted' statements and that cash accounting 'can delay recognition of financial problems'. Penn State lists payables, prepaid and supplies inventory adjustments. ISU CALT says it is 'often beneficial' for cash-method farmers to prepay supplies, with a 50% limit. USU Rural Tax Education (revised Aug 2025) gives the same 50% limit and conditions. NOT OBSERVED in the repo: budget.csv has no basis field (inspected header 'month,category,budget,actual').
rules.limitations: Full accrual books are a heavy lift for small ranches. A pragmatic dashboard may stay cash basis with clear labelling and a prepaid flag.
rules.configurable: Yes (basis label; netting of prepaid).
rules.missing_data_blocks: If the basis is unknown, label the variance 'basis not stated'. If a large prepaid row is present, avoid a serious call on that category until the manager tags it.
rules.recommendation: Add a basis field to meta.csv and show it next to the 'Spend vs budget' tile. Add entry_type 'prepaid' so prepayments are reported apart from operating overruns.

sources.publisher: Rural Tax Education (Utah State University; Colorado State; University of Minnesota)
sources.supports: 50% limit and the payment-not-deposit, business-purpose and no-material-distortion tests for prepaid feed and supplies.
sources.checker_note: 'Prepaid Farm Expenses', Rural Tax Education on a USU page. By Jeffrey E. Tranel (Colorado State), revised by C. Robert Holcomb (University of Minnesota). Page dated 2025-08-18, marked 'Revised August 2025'. Deductions are 'limited to 50% of other deductible farm expenses', with exceptions. rules.rule: PROPOSED: Split fuel variance into price and volume (gallons x $/gal). If price explains most of the overrun, the action is to reforecast or revisit purchasing. If volume does, check the use drivers (miles, hours, water hauling, feeding).
rules.decision_supported: Whether a fuel overrun is something the crew can manage (use) or a market condition to reforecast (price).
rules.required_inputs: Gallons purchased or delivered per month by fuel type (dyed diesel, gasoline); actual $/gal from invoices; planned gallons and planned $/gal behind the budget; optional EIA regional reference price.

rules.context_research: Northern and Central Plains ranches buy diesel and gasoline in a volatile market. In 2026 PADD 2 diesel peaked in May (5.732), fell in June and July (4.984, 4.825), then rose to 6.351 in September.
rules.classification_note: Kept at B for the idea (checker budget dispute 6).
rules.evidence: OBSERVED (WebFetch of EIA monthly series): Midwest (PADD 2) No 2 diesel retail 2026 'Jan 3.444 ... Jun 4.984, Jul 4.825, Aug 5.417, Sep 6.351' vs 2025 'Jun 3.569 ... Sep 3.730'. Rocky Mountain (PADD 4) 2026 'Jun 4.989, Jul 4.790, Aug 5.415, Sep 6.155'. Weekly table: 'Midwest (PADD2) ... 10/12/26 6.259 ... year ago 2.653' (change). OBSERVED (node docs/audit/diagnostics/budget.fuel.pricevolume.research.mjs, hypothetical pricing at Jan-2026 EIA): 'season price variance $4148 volume variance $-2108 sum $2040'. That is a D-class illustration only, because budget.csv has no gallons. EXTERNAL: extension machinery costing estimates fuel as quantity x price (MSU P3543: 0.044 gal/hp-hr x PTO hp x hours x price; ISU Edwards 2013: gal/acre x price). UNL, KSU and OSU budgets carry fuel as its own line (UNL 2026 'Fuel and energy' $35/cow; KSU 'Fuel' $20/cow and 'Utilities' $14/cow; OSU 2026 stocker 'Machinery fuel, lube, repairs' $29.37/head).
evidence_corrections: The cited sources (MSU P3543, ISU) model fuel as quantity x price for ex-ante machinery costing; none describes price/volume variance analysis.

EIA PADD 2 diesel peaked in May 2026 at 5.732, fell to 4.984 in June and 4.825 in July, then rose to 6.351 in September; 'rose sharply through the grazing season' holds only for a budget priced in January.
rules.limitations: EIA prices are on-highway retail including road taxes. Dyed farm diesel is priced differently, so EIA serves as an index, not the ranch's price. A WebFetch summarizer extracted the EIA numbers; a direct curl to eia.gov was refused by the session proxy (403), so the raw files were not independently downloaded.
rules.configurable: Yes: optional fields; the reference region (PADD 2 or 4) is selectable.
rules.missing_data_blocks: Without gallons the dashboard must not claim a cause. It shows the dollar variance and says 'price vs use unknown: gallons not recorded'.
rules.recommendation: Add optional fuel_gallons and fuel_price fields (from delivery tickets). Show a price/volume split in the Fuel tooltip. Change the Fuel action text to 'check whether price or gallons drove it; reforecast if price'.
rules.phase_note: Needs gallons from delivery tickets.

sources.title: Midwest No 2 Diesel Retail Prices (Dollars per Gallon), monthly
sources.supports: Monthly PADD 2 diesel: 2026 Jan 3.444, Jun 4.984, Jul 4.825, Aug 5.417, Sep 6.351; 2025 Jun 3.569, Sep 3.730. The same 2026 series has a spring peak (Mar 4.785, Apr 5.246, May 5.732), so June-July prices were below May.
sources.checker_note: 'Midwest No 2 Diesel Retail Prices (Dollars per Gallon)'. Release 10/14/2026, next 10/20/2026. Every quoted number matches: 2026 Jan 3.444, Jun 4.984, Jul 4.825, Aug 5.417, Sep 6.351; 2025 Jun 3.569, Sep 3.730. The research leaves out the 2026 spring peak: Mar 4.785, Apr 5.246, May 5.732. So the prose 'rose sharply through the grazing season' and 'rose from 3.444 (Jan) to 4.984 (Jun)' are partly misleading. Prices fell from May into Jun-Jul and rose only in Aug-Sep. A budget priced in spring would show Jun-Jul price UNDER-runs; only a January-priced budget gives the overrun illustrated. I read this through WebFetch, as the researcher did. My own direct curl was refused by the proxy ('CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'), so I did not check the raw file independently.

sources.pub_date: revision code POD-10-23 (no explicit date shown)

The cutoff wording differs between official pages ('8 a.m. EDT' on USDM; '7 a.m. Eastern Time' on SD DANR and sdresponse.gov; '7 am Eastern'/'7 a.m. EST' on drought.gov). The ArcGIS layer stores MapDate/ReleaseDate as epoch values that convert to 07:30 UTC (3:30 a.m. ET on release day, before the real 08:30 release), so its times must be treated as date-only.
rules.configurable: Schedule: no, it is fixed by the publisher. Ranch time zone: yes, it must be set per ranch because SD and NE each span Central and Mountain time.
rules.missing_data_blocks: If as_of has no offset or zone (true today: meta.csv holds '2026-09-30T18:00'), the page cannot decide confidently which map was public near Thursday morning. It should show 'time zone not set' and not pick silently.
rules.recommendation: Adopt. Store released_at and valid_date for every context row, and select rows by released_at <= as_of. Add a time zone to meta.csv.
rules.phase_note: Phase-3 item 'drought/precipitation context as a dated snapshot'. A naive lookup picks the 2026-09-29 map, released after as_of; the correct one is valid 2026-09-22.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: heat-stress days. From a dated forecast snapshot, show the USDA-ARS breathing-rate heat category (Normal, Alert, Danger, Emergency) as information. On days at or above a ranch-set heat level: (a) schedule an in-person water check for every tank with cattle on it, whatever the sensor shows, and record who checked and what they saw; (b) warn when a planned gather or processing task falls in a period with forecast THI at or above 84 (the BQA handling rule of thumb) and suggest working early in the day; (c) show the category beside planned gathers and moves. Never use NWS HeatRisk for cattle (RULE-CTX-08).
rules.decision_supported: [context research rule 6] Rescheduling cattle work and moves, and checking water, on hot days | [water research rule 10] Crew scheduling. Confirms sensor data against reality. | [health research rule 8] Picking a day and time to gather and work cattle that keeps heat and handling stress low.
rules.required_inputs: [context research rule 6] Location (lat/lon); NWS hourly forecast; planned work/move dates; cattle class | [water research rule 10] Forecast high (public dataset), tanks with cattle present, check log (manual observation). | [health research rule 8] planned work date and start/end time, location, hourly forecast temperature and relative humidity (or dewpoint), and THI computed from them.

rules.context_research: [context research rule 6] Summer, mainly June to August in the Northern/Central Plains. Developed at USDA-ARS Clay Center NE; press coverage frames it for cattle feeders. For pasture cattle the evidence is weaker. | [water research rule 10] Summer on Great Plains pastures. In heat, intake can more than double. | [health research rule 8] Summer handling (branding, preg check in hot falls, yearling processing). Not relevant in cold months.
rules.classification_research: context R6: B-context-dependent + water R10: B-context-dependent + health R8: B-context-dependent
rules.classification_note: CHANGED from B (all three research rules). Checker water dispute 4: no source gives a single trigger temperature for pasture cattle, so the heat-day water check's operative parameter is a ranch choice. Checker context dispute 2: the ARS breathing-rate maps were designed for cattle feeders; warning on Danger days is a ranch choice and B fits only the category display. THI 84 is a BQA rule of thumb for handling (B). The merged rule takes the stricter class C.
rules.evidence: [context research rule 6] The ARS 'Forecasting Heat Stress' page gives the equation and category table (Last Modified 8/12/2016). It suggests ~1000 W/m2 if no solar data and says the maps are 'an estimate of general trends' and 'cannot predict individual animal stress levels since there is much variability among animals'. The ARS index region page lists 7-day regional maps (Last Modified 7/26/2017); the forecast date is only in an image, which I could not read (forecastDate.png robots-blocked; curl to www.marc.ars.usda.gov returned 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'). Farm Progress (2020-07-08) and Drovers (2020-11-12) describe 7-day maps from NWS inputs. Drovers adds risk factors: 'high overnight lows (above 70 F)', low air movement, recent rain, and advises avoiding moving cattle during heat events. | [water research rule 10] NDSU (Hoppe): in 100F weather, daily checks 'may not be often enough'. Bartlett: hot weather can more than double needs. UNL BeefWatch (2024) and PREEC (2025) describe cameras and sensors as aids, without validated outcomes. The USDA ARS MARC heat stress forecast uses NWS 7-day forecasts (Normal, Alert, Danger, Emergency by predicted respiration rate), but it was built for feedlot cattle. | [health research rule 8] BQA Manual (p.27 per fetch): 'a general rule is to work them before the temperature humidity index (THI) reaches 84'. Avoid handling when heat-stress risk is high. Work heat-prone cattle first or earlier. UNL BeefWatch 2018 (Eirich, Woolsoncroft): 'Plan to handle cattle before 8:00 a.m. and never after 10:00 a.m. during summer months'. Core temperature peaks about 2 h after air temperature and takes 4-6 h to return. Keep holding to about 30 minutes or less. UNL IANR 2016 gives the same 8 a.m. / 10 a.m. guidance and says 'Work cattle slowly and use low-stress handling techniques.' USDA ARS MARC heat-stress forecast maps use NWS 7-day forecasts and are framed for feedlot cattle.
evidence_corrections: The weather.gov documentation does not support 'several times daily' as the refresh rate for a forecast THI field.
The ARS region-maps page does not support 'daily' updates; press coverage differs on cadence.
The ARS maps estimate breathing rate for 'cattle in a feedlot'; applying them to pasture cattle is extrapolation.
rules.limitations: [context research rule 6] Whether the ARS maps are still published in 2026 is UNVERIFIED. Category boundaries at exactly 110 and 130 are ambiguous on the page. Cloud cover to solar conversion is an approximation. Night-time cooling and coat colour are not in the equation. | [water research rule 10] The trigger temperature is a ranch choice. I found no source that gives a single trigger temperature for pasture cattle. | [health research rule 8] THI leaves out wind and solar load. The ARS model is for feedlot cattle and estimates general trends, not individual animals. Forecasts are uncertain. The two UNL summaries differed on evening handling, so no evening rule is proposed.
rules.configurable: [context research rule 6] Category cut-offs should stay as published. Which events trigger a warning (gathers, moves, shipping) is a ranch choice. | [water research rule 10] Yes. | [health research rule 8] Yes: THI cut-off, time window, whether to use a forecast at all.
rules.missing_data_blocks: [context research rule 6] No forecast or no location means no heat panel. Do not show 'Normal' by default. Off-season (as_of Sept 30), suppress the panel instead of showing an empty one. | [water research rule 10] If no forecast is available, keep the routine check schedule and say the heat adjustment is unavailable. | [health research rule 8] With no forecast available, show 'no forecast: check conditions on the day' and do not label the day safe.
rules.recommendation: [context research rule 6] Optional and seasonal. Compute at build time from an NWS forecast snapshot; label it 'estimate of general trend, not individual animals'. | [water research rule 10] Add a 'checked by eye' log. Show the last visual check per tank next to the sensor reading. | [health research rule 8] Optional phase-2 feature using the NWS API. For the static demo, any forecast must be clearly labelled synthetic.
rules.phase_note: Needs a dated weather-forecast snapshot; live integrations are deferred. Could later run on a manually entered forecast high.

sources.title: Forecasting Heat Stress
sources.publisher: USDA ARS U.S. Meat Animal Research Center, Clay Center NE
sources.supports: Breathing-rate equation, categories, caveats | 7-day NWS-based maps, breathing-rate categories (<90 normal, 90-110 alert, 110-130 danger, >130 emergency). For feedlot cattle; general trends only. | 7-day maps from NWS forecasts with categories Normal (<90 bpm), Alert, Danger and Emergency (>130 bpm). Framed for feedlot cattle. Does not predict individual animals.
sources.checker_note: Equation: 'Breathing Rate = (2.83 x Temperature) + (0.58 x Humidity) - (0.76 x Wind Speed) + (0.039 x Solar Radiation) - 196.4', 'For temperatures higher than 80°F'. Units: °F, % RH, mph, W/m2. Categories: Normal 'Less than 90', Alert 'From 90 - 110', Danger 'From 110 - 130', Emergency 'Above 130'. 110 appears in two categories, confirming the ambiguity. Page says 'a good number to use is about 1000 Watts/meter2'; the maps are 'an estimate of general trends' and 'cannot predict individual animal stress levels'. Last Modified 8/12/2016. Solar example 'Clay Center, NE on July 5, 2001'. Cites Brown-Brandl et al. 2005 and Eigenberg et al. 2005 (Biosystems Engineering).

sources.title: Beef Quality Assurance National Manual (bqa_manual_final.pdf)
sources.publisher: Beef Quality Assurance program (the PDF names no publisher; 'Funded by Beef Farmers and Ranchers'; NCBA is the Beef Checkoff contractor)
sources.pub_date: undated (no date in the PDF; newest data cited are the 2016 NBQA, a 2018 footnote and a 1998-2017 series). Likely superseded: NCBA announced an updated manual on 2024-12-19 (2025-01-06 is a trade-press reprint date), and bqa.org now links a 2026 edition that could not be fetched.
sources.data_years: newest data cited: 2016 National Beef Quality Audit; a 1998-2017 series
sources.supports: Work cattle before THI reaches 84 (Ch.2 Temperature Conditions, p.27 per fetch). Low-stress handling (p.44).
sources.checker_note: I fetched it three times. Every quoted claim was found. Sec 4.4 (pp.46-47): 'To establish immunity, almost all products recommend a second vaccination two (2) to four (4) weeks after the initial vaccination.' p.42 (also p.11): 'Follow all FDA/USDA/EPA guidelines and label directions for each product.' Sec 6.2 (pp.14-15) lists the individual record items, and group treatments record 'Group or lot identification' plus the same items. p.15: 'Keep records for a minimum of two years or longer as required by laws/regulations'. Ch.2 Temperature Conditions (pp.26-27): 'work them before the temperature humidity index (THI) reaches 84', 'Avoid handling cattle when the risk of heat stress is high', and 'Work cattle more prone to heat stress first, earlier in the day'. p.48: 'A VCPR cannot exist based solely on phone, video, or other telemedical interactions.' p.45: vaccines 'have either a 21 or 60 day withdrawal time'. p.42: VFD records are kept two years. Sec 4.3: 'Booster vaccinations as indicated in the herd health plan', 'Always read and follow label directions' and 'Keep records of all products administered including date, animal identification, product used, serial number, amount administered, route...'. Sec 4.5 (titled 'Judicious Use of Antimicrobials', not VCPR): protocols 'define when to quit treating and seek professional help'. Small drifts: the processing map (Sec 1.7.2, p.10) records 'where each injection was given', which is not 'how much'. The research cites the field guide for the withdrawal and sale point, but the manual gives stronger support: 'Verify withdrawal on any animals being sold' and 'Employ strict adherence to pre-harvest withdrawal periods'. METADATA PROBLEM: the PDF names no publisher. It shows only 'Funded by Beef Farmers and Ranchers'. NCBA's own release confirms that NCBA is a contractor to the Beef Checkoff. Its newest data are the 2016 NBQA, a 2018 'Unpublished' footnote and data for '1998 to 2017', which points to an edition from about 2019. NCBA announced an updated manual on 2024-12-19. The research's 2025-01-06 date is that of the trade-press reprints. bqa.org/resources/manuals now links bqa-national-manual-2026.pdf and does NOT link bqa_manual_final.pdf. The cited file is therefore very likely a superseded edition. My two fetches of the 2026 manual both failed with CLIENT_ERROR, so I could not confirm that the 2-4 week, THI 84, record-item, retention and VCPR wording is still in the current edition.
sources.metadata_note: Checker: likely superseded. bqa.org now links 2026 editions (NCBA announced an updated manual 2024-12-19); the 2026 manual could not be fetched, so claims are not re-verified against the current edition.

sources.title: Heat Stress: Handling Cattle Through High Heat Humidity Indexes
sources.supports: Handle before 8 a.m. and never after 10 a.m. in summer. Core temperature lag and 4-6 h recovery. Small groups with holding of about 30 minutes or less.
sources.checker_note: 'Heat Stress: Handling Cattle Through High Heat Humidity Indexes' by Rob Eirich and Mariah Woolsoncroft, BeefWatch Aug 1, 2018. The page is marked archived. Verbatim: 'Plan to handle cattle before 8:00 a.m. and never after 10:00 a.m. during summer months.' Core temperature peaks about 2 h after the environmental peak and takes 4-6 h to return to normal. Holding should not last much longer than 30 minutes, with smaller groups. It also says evening handling will not reduce heat-stress risk, which contradicts the 2016 piece.

sources.title: Extension educator offers tips on handling cattle in hot weather
sources.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln IANR News (no writer named; quotes R. Eirich)
sources.supports: Handle before 8 a.m. Low-stress handling. Process in small batches.
sources.checker_note: Originally published May 31, 2016 (IANR News / Nebraska Today). No writer is named. Rob Eirich is quoted, so '(R. Eirich)' identifies the source, not the author. Verbatim: 'Plan to handle cattle before 8 a.m. and never during daylight hours after 10 a.m.' and 'Work cattle slowly and use low-stress handling techniques.' Hold cattle about 30 minutes or less and work them in small groups. It also says 'Handling cattle in the early morning and evening will reduce the risk of heat stress', which confirms the conflict with 2018 that the research noted.
sources.metadata_note: Checker (health): no writer is named; Rob Eirich is quoted, so he is the source, not the author.

Use the newborn bands for calving pastures and the adult bands for others (e.g., Adult Cold Moderate -4 to 13 F; Newborn Cold Moderate 23 to 31 F). rules.classification_note: Kept at B for the CCI bands (checker context dispute 4 raised an evidence problem, not a class problem).
rules.evidence: NDAWN CCI page: CCI is 'calculated by adjusting the air temperature using relative humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation'. It 'does not take into account precipitation' and is 'not designed to predict apparent temperature for animals with wet hair coats'. 'Non-acclimated or sick animals should be evaluated using the Newborn CCI'. It gives a full band table and cites Mader, Johnson and Gaughan 2010 (J. Anim. Sci. 88:2153-2165). Per that abstract, the index was developed from 9 summer and 6 winter periods. KFYR (2026-02-19) quotes a livestock management specialist (employer not named) who uses NDAWN's index to plan feeding and shelter moves.
evidence_corrections: The KFYR article quotes a livestock management specialist whose employer is not named; it is not evidence of Extension or NDAWN endorsement.
rules.limitations: The NDAWN CCI page shows only North Dakota and Minnesota maps (Montana stations are not mentioned on it) and offers no download or API. SD/NE ranches would have to compute CCI themselves. Wet coats and precipitation are excluded, and calving losses depend on much more than weather.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: drought-plan review prompts. Record the ranch rain gauge and compare 30/60/90-day totals with a public normal; show a dated drought context line (county USDM category, optionally the Grass-Cast outlook); and at ranch-chosen trigger dates (for example spring rainfall as % of normal by a set date) prompt the drought-plan review. These prompts feed the plan review; they do not create move exceptions.
rules.decision_supported: [context research rule 9] Whether to start the drought contingency steps (destock, buy feed, defer pastures) on schedule | [grazing research rule 8] Lengthen recovery periods, slow the rotation, destock in stages, or bring feed in early.
rules.required_inputs: [context research rule 9] Daily ranch gauge precip (in); public precip/normal (PRISM, IEM, ACIS); ranch trigger dates and actions | [grazing research rule 8] Ranch rain gauge totals vs normal; USDM category for the county (weekly); Grass-Cast % change in production for the grid cell (about every 2 weeks during its season); optional RAP production history; ranch-defined trigger dates and actions.

context.season: Growing season; April-June precipitation largely drives annual production
context.geography: Northern and Central Great Plains
context.management: Written drought plan with trigger dates; ranch rain gauge

rules.context_research: [context research rule 9] Northern/Central Plains growing season; trigger dates are ranch-specific | [grazing research rule 8] Northern and Central Great Plains: April-June precipitation largely drives annual production. Grass-Cast is validated for the Great Plains only. Drought guidance extends recovery to 90+ days and removes animals in stages.
rules.classification_research: context R9: C-ranch-management-choice + grazing R8: B-context-dependent
rules.classification_note: CHANGED for the grazing part. Context research rule 9 was C; grazing research rule 8 was B. The merged rule's trigger dates and thresholds are ranch-set, so the stricter class C applies; the context banner alone is B.
rules.evidence: [context research rule 9] The NDMC 'Managing Drought Risk on the Ranch' plan page recommends 'Setting dates on the calendar when specific conditions warrant action'. It says monitoring 'helps you decide when it is time to act' and advises finding 'the earliest possible indicators of pending forage or water deficits'. It gives no numeric thresholds. Its Monitor page: 'If you suspect you may not produce enough forage to meet your herd's needs this year, it's time to take action', and it lists USDM, CoCoRaHS, VegDRI and Grass-Cast. PRISM web-service doc (26 Mar 2025): daily grids are updated 'eight times before becoming stable', and data older than six months are stable. So recent public precipitation values change after the fact. | [grazing research rule 8] SDSU 'Reading the Range' (updated Apr 13, 2022): April, May and June precipitation strongly predicts annual forage production in the central and northern Great Plains. SD TN9 App. B phases: Phase I remove 10% of the herd in the first month if drought is impending; Phase II 20-40%; Phase III 30%+, combine herds. SDSU MC-04340 example trigger: 'If rainfall totals fall 30% below average by May 15, initiate a 15% destocking plan.' Grass-Cast (Hartman et al. 2020, Ecosphere): agreed with the MODIS category 69% of the time; confidence 'increased substantially by late May or early June'; 'does not differentiate between desirable forage species and undesirable species'; does not account for prior-year grazing. The Grass-Cast site warns not to use it as the sole basis for stocking, turnout or permit decisions. The Grass-Cast home page says: 'As of August 31, 2026, all relevant precipitation data have been observed for the 2026 Grass-Cast season.' UNL BeefWatch (Aug 1, 2026): 'windshield green is not the same as cow days'; slow the rotation and extend recovery when regrowth is limited.
rules.limitations: [context research rule 9] No threshold is evidence-backed in what I gathered; they are ranch choices. PRISM limits: a file downloaded twice in 24 h is blocked; commercial use prohibited without arrangement; zipped grids are not browser-friendly. I could not verify ACIS and NCEI CDO terms or token rules (ACIS docs page rendered empty; the CDO page did not state token or limits). | [grazing research rule 8] These are coarse (10-km grid or county), lagged and model-based. They cannot say whether a given pasture is ready. Trigger values are ranch choices.
rules.configurable: [context research rule 9] Yes. Trigger dates, % of normal, and actions are all ranch-defined. | [grazing research rule 8] Yes. Triggers and actions are ranch-defined.
rules.missing_data_blocks: [context research rule 9] Gauge gaps longer than a few days should block a % of normal; show 'gauge record incomplete' and do not treat missing days as zero rain. | [grazing research rule 8] A stale feed (e.g. Grass-Cast off-season, USDM not updated) should be shown with its valid date and never read as 'normal'.
rules.recommendation: [context research rule 9] Adopt the ranch-gauge field and trigger-date checklist (cheap, credible). Treat public precip as optional build-time context with retrieved_at recorded. | [grazing research rule 8] Show as a context strip with source, valid date and caveat. Let the ranch configure a few drought triggers that create a 'review the grazing plan' task. Do not let regional products directly raise or lower pasture-level move severity.
rules.phase_note: Phase-3 item 'drought/precipitation context as a dated snapshot'. Needs a rain_gauge record and drought_plan.trigger rows; public precipitation is optional build-time context with retrieved_at.

sources.title: Seasonal grassland productivity forecast for the U.S. Great Plains using Grass-Cast. Ecosphere 11(11): e03280, doi:10.1002/ecs2.3280
sources.publisher: Ecological Society of America / Wiley (USDA ARS-hosted PDF)
sources.url: https://ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/52548/207. Hartman et al 2020 Ecoshpere - seasonal grassland productivity forcast for Great Plains using Grass-Cast.pdf
sources.data_years: Daymet 1980-2016; GIMMS NDVI 1982-2015; MODIS evaluation 2000-2018; forecasts 2017-2018
sources.supports: Method, skill (same category as MODIS 69% of the time), when it becomes reliable (late May/early June), and its limits (total production not forage; no management effects).
sources.checker_note: Hartman, Parton, Derner, Schulte, Smith, Peck, Day, Del Grosso, Lutz, Fuchs, Chen, Gao. Ecosphere 11(11): e03280, 2020, doi 10.1002/ecs2.3280. Daymet 1980-2016, GIMMS NDVI3g 1982-2015, MODIS evaluation 2000-2018, forecasts 2017-2018. All data years are correct. 'On average, Grass-Cast and MODIS were in the same category 69% of the time.' The abstract says over '20-yr', the results cover 19 years; this is a minor inconsistency in the paper. 'Confidence in Grass-Cast forecasts increased substantially by late May or early June.' 'does not differentiate between desirable forage species and undesirable species'; 'does not directly account for local management practices such as grazing intensity in the previous year'. County level in 2017-18 and a 10x10 km grid from 2019. 'updated approximately every two weeks from April through July'. Ten Great Plains states.

sources.checker_note: 'About Our Maps | Grassland Productivity Forecast'. Partners: CSU, USDA, NDMC, University of Arizona. Example maps 'produced on April 29, 2019'; footer '(c)2026'. '10 km x 10km'. 'Grass-Cast is updated every two weeks to incorporate newly observed weather data'; the page itself does not limit this to the growing season. 'almost 40 years of historical data' and a '38-year average'. 'cannot tell the difference between desirable forage species and undesirable species'. 'does not directly account for local management practices'. 'Producers should not rely on Grass-Cast as a sole source for making management decisions'. Public land managers should not use it 'as a sole source of information for setting stocking rates, determining turnout dates, or other aspects of lease agreements, allotments or permits', which supports the 'stocking, turnout or permit' wording. Gray or white cells: 'no forecast is available due to insufficient data or weak statistical relationships'.

sources.title: Reading the Range: Range readiness, grazing timing and drought considerations
sources.publisher: SDSU Extension (Krista Ehlert; originally Jessalyn Bachler)
sources.supports: April-June precipitation predicts annual production; drought delays turnout; heavily overgrazed pastures may need up to a year to recover.
sources.checker_note: Krista Ehlert, originally by Jessalyn Bachler; 'updated April 13, 2022'. 'Research has demonstrated that precipitation received during these months [April, May, June] accurately predicts annual forage production in the central and northern Great Plains (Smart et al. 2020)'. The research's word 'strongly' is a paraphrase; the source says 'accurately'. The reference list gives 2021, an in-text/reference mismatch in the source. Native cool-season grasses 'should not be grazed until they reach the 3.5-leaf stage'; tame grasses are ready at three-leaf. NW SD native turnout is 'generally around the end of May or beginning of June', tame 'beginning of May'. 'general rules of thumb'. Inadequate spring moisture means turnout will be later. Overgrazed pastures 'need adequate time (up to a year) to recover'.

sources.title: Green Is Not Always Growth: Nebraska Pasture Conditions After Late Rains
sources.publisher: Nebraska Extension / UNL BeefWatch (Beckman, Benjamin, Stephenson)
sources.data_years: USDA NASS condition ratings, week ending July 20, 2026
sources.supports: Green colour is not forage; walk pastures for height, leaf area, residual and regrowth; slow rotations and extend recovery when regrowth is limited; NE pasture and range 35% very poor and 33% poor on July 20, 2026.
sources.checker_note: 'Green Is Not Always Growth: Nebraska Pasture Conditions After Late Rains', Ben Beckman, Ryan Benjamin (Nebraska Extension Educators) and Mitch Stephenson (UNL), August 1, 2026, BeefWatch. Verbatim 'windshield green is not the same as cow days'. 'Pastures need to be walked. Look at plant height, leaf area, residual forage' (also bare ground, regrowth, evenness of use). 'consider slowing rotations, increasing recovery time, reducing stocking pressure, or finding additional feed resources.' 'For the week ending July 20, 2026, USDA/NASS rated Nebraska pasture and range condition at 35% very poor', with 33% poor, 24% fair and 8% good. The page does not name a publisher; 'Nebraska Extension / UNL BeefWatch' is inferred from the domain and affiliations, which is reasonable.

sources.title: Prescribed Grazing, Range Technical Note No. 9 (Appendix B)
sources.supports: Drought-phase triggers and staged herd reductions; weekly monitoring of soil moisture and plant growth in Phase II.
sources.checker_note: Fetched with WebFetch; curl gave 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Metadata is correct: 'Prescribed Grazing', Range Technical Note No. 9, April 2017, running header 'SOUTH DAKOTA TECHNICAL GUIDE NOTICE SD-424'. VERIFIED: p.4 'Livestock movements should be based on plant growth and utilization and not calendar dates.' and 'Calendar dates may be used as a guide when developing grazing schedules.' p.3 'Keeping the grazing periods as short as practical, especially during periods of fast plant growth, will minimize the opportunity ... to graze plant regrowth prior to plant recovery.' p.3, once-over use ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed only one time'): rangeland 'minimum of 45 consecutive days of rest during the growing season', pasture 30. p.3, 2+ grazings ('When two or more pastures are planned to be grazed two or more times during a growing season'): 'Each pasture will be deferred for a minimum of 90 days during the growing season.' The p.4 Table 1 range values match the research: 20-30%* West fast 40, slow 60; East 35/55. 40-50%: West 50/70, East 45/65. Footnote: 'Fast growth usually refers to grasses in a vegetative, pre-boot stage.' Note: 'Under drought conditions, recovery periods may need to be extended to 90 days or longer'. Utilization limits match: 50% seasonal and 30% temporal (p.4), 65% browse and 60% dormant season (p.6). Table 3 (p.6, titled 'Minimum Height of Pasture Species') gives end stubble WWG 4, CWG 3, switchgrass 8, big & sand bluestem 6, KBG 2, sideoats 2, and begin heights WWG 6-10 etc., all as cited. Riparian 'residual heights of 4 to 8 inches is commonly cited as adequate' (Section IV, p.7). App. B p.16: 'Monitor grazing lands frequently and ensure animals have access to dependable water.' Phase I removes 10% in the first month; Phase II removes 20-40% and says 'Routinely monitor conditions such as soil moisture and plant growth on a weekly basis'; Phase III says 'measure remaining forage in all pastures', 'combine remaining herds into one herd', with 30%+ removal on p.16. All verified. MISREAD: the research says '>1 mile to water = very large field needing herding or water relocation'. The source says 'A very large field would roughly be where the distance to water is greater than one mile' ('could be considerably larger on smooth terrain'). Its point is that continuous season-long use gives adequate recovery only on very large fields where livestock are herded or redistributed by changing water. It does not say every field over 1 mile needs herding. The page number for this passage came back inconsistently from two fetches (p.2 and p.3).

sources.title: Alarm Management and ISA-18 - A Journey, Not a Destination (white paper)
sources.publisher: exida.com LLC (consultancy). Authors Stauffer, Sands, Dunn.
sources.pub_date: Copyright 2018-2020. The revision history says it was presented in 2010; the document leaves this unresolved.
sources.supports: ISA-18.2 alarm definition 'requiring a response'; the 10-stage lifecycle; rationalization
sources.checker_note: Used in rules 9, 10, 13 and 19 and the severity data field. Authors are 'Todd Stauffer, Nicholas P. Sands, Donald G. Dunn'. The copyright line reads 'Copyright © exida.com LLC 2018-2020'. The paper says 'Presented at the 2010 Texas A&M Instrumentation Symposium', so the date inconsistency is real and was disclosed. The alarm definition ends '...abnormal condition requiring a response.' MISQUOTE: the research quotes 'If the operator does not need to respond, there should be no alarm.' The paper says 'This means if the operator does not need to respond, then there should not be an alarm.' Priority: 'Alarm priority should be set based on the severity of the consequences and the time to respond'; 'no more than three or four different alarm priorities'; '3 priorities: ~80% Low, ~15% Medium, ~5% High'. Table 1 is 'Based upon at least 30 days of data', with ~150/day 'Very Likely to be Acceptable' and ~300/day 'Maximum Manageable' (~1 and ~2 per 10 min). Stale Alarms: 'Less than 5 present on any day, with action plans to address.' The 10 lifecycle stages include MOC and Audit.

sources.title: Better alarm handling (Chemicals Sheet No 6, CHIS6)
sources.supports: Every alarm needs a defined operator action; status indicators should not be alarms
sources.checker_note: Title 'Better alarm handling', Chemicals Sheet No 6, 'current at 3/00', which matches 2000-03. Verbatim: 'Have a defined response to each alarm'; 'eliminate/review alarms with no defined operator response'; '(Note: process status indicators should not be designated as alarms.)'; 'Prioritise proportionately, eg 5% high priority, 15% medium, and 80% low', based on 'the potential consequences if the operator fails to respond'. Milford Haven 1994: 'In the last 11 minutes before the explosion the two operators had to recognise, acknowledge and act on 275 alarms.' Nuisance sign: 'large numbers of alarms acknowledged in quick succession, or are audible alarms regularly turned off?' The sheet lists 'suppress alarms from out-of-service plant' as a quick fix, says to 'reduce the number of standing alarms', and calls for 'a mechanism for regular review and alarm change-control', 'formal audits and reviews', and 'How many new alarms did your last HAZOP produce and how were they justified?' Caveat for rule 11: 'acknowledging is distinct from acting' is implied only by 'recognise, acknowledge and act'.

rules.rule: PROPOSED: assign severity by consequence of no response and the time available to respond, with about 3 documented levels (e.g. Critical = act today, animals or water at risk; Serious = act this week; Warning = plan at the next gather or month).
rules.decision_supported: Decides what the crew does first this morning and what waits.
rules.required_inputs: Per rule: consequence class and response window. Ranch staffing.
